info.description: Enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus at T12 and descends in front of the lumbar vertebral bodies, slightly left of the midline, dividing into the two common iliac arteries at L4 (about the level of the umbilicus and iliac crests).
info.function: Supplies the gut (coeliac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries), kidneys, adrenals, gonads and the posterior body wall.
info.size: ~13 cm long; ~2 cm tapering to ~1.7 cm diameter (over 3 cm counts as aneurysmal).
info.notes: Abdominal aortic aneurysms are mostly below the renal arteries; a pulsatile mass above the umbilicus can be felt in thin people, and ultrasound screening is offered to older men.

info.description: Leaves the front of the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction, close to the midline above the pyramid. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to the lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 1.6 mm thick
info.notes: Its long climb over the petrous apex makes it a false-localising sign: raised intracranial pressure from any cause can paralyse it.

info.description: Its cranial rootlets leave the lower medulla behind the olive, where the spinal root, which climbs from the upper cervical cord through the foramen magnum, joins them. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (spinal part); the cranial part joins the vagus for the larynx.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 1.6 mm thick
info.notes: Often injured in posterior-triangle neck surgery, causing a drooping shoulder.

info.description: A dense mesh of pulmonary capillaries wrapped over the alveolar walls, fed by branches of the pulmonary artery.
info.function: Brings deoxygenated blood within half a micrometre of alveolar air; each red cell crosses in about 0.75 s, time enough to load oxygen.
info.size: Capillaries are 5–8 µm wide, just enough for red cells in single file; together they hold ~70–100 ml of blood at rest.
info.notes: Thickening of this barrier (pulmonary fibrosis) or loss of capillaries (emphysema) lowers the lung's diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO).

info.description: Grape-like clusters of alveoli at the ends of the alveolar ducts, where the airway ends in thin-walled air sacs.
info.function: Gas exchange: oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into capillary blood and carbon dioxide diffuses out across a barrier only ~0.5 µm thick.
info.size: Each alveolus is about 0.2–0.3 mm across; the lungs hold roughly 300–500 million, a surface of ~70 m².
info.notes: Type II cells make surfactant that stops alveoli collapsing; premature babies lacking it develop respiratory distress syndrome.

info.description: Last 3-4 cm of the gut. At the anorectal junction the puborectalis sling pulls the gut forward, and the canal then runs down and back through the pelvic floor to the anus.
info.function: Keeps faeces and gas in with the internal (involuntary) and external (voluntary) anal sphincters, relaxing during defecation.
info.size: About 3-4 cm long.
info.notes: The pectinate (dentate) line marks an embryological boundary: haemorrhoids above it are painless, those below it painful, because of different nerve supply.

info.description: The front three-quarters of the pituitary gland, a pea-sized gland hanging from the base of the brain in a bony cup (the sella turcica) behind the nose. It is true glandular tissue, controlled by releasing hormones that reach it through a private portal blood supply from the hypothalamus.
info.function: Secretes growth hormone, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH — the "master gland" signals that drive the adrenal cortex, thyroid, gonads, growth and lactation.
info.size: Whole pituitary about 12 × 8 × 6 mm, 0.5–0.6 g; the anterior lobe is ~75–80 % of it
info.notes: Pituitary adenomas are common (≈10 % of intracranial tumours). A growing one presses upward on the optic chiasm and classically causes bitemporal hemianopia (loss of both outer visual fields).

info.description: Curves backwards and to the left from the level of the sternal angle, arching over the pulmonary trunk bifurcation and the left main bronchus to reach the left side of T4. It gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries.
info.function: Distributes blood to the head, neck and upper limbs and turns the flow downward into the descending aorta.
info.size: ~4.5 cm long, ~2.5 cm diameter; its top lies ~2.5 cm below the jugular notch.
info.notes: The ligamentum arteriosum (remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus) tethers its underside to the left pulmonary artery; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under it, so an arch aneurysm can cause hoarseness.

info.description: Arched opening behind the diaphragm at T12, bounded in front by the median arcuate ligament that joins the two crura across the vertebral column; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and often the azygos vein.
info.function: Lets the aorta pass behind the muscle rather than through it, so breathing does not squeeze it.
info.size: About 2.5–3 cm across.
info.notes: A low-lying median arcuate ligament can compress the coeliac trunk, causing pain after meals (median arcuate ligament syndrome).

info.description: Three half-moon (semilunar) cusps — right, left and posterior (non-coronary) — at the outlet of the left ventricle. Behind each cusp the aortic wall bulges into a sinus of Valsalva; the coronary arteries arise from the right and left sinuses.
info.function: Opens during systole to let blood into the aorta and snaps shut in diastole to stop it flowing back into the left ventricle.
info.size: Annulus ~20–25 mm diameter; opening area 3–4 cm².
info.notes: Its closure makes the second heart sound (S2); age-related calcific aortic stenosis and a congenitally bicuspid valve (1–2% of people) are the commonest reasons for valve replacement.

info.description: The thin, cobweb-like middle membrane lying against the inner dura. Fine trabeculae cross the CSF-filled subarachnoid space beneath it to the pia mater, which clings to every gyrus and sulcus of the brain surface.
info.function: Encloses the subarachnoid space where CSF cushions the brain and the large cerebral arteries run; arachnoid granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses.
info.size: Microscopically thin (tens of micrometres); subarachnoid space holds ~125-150 ml of CSF in total
info.notes: A ruptured berry aneurysm bleeds into the subarachnoid space, classically causing a sudden "worst headache of my life"; meningitis inflames the arachnoid and pia.

info.description: A tiny band of smooth muscle running from the follicle bulge region to the papillary dermis on the obtuse-angle side of the hair.
info.function: Contracts under sympathetic control to stand the hair upright ("goose bumps") and squeeze sebum from the gland.
info.size: ~0.5–1 mm long, a few cells thick
info.notes: Goose bumps are a vestige of fur-fluffing for warmth and display seen in other mammals.

info.description: The first ~5 cm of the aorta, rising from the aortic valve behind the sternum upward, forward and to the right inside the pericardial sac. Its root bulges into three aortic sinuses, from which the coronary arteries arise.
info.function: Carries the entire output of the left ventricle (~5 L/min at rest) towards the arch.
info.size: ~5 cm long; 2.5–3.5 cm diameter (root up to ~3.7 cm).
info.notes: Commonest site of thoracic aortic aneurysm and of type A aortic dissection, a surgical emergency.

info.description: Rises from the cecum up the right flank to the hepatic (right colic) flexure under the liver; it is retroperitoneal, fixed to the back wall.
info.function: Absorbs water and salts from the liquid contents arriving from the ileum and moves them upward by periodic mass movements.
info.size: About 15 cm long and 5-6 cm wide.
info.notes: Its surface shows the colon's hallmarks: three longitudinal muscle bands (taeniae coli), pouches between them (haustra) and small fatty tags (epiploic appendages).

info.description: A compact knot of conducting tissue in the lower interatrial septum, inside the triangle of Koch just above the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve and near the coronary sinus opening.
info.function: Delays the electrical impulse by ~0.1 s so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract; it is the only normal electrical path from atria to ventricles.
info.size: About 5 × 3 × 1 mm.
info.notes: The delay shows as the PR interval on an ECG; damage to it causes heart block, often treated with a pacemaker.

info.description: The single long output fibre. It leaves the soma at a cone-shaped axon hillock, runs inside its myelin sheath and ends in terminal branches at the synapse.
info.function: Conducts the action potential - an all-or-nothing electrical impulse - away from the cell body, and transports proteins and organelles along its length in both directions.
info.size: 1-20 micrometres thick; from under 1 mm to over 1 m long (spinal cord to big toe)
info.notes: After a peripheral nerve injury the axon can regrow about 1 mm a day inside its old sheath, which is why feeling returns to the fingertips months after a wrist injury.

info.description: Ascends on the right side of the thoracic vertebral bodies from the upper abdomen, then arches forward over the root of the right lung at T4 to enter the back of the superior vena cava.
info.function: Drains the posterior intercostal veins and the chest wall, oesophagus and bronchi; it is a collateral route between the inferior and superior venae cavae.
info.size: ~1 cm diameter at its arch.
info.notes: Its name is Greek for "unpaired"; if the IVC is blocked, the azygos system can carry lower-body blood back to the heart.

info.description: Formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the lower border of the pons; it runs up the groove on the front of the pons and divides at its upper border into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
info.function: Supplies the pons, cerebellum (via superior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries), inner ear and, through its terminal branches, the occipital lobes.
info.size: ~3 cm long, ~3–4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Basilar artery occlusion can cause "locked-in syndrome" — full consciousness with paralysis of all muscles except those moving the eyes.

info.description: The fibrous sheet stretched across the cochlear duct from the bony spiral lamina to the outer wall, on which the organ of Corti sits. Its radial fibres are short and stiff at the base of the cochlea and long and floppy at the apex.
info.function: Its graded stiffness turns each sound frequency into a peak of vibration at one place along the spiral: the cochlea's frequency map.
info.size: Real width 0.1 mm at the base to 0.5 mm at the apex; about 35 mm long.
info.notes: Georg von Bekesy won the 1961 Nobel Prize for showing the travelling wave that runs along this membrane.

info.description: Smooth triangular area of the bladder base whose corners are the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; its lining is fixed to the muscle beneath, so it never forms folds.
info.function: Funnels urine toward the urethra; the interureteric ridge between its upper corners guides the cystoscopist to the ureteric orifices.
info.size: Each side about 2.5–3 cm.
info.notes: It develops from the absorbed ends of the mesonephric ducts and is a common site of infection and of bladder tumours.

info.description: Main central part, crossing the aorta, left adrenal and left kidney behind the stomach, from which it is separated by the lesser sac.
info.function: Its acinar cells secrete about 1.5 L a day of enzyme-rich alkaline juice into the duodenum; scattered islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
info.size: About 2.5 cm high and 1.5 cm thick.
info.notes: Lying over the vertebral column, it can be crushed against the spine in blunt trauma such as steering-wheel or bicycle-handlebar injuries.

info.description: The long flat middle part of the breastbone, formed from four fused segments (sternebrae), with notches for costal cartilages 2–7.
info.function: Forms the front of the rib cage and shields the heart; ribs 2–7 attach to it through their cartilages.
info.size: ≈ 100 mm long, 25–35 mm wide, 10 mm thick
info.notes: Red marrow persists here throughout life, so it is a site for bone-marrow aspiration; it is split for open-heart surgery.

info.description: The red, blood-forming marrow filling the spongy interior of the breastbone, shown here as a slab inside the manubrium and body of the sternum. In adults red marrow survives only in the flat bones (sternum, ribs, pelvis, skull), the vertebrae and the upper ends of the femur and humerus.
info.function: Makes all blood cells, about 500 billion a day, including the B lymphocytes that mature here and the T-cell precursors sent to the thymus.
info.size: Slab about 15 cm long, 2-5 cm wide and 5 mm thick; the body holds about 2.6 kg of marrow, half of it red
info.notes: The sternum is a classic site for marrow aspiration with a needle (the posterior iliac crest is now preferred), and its marrow is what a bone-marrow transplant replaces after high-dose chemotherapy.

info.description: Soft tissue filling the medullary cavity of the femoral shaft, revealed by peeling away the compact bone; in adults the shaft holds mostly fatty yellow marrow.
info.function: Red marrow (in the ends of long bones, pelvis, sternum and vertebrae) makes about 500 billion blood cells a day; yellow marrow stores fat and can convert back when needed.
info.size: Medullary cavity ≈ 15 mm across, ≈ 25 cm long
info.notes: A large femoral fracture can release marrow fat into the bloodstream (fat embolism syndrome).

info.description: Double-walled cup around the glomerulus: an inner layer of podocytes clasping the capillaries and an outer parietal layer, with the urinary space between. Glomerulus plus capsule form the renal corpuscle.
info.function: Collects the glomerular filtrate and channels it into the proximal tubule at the urinary pole.
info.size: About 0.2 mm across.
info.notes: In crescentic glomerulonephritis cells proliferate inside the capsule and form crescents that crush the glomerulus.

info.description: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It rises behind the manubrium to the right of the trachea and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries.
info.function: Supplies the right side of the head and neck and the right upper limb.
info.size: 4–5 cm long, ~1.2 cm diameter.
info.notes: Exists only on the right; in a common variant (so-called "bovine arch", ~15–25%) the left common carotid also arises from it.

info.description: The short continuation of the right main bronchus between the upper lobe origin and the middle/lower lobe bronchi.
info.function: Secondary (lobar) bronchus: conducts air to one lobe of the lung.
info.size: About 2–3 cm long, 10–12 mm wide.
info.notes: Lobar bronchi are the level at which the lung is removed in a lobectomy; their walls contain irregular cartilage plates instead of rings.

name: Bundle of His and bundle branches

info.description: The ventricular conduction pathway: the bundle of His runs from the AV node through the top of the septum and splits into a right bundle branch (reaching the RV via the moderator band) and a fan-like left bundle branch with anterior and posterior fascicles that end in Purkinje fibres.
info.function: Spreads the impulse rapidly (up to 4 m/s) down the septum to the apex and papillary muscles so the ventricles contract from apex to base.
info.size: His bundle ~1 cm long and 1–4 mm thick; bundle branches a few millimetres wide (exaggerated here for visibility).
info.notes: Block of either bundle branch widens the QRS complex on the ECG (right or left bundle branch block).

info.description: The atlas: a bony ring with no body and no spinous process; two lateral masses carry the occipital condyles of the skull.
info.function: Supports the skull and allows nodding at the atlanto-occipital joints.
info.size: Body 22 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Named after the Titan Atlas who held up the heavens.

info.description: The axis: carries the dens (odontoid peg), which projects up through the ring of the atlas and is held by the transverse ligament.
info.function: Acts as the pivot for about half of all head rotation.
info.size: Body 23 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: A "hangman's fracture" breaks both pedicles of C2.

info.description: A cervical (neck) vertebra: small oval body, large triangular canal and transverse processes pierced by foramina for the vertebral artery.
info.function: Supports the head and gives the neck its wide range of flexion, extension and rotation.
info.size: Body 24 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Cervical vertebrae C3–C6 have short bifid (forked) spinous processes.

info.description: A cervical (neck) vertebra: small oval body, large triangular canal and transverse processes pierced by foramina for the vertebral artery.
info.function: Supports the head and gives the neck its wide range of flexion, extension and rotation.
info.size: Body 25 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Cervical vertebrae C3–C6 have short bifid (forked) spinous processes.

info.description: A cervical (neck) vertebra: small oval body, large triangular canal and transverse processes pierced by foramina for the vertebral artery.
info.function: Supports the head and gives the neck its wide range of flexion, extension and rotation.
info.size: Body 26 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Cervical vertebrae C3–C6 have short bifid (forked) spinous processes.

info.description: A cervical (neck) vertebra: small oval body, large triangular canal and transverse processes pierced by foramina for the vertebral artery.
info.function: Supports the head and gives the neck its wide range of flexion, extension and rotation.
info.size: Body 27 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Cervical vertebrae C3–C6 have short bifid (forked) spinous processes.

info.description: Vertebra prominens: the last cervical vertebra, with a long non-bifid spinous process easily felt at the base of the neck.
info.function: Transitions the flexible cervical spine to the rigid thoracic spine and anchors the nuchal ligament.
info.size: Body 28 mm wide × 16 mm deep × 14 mm tall; canal ≈ 18 mm
info.notes: Its spine is the usual landmark for counting vertebrae on the back.

info.description: A web of autonomic nerves at the base of the heart - its superficial part below the aortic arch, its deep part between the arch and the tracheal bifurcation - fed by cardiac branches of both sympathetic trunks (cervical and upper thoracic ganglia) and both vagus nerves; it continues along the coronary arteries and into the lung roots.
info.function: Sets heart rate and force: sympathetic fibres speed the SA node and strengthen contraction, vagal fibres slow the rate and AV conduction; it also carries cardiac pain fibres back to T1-T4.
info.size: About 3-4 cm across; individual cardiac nerves 0.5-1 mm
info.notes: Heart pain travels with the sympathetic fibres to T1-T4, so angina is felt in the chest, left arm and jaw (referred pain). A transplanted heart has no plexus connections, so its rate only rises slowly with circulating adrenaline.

info.description: A keel-shaped ridge of cartilage at the tracheal bifurcation, where the trachea divides into the two main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle (T4/T5).
info.function: Splits the airflow between the two lungs; its mucosa is the most sensitive trigger zone of the cough reflex.
info.size: The bifurcation angle is about 60–75°; the carina lies ~12 cm below the vocal folds and ~25 cm from the incisor teeth.
info.notes: Widening or blunting of the carina on bronchoscopy suggests enlarged subcarinal lymph nodes or a dilated left atrium.

info.description: The "horse's tail": the bundle of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots (L2-Co1) that stream down the dural sac below the end of the cord to reach their exit foramina.
info.function: Carries motor and sensory fibres for the legs, bladder, bowel and genitals.
info.size: About 20 pairs of roots filling the lumbar dural sac from L1/L2 to S2 (~15-20 cm)
info.notes: Compression by a large central disc herniation (cauda equina syndrome) causes saddle numbness and bladder retention - a surgical emergency.

info.description: Opening in the central tendon at about the T8 level, just right of the midline, transmitting the inferior vena cava and branches of the right phrenic nerve.
info.function: Lets the inferior vena cava through; its tendinous rim is pulled open during inspiration.
info.size: About 2.5 cm across.
info.notes: The highest of the three large openings: "I 8 10 Eggs At 12" — IVC T8, oesophagus T10, aorta T12.

info.description: Blind pouch that begins the large intestine in the right iliac fossa, below the point where the ileum enters through the ileocecal valve; the appendix hangs from it.
info.function: Receives liquid contents from the ileum and begins absorbing water and salts; the ileocecal valve limits backflow of colonic bacteria.
info.size: About 6 cm long and 7.5 cm wide.
info.notes: As the widest part of the colon it is the part most likely to split when the large bowel is obstructed (law of Laplace).

info.description: The largest autonomic plexus ("solar plexus"): a dense web of nerve fibres and two irregular crescent-shaped celiac ganglia wrapped around the origin of the celiac trunk on the front of the aorta at the T12-L1 level, just behind the stomach and pancreas.
info.function: Sympathetic relay (from the greater splanchnic nerves) and parasympathetic crossroads (vagal fibres) for the stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, kidneys, adrenals and small intestine; it also carries their pain signals.
info.size: Ganglia 1.5-2 cm each; the plexus spans ~4 cm
info.notes: A blow to the "solar plexus" knocks the wind out of you by jarring the diaphragm and this plexus; a celiac plexus block, guided by CT or endoscopic ultrasound, is the standard treatment for pain from pancreatic cancer.

info.description: Thin, strong trefoil-shaped aponeurosis at the top of the diaphragm with anterior, right and left leaflets; the fibrous pericardium is fused to its upper surface and the inferior vena cava passes through it.
info.function: Gives all the diaphragm's muscle fibres a common insertion, so their contraction pulls the dome down.
info.size: About 10 cm across the leaflets and ~1 mm thick.
info.notes: Because the vena caval opening lies in the tendon, inspiration stretches it open, helping blood return to the heart.

info.description: The narrow, worm-like midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres, raised on top (culmen) under the tentorium and sunk below between the hemispheres (vallecula).
info.function: Controls posture, balance, gait and eye movements via the fastigial and vestibular nuclei.
info.size: About 1-2 cm wide and 5 cm long around its curve
info.notes: Chronic alcohol damage typically hits the anterior superior vermis, causing a wide-based, staggering gait while arm coordination is relatively spared.

info.description: The branching white-matter core of the cerebellum: a central body (corpus medullare) sends thin lamellae out into every folium, so a midline cut shows a tree-like pattern, the "tree of life". The deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, interposed, fastigial) sit inside it.
info.function: Carries fibres into the cerebellar cortex (mossy and climbing fibres) and Purkinje-cell output to the deep nuclei, which send the cerebellum's signals out through the peduncles.
info.size: Core about 3 x 1.5 cm; lamellae under 1 mm thick
info.notes: The dentate nucleus, the largest deep cerebellar nucleus, relays the lateral cerebellum to the thalamus and motor cortex; damage to it or its outflow causes intention tremor.

info.description: The narrow canal through the midbrain, between the tectum behind and the tegmentum in front, joining the third and fourth ventricles.
info.function: The only route for CSF from the forebrain ventricles to the fourth ventricle.
info.size: About 1.5 cm long and only 1-2 mm wide
info.notes: Being the narrowest point of the ventricular system, it is the commonest site of congenital obstruction (aqueduct stenosis) causing hydrocephalus in infants.

info.description: Narrow, firm lower third of the uterus; its lower part projects into the top of the vagina and carries the small external os.
info.function: Keeps the uterus closed with a mucus plug whose consistency changes through the cycle, then softens and dilates to about 10 cm in labour.
info.size: About 2.5–3 cm long and 2.5 cm across.
info.notes: The transformation zone at the external os is where HPV-related cervical cancer starts, which is why it is sampled in screening (Pap/HPV test).

info.description: A ring of arteries on the base of the brain around the optic chiasm and pituitary stalk, linking the two internal carotids (via the anterior communicating artery and the anterior cerebral arteries) with the basilar system (via the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries). Stubs of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries leave it.
info.function: Provides alternative routes so that blood can still reach all parts of the brain if one feeding artery narrows; ACA supplies the medial frontal and parietal lobes, MCA most of the lateral cortex, PCA the occipital lobe.
info.size: Ring ~3 × 2.5 cm; component arteries 1–4 mm diameter.
info.notes: A complete, symmetric circle is present in fewer than half of people; berry aneurysms at its junctions (especially the anterior communicating artery) cause most subarachnoid haemorrhages.

info.description: A thin-walled, spindle-shaped sac on the back wall of the upper abdomen, in front of the first two lumbar vertebrae just to the right of the aorta and behind the right crus of the diaphragm. It is formed by the union of the right and left lumbar trunks with the intestinal trunk, and narrows upward into the thoracic duct.
info.function: Collects lymph from both legs, the pelvis and the abdominal organs, including the milky, fat-rich chyle from the intestine, and feeds it into the thoracic duct.
info.size: About 5-7 cm long and 5-6 mm wide (absent or replaced by a plexus in about half of people)
info.notes: Its content is chyle: after a fatty meal the lymph turns white with chylomicrons. Injury during spine or aortic surgery leaks chyle into the abdomen (chylous ascites).

info.description: Erectile organ made of a small glans under its hood, a body that bends back under the pubic symphysis, and two crura that run along the ischiopubic rami (the vestibular bulbs lie alongside the vestibule).
info.function: Densely innervated organ whose only known role is sexual sensation; it engorges with blood during arousal.
info.size: Glans about 5 mm; body plus crura about 9–11 cm in total.
info.notes: It is the counterpart of the penis (glans and corpora cavernosa); most of it lies hidden beneath the skin.

info.description: The tailbone: three to five small rudimentary vertebrae fused into a tapering, forward-curving triangle.
info.function: Anchors the gluteus maximus, the anococcygeal ligament and pelvic-floor muscles.
info.size: ≈ 40 mm long
info.notes: It is the vestigial remnant of a tail; a fall on the buttocks can bruise or fracture it (coccydynia).

info.description: Afferent fibres of the spiral ganglion neurons: thick type I fibres (95 per cent) each contact a single inner hair cell, while thin type II fibres branch across many outer hair cells. They leave through the habenula perforata and run to the modiolus.
info.function: Carry the electrical signal from the hair cells toward the brainstem, each fibre tuned to one frequency.
info.size: Type I fibres 2-4 micrometres, myelinated; about 30,000 per cochlea.
info.notes: Loud noise can destroy these synapses before any hair cell dies: "hidden hearing loss" with a normal audiogram but poor hearing in background noise.

info.description: A short, wide artery leaving the front of the aorta just below the aortic hiatus (T12) and dividing almost at once into the left gastric, common hepatic and splenic arteries (the "tripod of Haller").
info.function: Supplies the foregut: lower oesophagus, stomach, first half of the duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen.
info.size: ~1–2 cm long, ~7 mm diameter.
info.notes: In median arcuate ligament syndrome the diaphragm's tendinous arch compresses it, causing pain after meals.

info.description: Duct that collects urine from several nephrons and runs straight down through the medulla, merging with others to open at the tip of a renal papilla (papillary ducts of Bellini).
info.function: Makes the final adjustment of urine: antidiuretic hormone inserts aquaporin-2 water channels, and aldosterone controls sodium and potassium exchange.
info.size: About 20 mm long, widening toward the papilla.
info.notes: Without ADH or a response to it (diabetes insipidus), many litres of dilute urine are passed each day.

info.description: Formed where the cystic and common hepatic ducts join; runs down behind the first part of the duodenum and through the back of the pancreatic head, then unites with the pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla on the descending duodenum.
info.function: Delivers bile into the duodenum through the sphincter of Oddi.
info.size: About 8 cm long and up to 6 mm wide.
info.notes: A stone or pancreatic-head tumour blocking it causes obstructive jaundice with pale stools and dark urine; a painless palpable gallbladder suggests cancer (Courvoisier's law).

info.description: Runs to the right from the coeliac trunk along the upper border of the pancreatic head, gives off the gastroduodenal artery and continues as the proper hepatic artery up the free edge of the lesser omentum to the porta hepatis, where it splits into right and left hepatic arteries.
info.function: Supplies the liver, gallbladder (cystic artery), stomach (right gastric) and duodenum and pancreatic head (gastroduodenal).
info.size: ~5 mm diameter.
info.notes: Provides only ~25% of the liver's blood (the portal vein gives the rest) but about half its oxygen; variant origins (e.g. a replaced right hepatic artery from the SMA) are common and matter in surgery.

info.description: Formed at the porta hepatis by the union of the right and left hepatic ducts; descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum to meet the cystic duct.
info.function: Carries all the bile leaving the liver.
info.size: About 3 cm long and 6 mm wide.
info.notes: With the cystic duct and the liver it bounds the hepatocystic (Calot's) triangle, which surgeons clear before clipping the cystic duct and artery.

info.description: A wide venous channel lying in the posterior atrioventricular groove between the left atrium and left ventricle, opening into the right atrium between the IVC opening and the tricuspid valve. Shown with its tributary the middle cardiac vein in the posterior interventricular groove.
info.function: Collects most of the venous blood of the heart wall (great, middle and small cardiac veins) and returns it to the right atrium.
info.size: About 3–5 cm long and ~1 cm wide at its opening.
info.notes: Its opening is guarded by the thin Thebesian valve; the heart muscle extracts ~70% of the oxygen delivered, so coronary-sinus blood is the most deoxygenated in the body.

info.description: The great arched bridge of white matter at the bottom of the longitudinal fissure, joining the two hemispheres. From front to back: rostrum, genu, body and the thick splenium; it forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
info.function: Carries about 200 million axons between matching areas of the left and right cortex so the hemispheres share information.
info.size: About 7-8 cm long; 0.5-1 cm thick (thickest at the splenium)
info.notes: Cutting it (callosotomy) for intractable epilepsy produces "split-brain" patients who cannot name an object felt with the left hand alone.

info.description: Single ventral erectile body surrounding the spongy urethra; it swells into the bulb in the perineum and expands at its far end into the glans.
info.function: Engorges less than the corpora cavernosa, so the urethra stays open for ejaculation during erection.
info.size: About 1 cm across in the shaft; the bulb is about 3 cm wide.
info.notes: The bulbospongiosus muscle wraps its bulb and squeezes out the last drops of urine and semen.

info.description: The only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, shaped like a signet ring: a narrow arch in front and a tall lamina behind.
info.function: Forms the base of the larynx, carrying the arytenoid and thyroid cartilages on synovial joints, and holds the airway open at the laryngo-tracheal junction.
info.size: About 2.5 cm across; arch 5–7 mm high, lamina 2–3 cm high; at the level of C6.
info.notes: An emergency airway (cricothyrotomy) is made through the cricothyroid membrane just above its arch; it is the narrowest point of a young child's airway.

info.description: Short, tortuous duct from the neck of the gallbladder to the common hepatic duct; its lining forms a spiral fold (valve of Heister).
info.function: Lets bile flow into the gallbladder for storage and out again when it contracts.
info.size: About 3-4 cm long and 2-3 mm wide.
info.notes: A stone impacted here causes biliary colic or acute cholecystitis.

info.description: Several thick, tapering processes that leave the soma and branch again and again into a tree; their surfaces are studded with tiny spines where other neurons make contact.
info.function: Collect thousands of incoming synaptic signals and carry the resulting graded potentials toward the soma, where they are added up at the axon hillock.
info.size: A real dendritic tree spans 0.2-1 mm; branches taper from ~5 to under 1 micrometre
info.notes: Dendritic spines grow and shrink with learning; their loss is an early change in Alzheimer disease.

info.description: Two horizontal networks of small vessels — a deep plexus at the dermis–hypodermis border and a superficial plexus under the papillae — joined by vertical vessels, with hairpin capillary loops rising into each dermal papilla.
info.function: Nourish the avascular epidermis by diffusion and regulate heat loss by opening (flushing) or closing (pallor) the superficial blood flow.
info.size: Capillaries ~5–10 µm diameter; papillary loops ~0.2–0.4 mm tall (magnified here)
info.notes: Skin blood flow can rise from ~0.25 to ~8 litres per minute in heat stress — almost a third of cardiac output — to dump heat.

info.description: The tough connective-tissue layer under the epidermis: a thin papillary layer of loose tissue in the dermal papillae over a thick reticular layer of dense collagen and elastic fibres. It holds the vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands (shown translucent here).
info.function: Gives skin its strength and elasticity, nourishes the epidermis and houses its appendages and sensory receptors.
info.size: Real thickness ~0.6 mm (eyelids) to ~3–4 mm (back)
info.notes: Leather is tanned dermis. Stretch marks (striae) are tears in the dermal collagen; a burn is "full thickness" once the whole dermis is destroyed.

info.description: Runs down the left flank from the splenic flexure to the left iliac fossa; retroperitoneal and narrower than the right colon.
info.function: Stores and propels increasingly solid faeces toward the sigmoid colon.
info.size: About 25 cm long and about 4 cm wide.
info.notes: Diverticula - pouches pushed out where vessels pierce the wall - are common here and in the sigmoid in people on low-fibre diets.

info.description: Runs down the posterior mediastinum from T4 to T12, just left of the vertebral bodies and behind the left atrium and oesophagus, and leaves the chest through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm.
info.function: Gives posterior intercostal, bronchial, oesophageal and superior phrenic branches and conveys blood to the abdomen and legs.
info.size: ~20 cm long, ~2.3–2.5 cm diameter.
info.notes: The isthmus just beyond the left subclavian origin is where coarctation occurs and where the aorta tears in high-speed deceleration injuries.

info.description: Dome-shaped musculotendinous sheet separating the chest from the abdomen. Its muscle fibres arise from the xiphoid process, the inner surfaces of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages, the arcuate ligaments and — through the right and left crura — the upper lumbar vertebral bodies, and converge on the central tendon. The right dome sits higher, over the liver.
info.function: The main muscle of breathing: contracting, it flattens and descends, enlarging the chest to draw air in; it also raises abdominal pressure for coughing, vomiting, childbirth and defecation.
info.size: About 30 cm across and 2–5 mm thick; the domes reach about the 5th rib, and it descends 1–2 cm in quiet breathing and up to 10 cm in a deep breath.
info.notes: Supplied by the phrenic nerves ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"); irritation of it is felt as shoulder-tip pain.

info.description: Short coiled tubule in the cortex that begins at the macula densa, where the tubule touches its own glomerulus to form the juxtaglomerular apparatus, and drains via a connecting tubule into a collecting duct.
info.function: Fine-tunes sodium, chloride and calcium reabsorption (thiazide-sensitive NCC cotransporter; calcium under parathyroid hormone control).
info.size: About 5 mm long.
info.notes: The macula densa senses tubular salt and signals the neighbouring cells to release renin when it falls.

info.description: First part of the small intestine: a C-shaped loop in four parts (superior, descending, horizontal, ascending) wrapped around the head of the pancreas, mostly fixed to the back wall of the abdomen.
info.function: Receives chyme from the stomach plus bile and pancreatic juice through the major duodenal papilla in its descending part, neutralising the acid and starting most chemical digestion.
info.size: About 25 cm long and 3-4 cm wide; the flexure where it becomes the jejunum lies left of L2.
info.notes: Its name means "twelve finger-breadths". Most peptic ulcers occur in its first 2-3 cm, the duodenal bulb.

info.description: The thick, tough outer membrane lining the inside of the skull, fused with the periosteum. Its inner layer folds inward to form the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli, and the dural venous sinuses run between its layers.
info.function: Protects the brain, holds it in place and drains its venous blood through the dural sinuses.
info.size: About 0.5-1 mm thick; encloses ~1,400 ml of brain and CSF
info.notes: Arterial bleeding between skull and dura (extradural haematoma, often from the middle meningeal artery) can kill within hours after a "lucid interval"; the dura itself is pain-sensitive, unlike the brain.

info.description: A single long tube whose lower end is a tight secretory coil in the deep dermis; its duct climbs through the dermis and corkscrews through the epidermis to open at a sweat pore.
info.function: Secretes watery sweat whose evaporation cools the body; up to 2–4 litres an hour in extreme heat.
info.size: Coil ~0.4 mm across; 2–4 million glands, densest on palms and soles (~600 per cm²)
info.notes: Cystic fibrosis raises the salt content of sweat (faulty CFTR chloride channels in the duct), which is the basis of the sweat test.

info.description: Glandular mucous lining of the uterine cavity with a permanent basal layer and a functional layer that thickens and is shed every cycle.
info.function: Prepares a blood-rich bed for implantation under oestrogen and progesterone; if no embryo implants, its functional layer breaks down as menstruation.
info.size: 2–4 mm thick after menstruation, up to 10–14 mm in the secretory phase.
info.notes: Endometriosis is endometrium-like tissue growing outside the uterus, a common cause of pelvic pain and infertility.

info.description: A representative piece of the enteric nervous system: a net of small ganglia and fibre bundles lying between the muscle layers of the gut wall (myenteric plexus), with a finer submucosal plexus inside it. It runs continuously from the oesophagus to the anus; only a short segment is shown.
info.function: The "second brain" of the gut: its roughly 500 million neurons coordinate peristalsis, secretion and local blood flow on their own, merely adjusted by vagal and sympathetic input.
info.size: Ganglia 0.1-0.5 mm (enlarged here); network mesh a few millimetres
info.notes: Congenital absence of these ganglia in the last part of the colon (Hirschsprung disease) leaves a segment that cannot relax, causing severe constipation in newborns.

info.description: The outer, cell-only layer of skin: a keratinised stratified squamous epithelium (basal, spinous, granular and horny layers) whose underside interlocks with the dermal papillae in rete ridges. It has no blood vessels.
info.function: Waterproof, microbe- and UV-resistant barrier; melanocytes add pigment, Langerhans cells police for pathogens, Merkel cells sense light touch.
info.size: Real thickness ~0.05–0.1 mm (eyelids) to ~1.5 mm (palms, soles); shown magnified ~x20
info.notes: The epidermis renews itself about every 4 weeks: basal cells divide, flatten and die as they rise, and ~500 million dead cells are shed daily.

info.description: A leaf-shaped plate of elastic cartilage behind the root of the tongue, attached by its stalk to the inside of the thyroid angle and free above.
info.function: During swallowing it tips back over the laryngeal inlet as the larynx rises, helping steer food into the oesophagus.
info.size: About 3 cm long and 2.5 cm wide.
info.notes: Acute epiglottitis can swell it within hours and block the airway, especially in children; do not examine the throat with a spatula if it is suspected.

info.description: Muscular tube carrying food from the pharynx to the stomach. It runs behind the trachea and the heart, slightly left of the midline, and passes through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm at T10 to reach the cardia of the stomach.
info.function: Moves swallowed food down by waves of peristalsis; the lower esophageal sphincter keeps stomach acid from refluxing upward.
info.size: About 25 cm long (C6 to T11), about 2 cm wide when distended; flattened front-to-back when empty.
info.notes: It narrows at three points - the cricoid, where the aortic arch and left main bronchus cross it, and the diaphragm - where swallowed objects most often lodge.

info.description: Light, box-like bone between the orbits: the sieve-like cribriform plate and crista galli above, a midline perpendicular plate (upper nasal septum) and air-cell labyrinths forming the medial orbital walls.
info.function: Separates the nasal cavity from the brain and orbits; olfactory nerve fibres pass through its cribriform plate.
info.size: ≈ 2.5 cm wide, 4 cm deep
info.notes: A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell and CSF leaking from the nose.

info.description: Emerges at the cerebellopontine angle at the lateral end of the pontomedullary junction, with the smaller nervus intermedius between it and CN VIII. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to the muscles of facial expression; taste from the front of the tongue; tear and saliva secretion.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 2.6 mm thick
info.notes: An acoustic neuroma in the cerebellopontine angle stretches it together with CN VIII.

info.description: Sickle-shaped double fold of peritoneum attaching the front of the liver to the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall. Its free lower edge carries the ligamentum teres (round ligament), the fibrous remnant of the fetal umbilical vein, down to the umbilicus.
info.function: Anchors the liver to the abdominal wall and marks the boundary between the anatomical right and left lobes.
info.size: A thin sheet a few millimetres thick running from the diaphragm to the umbilicus.
info.notes: In portal hypertension, small paraumbilical veins alongside it enlarge and radiate from the umbilicus as "caput medusae".

info.description: A sickle-shaped fold of dura hanging down into the longitudinal fissure between the hemispheres, from the crista galli in front to the internal occipital protuberance behind, where it joins the tentorium. Its free lower edge arches above the corpus callosum.
info.function: Limits side-to-side movement of the hemispheres and carries the superior and inferior sagittal sinuses (and the straight sinus at its junction with the tentorium).
info.size: About 3-4 cm deep at the back, narrow in front; ~15 cm long along its attached edge
info.notes: A mass in one hemisphere can push the cingulate gyrus under the free edge of the falx (subfalcine herniation), compressing the anterior cerebral artery.

info.description: Short tube running down and forward from the bladder neck behind the pubic symphysis, embedded in the front wall of the vagina, to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule between the clitoris and the vaginal opening.
info.function: Carries urine out of the bladder; the external urethral sphincter surrounds its middle third.
info.size: About 4 cm long and 6 mm wide.
info.notes: Its shortness is the main reason bladder infections are far commoner in women than in men.

info.description: A thin thread of pia mater running from the tip of the conus medullaris down through the dural sac (internal part) and, wrapped in dura, on to the back of the coccyx (external part).
info.function: Anchors the lower end of the spinal cord and steadies it within the vertebral canal.
info.size: About 20 cm long and 1 mm thick
info.notes: A short, thick filum (tethered cord) pulls on the conus as a child grows, causing back pain, leg weakness and bladder problems; it is treated by cutting the filum.

info.description: A paired arch of white matter that leaves the tail of each hippocampus, runs forward under the corpus callosum and plunges down as the columns of the fornix into the hypothalamus to end in the mammillary bodies.
info.function: The main output pathway of the hippocampus, part of the Papez memory circuit.
info.size: About 3.5 cm long; 3-4 mm thick
info.notes: Damage to both fornices (e.g. during removal of a colloid cyst of the third ventricle) can cause lasting amnesia for new events.

info.description: A tent-shaped cavity between the pons and upper medulla in front (its diamond-shaped floor, the rhomboid fossa) and the cerebellum behind (the roof peaks at the fastigium); lateral recesses reach round the brainstem.
info.function: Lets CSF escape from the ventricles into the subarachnoid space through the median aperture (Magendie) and two lateral apertures (Luschka).
info.size: About 3 cm long and 1.5-2 cm wide at the lateral recesses
info.notes: Its floor holds the facial colliculus, vagal and hypoglossal triangles and the area postrema, the vomiting centre that senses toxins in the blood.

info.description: The forehead bone: a curved squama rising from the brow ridges and supraorbital margins, plus thin orbital plates forming the roofs of both orbits; it meets the parietals at the coronal suture.
info.function: Protects the frontal lobes, forms the forehead and orbital roofs, and contains the frontal sinuses.
info.size: ≈ 12 cm wide, 12 cm tall; 5–7 mm thick
info.notes: It forms from two halves; a persistent midline metopic suture is seen in a few percent of adults.

info.description: Pear-shaped sac lying in a fossa on the underside of the right liver. Its rounded fundus projects just beyond the liver's lower border at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage; the body narrows into a neck that continues as the cystic duct.
info.function: Stores bile between meals and concentrates it up to 10-fold, then contracts under the hormone cholecystokinin when fatty food reaches the duodenum.
info.size: 7-10 cm long and 3-4 cm wide; holds about 30-50 mL.
info.notes: Gallstones affect 10-15% of adults. Inflammation (cholecystitis) causes Murphy's sign: pain that stops a deep breath when the examiner presses under the right ribs.

info.description: The single, unpaired ganglion in front of the coccyx where the lower ends of the two sympathetic trunks fuse.
info.function: Supplies sympathetic fibres to the perineum, distal rectum, anus and the end of the urethra and vagina.
info.size: About 3-5 mm
info.notes: Injecting local anaesthetic at the ganglion impar (through the sacrococcygeal joint) relieves otherwise intractable perineal and tailbone (coccydynia) pain.

info.description: Longitudinal folds of the gastric mucosa lining the inside of the stomach, most prominent along the greater curvature and in the body.
info.function: Let the stomach expand as it fills and increase the surface of the acid- and enzyme-secreting gastric glands.
info.size: Folds 3-5 mm high; they flatten out when the stomach is distended.
info.notes: Along the lesser curvature the folds run straight toward the pylorus (the "gastric canal"), channelling swallowed liquids quickly past the food mass.

info.description: Cone-shaped cap formed by the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum, bordered by the raised corona and bearing the slit-like external urethral meatus.
info.function: Densely innervated sensory tip of the penis that also directs the urinary stream.
info.size: About 2 cm long and 3 cm across the corona.
info.notes: Covered by the prepuce (foreskin) unless circumcised; in hypospadias the meatus opens on its underside.

info.description: Tuft of looping capillaries fed by the wider afferent arteriole and drained by the narrower efferent arteriole, which keeps the pressure inside high.
info.function: Filters plasma through fenestrated endothelium, a basement membrane and podocyte filtration slits; together the kidneys make about 180 L of filtrate a day (GFR ~125 mL/min).
info.size: About 0.2 mm across.
info.notes: Damage to the filter (diabetic nephropathy, glomerulonephritis) lets protein and blood leak into the urine.

info.description: The uppermost of a row of rootlets leaving the postolivary sulcus of the medulla, behind the olive. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Taste and sensation from the back of the tongue and pharynx; carotid sinus and body reflexes; parotid secretion.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 1.8 mm thick
info.notes: Leaves the skull through the jugular foramen with X and XI, so tumours there affect all three.

info.description: Begins near the apex, ascends in the anterior interventricular groove beside the LAD, then turns left in the atrioventricular groove alongside the circumflex artery to become the coronary sinus at the back of the heart.
info.function: Drains blood from the territory of the left coronary artery (front of both ventricles and the septum).
info.size: About 2–3 mm wide, widening to ~4 mm near the coronary sinus.
info.notes: The coronary sinus and great cardiac vein are the route used to place the left-ventricular lead of a biventricular pacemaker (CRT).

info.description: Apron-like, four-layered fold of peritoneum hanging from the greater curvature of the stomach in front of the intestines and folding back up to the transverse colon; it is usually laden with fat.
info.function: Stores fat and, through immune "milky spots", sticks to and walls off areas of infection or inflammation - the "policeman of the abdomen".
info.size: Hangs about 20-25 cm down in front of the small intestine; from paper-thin to several centimetres of fat thick.
info.notes: Surgeons use it as a vascularised flap to patch perforations, and ovarian cancer often spreads into it ("omental cake").

info.description: A tubular pocket of epidermis sunk obliquely into the dermis; its swollen base, the hair bulb, wraps a dermal papilla of capillaries that feeds the dividing matrix cells which build the hair.
info.function: Produces the hair shaft; its bulge region holds stem cells that regenerate the follicle and help re-surface wounds.
info.size: Terminal scalp follicles ~3–4 mm deep, bulb ~0.3 mm wide (magnified here)
info.notes: Follicles cycle through growth (anagen), regression (catagen) and rest (telogen); chemotherapy attacks the rapidly dividing matrix cells, causing hair loss.

info.description: The dead, keratinised hair emerging from the follicle, made of a medulla, a pigmented cortex and a scaly cuticle.
info.function: Insulation, protection and touch sensing (bending the hair stimulates nerve endings around the follicle).
info.size: Scalp hair ~50–100 µm diameter (magnified here)
info.notes: Hair records exposure to drugs and toxins as it grows, so a segment of hair can date exposure month by month.

info.description: Bony front two-thirds of the roof of the mouth (palatine processes of the maxillae and horizontal plates of the palatine bones) covered by firm mucosa with a midline raphe and transverse ridges called palatine rugae.
info.function: Separates the mouth from the nasal cavity and gives the tongue a rigid surface to press food against while chewing and swallowing.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 3.5-4 cm wide between the teeth; the vault is 1-1.5 cm high.
info.notes: Incomplete fusion of the two palatal shelves in the embryo causes cleft palate, one of the most common birth defects; it disturbs feeding and speech until repaired.

info.description: Widest part of the pancreas, nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum; its hook-like uncinate process tucks behind the superior mesenteric vessels. The common bile duct runs through its back.
info.function: Its acinar cells secrete about 1.5 L a day of enzyme-rich alkaline juice into the duodenum; scattered islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
info.size: About 5 cm high and up to 3 cm thick; the whole pancreas is 12-15 cm long and weighs 70-100 g.
info.notes: About two-thirds of pancreatic cancers arise in the head, where they often first show as painless jaundice by squeezing the common bile duct.

info.description: Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins; it runs up behind the first part of the duodenum and in the free edge of the lesser omentum (behind the bile duct and hepatic artery) to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches.
info.function: Carries nutrient-rich blood from the stomach, intestines, pancreas and spleen to the liver for processing before it reaches the general circulation.
info.size: ~8 cm long, ~1.2–1.5 cm diameter.
info.notes: Supplies ~75% of the liver's blood; in cirrhosis high portal pressure opens collaterals such as oesophageal varices, which can bleed torrentially.

info.description: Three large valveless veins (right, middle and left) running within the liver between its segments and opening into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm.
info.function: Return all the blood that has passed through the liver (from both the portal vein and hepatic artery) to the inferior vena cava.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm diameter near the IVC.
info.notes: Their obstruction causes Budd–Chiari syndrome (painful enlarged liver and ascites); the middle hepatic vein marks the plane between the functional right and left halves of the liver.

info.description: U-shaped bone in the front of the neck at the level of C3, with a body and greater and lesser horns; it touches no other bone and hangs from muscles and ligaments.
info.function: Anchors the tongue and the muscles that raise and lower the larynx during swallowing and speech.
info.size: ≈ 4 cm across, body 2.5 cm wide
info.notes: A fractured hyoid is a classic forensic sign of strangulation.

info.description: The subcutaneous layer below the dermis: lobules of fat cells (adipocytes) separated by thin fibrous septa that tether the skin to the deep fascia.
info.function: Insulates, stores energy, cushions and lets the skin move over deeper structures.
info.size: Real thickness a few mm to several cm depending on site and body fat; lobules ~1 cm, adipocytes ~0.1 mm
info.notes: Insulin and many vaccines are injected into this layer (subcutaneous injection) because its blood supply gives slow, steady absorption.

info.description: A line of rootlets leaving the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and the olive of the medulla. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to the muscles of the tongue.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 1.4 mm thick
info.notes: A lesion makes the protruded tongue deviate toward the weak side.

info.description: The floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, below the thalamus and above the optic chiasm; the paired mammillary bodies bulge from its back and the funnel-shaped infundibulum carries the pituitary stalk down to the pituitary gland (built with the glands).
info.function: Keeps the internal environment constant: body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance, sleep-wake rhythm, sexual behaviour and the stress response, largely by controlling the pituitary.
info.size: About 4 g - under 1% of the brain; roughly the size of an almond
info.notes: It makes antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin, which travel down axons to the posterior pituitary; damage causes diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine).

info.description: Final and longest part of the small intestine, coiled in the lower right abdomen and pelvis, ending at the ileocecal valve in the medial wall of the cecum; its wall contains Peyer's patches.
info.function: Absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts, plus any nutrients that escaped the jejunum.
info.size: About 3.5 m long (three-fifths of the jejunoileum), 2-2.5 cm wide; a representative 1.2 m of coil is modelled.
info.notes: Crohn's disease most often affects the terminal ileum; a Meckel's diverticulum (about 2% of people) lies about 60 cm from its end.

info.description: Arises from the front-left of the aorta at L3, about 4 cm above the bifurcation, and runs down and to the left behind the peritoneum, giving the left colic and sigmoid arteries and ending as the superior rectal artery in the pelvis.
info.function: Supplies the hindgut: the distal third of the transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon and upper rectum.
info.size: ~4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Often sacrificed during abdominal aortic aneurysm repair because the marginal artery along the colon keeps the gut alive; the splenic flexure is a watershed prone to ischaemic colitis.

info.description: The largest vein, formed at L5 by the union of the common iliac veins. It ascends to the right of the aorta, grooves the back of the liver (receiving the hepatic veins), pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8 and opens into the lower right atrium.
info.function: Returns blood from the legs, pelvis and abdomen to the heart.
info.size: ~22–25 cm long, ~2–2.5 cm diameter.
info.notes: In late pregnancy the uterus can compress it when the mother lies on her back, dropping blood pressure; filters are placed in it below the renal veins to catch leg clots.

info.description: A single row of flask-shaped sensory cells, about 3,500 per ear, each crowned by a shallow line of stereocilia in three rows of graded height. Every inner hair cell is contacted by 10-20 afferent nerve fibres.
info.function: The true sound receptors: bending of the stereocilia opens ion channels, depolarises the cell and releases glutamate onto cochlear-nerve endings.
info.size: Real length about 35 micrometres; stereocilia 2-8 micrometres tall.
info.notes: Loss of inner hair cells causes permanent deafness because mammalian hair cells do not regenerate.

info.description: The thick muscular wall between the two ventricles. It bulges into the right ventricle, which is why the RV cavity is crescent-shaped in cross-section; a small thin membranous part lies just below the aortic valve.
info.function: Separates oxygenated from deoxygenated blood and contracts with the left ventricle; it carries the bundle of His and the bundle branches.
info.size: About 10–12 mm thick (up to ~15 mm is normal on echo); ~9 cm long from base to apex.
info.notes: Ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the commonest congenital heart defect; abnormal thickening of the septum occurs in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C2 and C3 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 24 × 16 mm, 5 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C3 and C4 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 25 × 16 mm, 5 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C4 and C5 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 26 × 16 mm, 5 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C5 and C6 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 27 × 16 mm, 6 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C6 and C7 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 27 × 16 mm, 6 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the C7 and T1 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 28 × 19 mm, 4 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)
info.notes: Discs lose water with age, which is why people get slightly shorter; a torn annulus lets the nucleus herniate onto a nerve root.

info.description: Fibrocartilage cushion between the L1 and L2 vertebral bodies: a tough ring (annulus fibrosus) around a gel core (nucleus pulposus).
info.function: Absorbs shock and lets adjacent vertebrae rock and twist on each other.
info.size: ≈ 46 × 32 mm, 7 mm thick here (discs make up ~25% of spinal length)

info.description: Middle part of the small intestine, starting at the duodenojejunal flexure and coiling mostly in the upper left of the infracolic abdomen; thicker-walled, wider and redder than the ileum, with tall, closely packed circular folds inside.
info.function: Main site of absorption of sugars, amino acids and fatty acids through its villi.
info.size: About 2.5 m long (two-fifths of the jejunoileum) and 2.5-3 cm wide; a representative 1.2 m of coil is modelled.
info.notes: Its name comes from Latin jejunus, "empty", because it was usually found empty at autopsy.

info.description: A lumbar vertebra: the largest vertebral bodies, kidney-shaped, with short hatchet-shaped spinous processes and long thin transverse processes.
info.function: Bears most of the upper-body weight and allows bending forward and backward.
info.size: Body 45 mm wide × 32 mm deep × 27 mm tall; canal ≈ 20 mm
info.notes: Lumbar discs (L4–L5, L5–S1) are the commonest site of disc herniation and sciatica.

info.description: A lumbar vertebra: the largest vertebral bodies, kidney-shaped, with short hatchet-shaped spinous processes and long thin transverse processes.
info.function: Bears most of the upper-body weight and allows bending forward and backward.
info.size: Body 47 mm wide × 32 mm deep × 27 mm tall; canal ≈ 20 mm
info.notes: Lumbar discs (L4–L5, L5–S1) are the commonest site of disc herniation and sciatica.

info.function: Bears most of the upper-body weight and allows bending forward and backward.
info.size: Body 49 mm wide × 32 mm deep × 27 mm tall; canal ≈ 20 mm
info.notes: Lumbar discs (L4–L5, L5–S1) are the commonest site of disc herniation and sciatica.

info.size: Body 53 mm wide × 32 mm deep × 27 mm tall; canal ≈ 20 mm
info.notes: Lumbar discs (L4–L5, L5–S1) are the commonest site of disc herniation and sciatica.

info.description: The air space inside the larynx from the inlet behind the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid, pinched at the vocal folds (glottis) into an upper vestibule, the small lateral ventricles and a lower infraglottic cavity.
info.function: Air passage between pharynx and trachea; the glottis acts as the valve controlling voice and airway protection.
info.size: About 5 cm long; the glottis is its narrowest part in adults.
info.notes: The laryngeal ventricles between the true and false vocal folds contain mucous glands that keep the vocal folds lubricated.

info.description: The lowest part of the pharynx (hypopharynx), from the epiglottis to the cricoid cartilage, lying behind the larynx with a piriform recess on either side.
info.function: Channels swallowed food around the laryngeal inlet into the oesophagus.
info.size: About 4–5 cm long, narrowing to ~1.5 cm at the upper oesophageal sphincter (level of C6).
info.notes: Fish bones often lodge in the piriform recesses; a Zenker's diverticulum bulges through its back wall just above the cricopharyngeus.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 10th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 10th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: The tenth thoracic dermatome encircles the body at the umbilicus.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 11th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 11th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 30-35 cm long
info.notes: The last intercostal nerve; below it runs the subcostal nerve (T12). Transverse abdominal incisions spare these segmental nerves better than vertical ones.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 1st thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 1st rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 17-22 cm long
info.notes: The first intercostal nerve is tiny because most of T1 goes up into the brachial plexus; it has no anterior cutaneous branch.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 2nd thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 2nd rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 22-27 cm long
info.notes: Its lateral cutaneous branch, the intercostobrachial nerve, crosses the armpit to the inner arm and is commonly cut during axillary lymph-node surgery.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 3rd thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 3rd rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 25-30 cm long
info.notes: An intercostal nerve block is given just below the lower edge of the rib, where the nerve lies under the intercostal vein and artery.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 4th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 4th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 27-32 cm long
info.notes: Supplies the skin at the nipple (T4 dermatome) - the landmark used to map the level of a spinal-cord injury.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 5th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 5th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 29-34 cm long
info.notes: Chest drains are pushed in just ABOVE a rib so that the needle misses this nerve and its vessels in the groove below the rib above.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 6th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 6th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 30-35 cm long
info.notes: Shingles most often erupts along a mid-thoracic intercostal nerve as a one-sided painful band of blisters that stops at the midline.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 7th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 7th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: The seventh to eleventh nerves continue into the abdominal wall (thoracoabdominal nerves), so lower-lobe pneumonia can present as abdominal pain.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 8th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 8th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: Supplies the upper rectus abdominis; cutting it in an upper abdominal incision weakens the muscle segment below.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 9th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 9th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: Anterior cutaneous branches can become trapped where they pierce the rectus sheath (ACNES), a cause of chronic abdominal-wall pain.

info.description: A slender nerve that leaves the junction of the pons and medulla, climbs the clivus inside the dura, bends sharply over the petrous apex and runs through the middle of the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery to the orbit.
info.function: Supplies only the lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward (abduction).
info.size: About 1-1.5 mm thick; ~4 cm intracranial course
info.notes: Its long climb up the clivus makes it vulnerable to any rise in intracranial pressure: a sixth-nerve palsy (eye cannot look outward, horizontal double vision) is a classic "false localising sign".

info.description: Forms the soft medial border of the sole, from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and flexor retinaculum to the medial side of the base of the great toe's proximal phalanx.
info.function: Abducts and flexes the great toe and helps support the medial arch.
info.size: About 12-14 cm long.
info.notes: The plantar nerves and vessels pass deep to it - it can compress them in tarsal tunnel syndrome; it is often weak in hallux valgus (bunions).

info.description: Formed mainly by a spinal root that rises from the upper five cervical cord segments, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves again through the jugular foramen. It then runs down and back across the side of the neck, piercing the sternocleidomastoid and crossing the posterior triangle to the trapezius.
info.function: Motor to the sternocleidomastoid (turns the head) and trapezius (shrugs the shoulder and rotates the shoulder blade).
info.size: About 1.5 mm thick; ~12 cm from foramen magnum to trapezius
info.notes: Its superficial course through the posterior triangle makes it the nerve most often injured in lymph-node biopsies of the neck, leaving a dropped shoulder and difficulty lifting the arm.

info.description: Deep cup-shaped socket on the outer hip bone, formed where the ilium, ischium and pubis fuse (the triradiate cartilage in children).
info.function: Holds the femoral head in the hip joint, facing outward, downward and forward.
info.size: ≈ 5–5.5 cm across, 2.5–3 cm deep
info.notes: Shallow acetabula (developmental dysplasia of the hip) are screened for in newborns.

info.description: The calcaneal tendon, thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed by the union of gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the middle of the back of the calcaneus.
info.function: Transmits the force of the triceps surae to plantarflex the foot in walking, running and jumping - loads of several times body weight.
info.size: About 15 cm long; about 1.5 cm wide and 6 mm thick at its narrowest.
info.notes: Usually ruptures 2-6 cm above its insertion where the blood supply is poorest; the Thompson (calf-squeeze) test detects a complete tear.

info.description: Short triangular adductor lying behind pectineus and adductor longus, from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper third of the linea aspera.
info.function: Adducts the hip and helps flex it.
info.size: About 12-15 cm long.
info.notes: The obturator nerve divides around it - the anterior division runs in front of it and the posterior division behind it.

info.description: Triangular fan arising by a narrow tendon from the body of the pubis just below the pubic tubercle and widening to insert on the middle third of the linea aspera. The most anterior adductor; its medial border bounds the femoral triangle.
info.function: Adducts and flexes the hip and assists medial rotation.
info.size: About 20-25 cm long and up to 6 cm wide.
info.notes: Its tendinous origin is the usual site of a "groin strain" in football, ice hockey and other kicking or cutting sports.

info.description: The largest adductor: a huge triangular sheet from the inferior pubic ramus, ischial ramus and ischial tuberosity to the whole length of the linea aspera (adductor part) and the adductor tubercle above the medial femoral condyle (hamstring part).
info.function: Adducts the hip; its adductor part also flexes and its hamstring part extends the hip.
info.size: About 30 cm long and up to 15 cm wide.
info.notes: The adductor hiatus in its lower tendon lets the femoral vessels pass to the back of the knee, where they become the popliteal vessels; dual nerve supply (obturator and tibial).

info.description: A flat, crescent-shaped (semilunar) gland draped over the inner upper pole of the left kidney, behind the stomach and pancreas. Like its partner it has an outer yellow cortex and an inner red-brown medulla, which are really two glands in one capsule.
info.function: Cortex: aldosterone (salt and blood-pressure control), cortisol (stress, glucose, immune suppression) and weak androgens; medulla: adrenaline and noradrenaline for fight-or-flight.
info.size: About 4–5 × 3 × 1 cm, 4–5 g
info.notes: The left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein, unlike the right, which empties straight into the inferior vena cava. Adrenal failure (Addison's disease) causes fatigue, low blood pressure and a bronze tan from excess ACTH.

info.description: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei in the front of the medial temporal lobe (the uncus), just in front of the hippocampal head and the tip of the temporal horn.
info.function: Detects threat and emotional significance, triggers fear responses and tags memories with emotion.
info.size: About 1.5-2 cm across; roughly 1.2-1.7 cm3
info.notes: Rare bilateral amygdala damage (Urbach-Wiethe disease) leaves people unable to feel or recognise fear.
