info.notes: It drains through the frontonasal duct into the middle meatus; infection can spread to the orbit or through the thin posterior wall to the brain.

info.description: Frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis: a thin quadrilateral sheet over the forehead that arises from the galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) and inserts into the skin of the eyebrow, blending with orbicularis oculi. It has no bony attachment.
info.function: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead horizontally.
info.size: About 6 cm tall and 5 cm wide per side, 1–2 mm thick.
info.notes: Supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve: in Bell's palsy the forehead cannot be wrinkled on that side, whereas it is spared in a stroke.

info.description: The smallest coeliac branch; it climbs to the cardia of the stomach, gives oesophageal branches, then runs down the lesser curvature to join the right gastric artery.
info.function: Supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach and the lower oesophagus.
info.size: ~3–4 mm diameter.
info.notes: A bleeding gastric ulcer high on the lesser curvature can erode it, causing major haematemesis.

info.description: The smaller, shorter head of gastrocnemius, arising from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and joining the medial head in the calcaneal tendon.
info.function: Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee.
info.size: Belly about 15-18 cm long, 4-5 cm wide.
info.notes: A small sesamoid bone, the fabella, is found in its tendon in a minority of people and can be mistaken for a loose body on knee X-rays.

info.description: The larger head of gastrocnemius, arising from the back of the medial femoral condyle. It forms the prominent inner bulge of the calf, extends lower than the lateral head and blends into the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
info.function: Plantarflexes the ankle (push-off, standing on tiptoe) and flexes the knee.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm long, 6-7 cm wide.
info.notes: "Tennis leg" is a tear of its musculotendinous junction on the inner calf, typically in middle-aged recreational athletes.

name: Left gemelli and quadratus femoris
latin: Musculi gemelli superior et inferior; musculus quadratus femoris

info.description: Three small deep rotators behind the hip: the superior gemellus (from the ischial spine) and inferior gemellus (from the ischial tuberosity) run alongside the obturator internus tendon to the greater trochanter; below them quadratus femoris, a flat rectangle, passes from the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest.
info.function: Laterally rotate the hip and hold the femoral head in its socket.
info.size: Gemelli about 6-8 cm long and 1 cm thick; quadratus femoris about 7 x 4 cm.
info.notes: With piriformis and the obturators they form the "short external rotators" that are detached and repaired in the posterior approach to hip replacement.

info.description: Ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the glenoid cavity, to which the long head of biceps is anchored above.
info.function: Deepens the shallow socket by about 50% and stabilises the shoulder.
info.size: Ring ≈ 30 × 22 mm, 4 mm thick
info.notes: A SLAP tear (superior labrum anterior-to-posterior) is common in throwing athletes.

info.description: The inner, wedge-shaped part of the lentiform nucleus pointing toward the internal capsule; it looks pale because of the many myelinated fibres crossing it.
info.function: The main output station of the basal ganglia: its inhibitory signals to the thalamus act as a brake on movement that the striatum releases selectively.
info.size: About 2 cm long and 1 cm across at its base
info.notes: Deep brain stimulation of the internal pallidum relieves dystonia and levodopa-induced dyskinesia in Parkinson disease.

info.description: Leaves the side of the medulla as a row of rootlets, passes through the jugular foramen with the vagus and accessory nerves, descends between the internal carotid artery and jugular vein, winds forward around the stylopharyngeus muscle and ends in the back of the tongue and the tonsil.
info.function: Taste and sensation from the back third of the tongue, sensation from the pharynx, tonsil and middle ear; motor to stylopharyngeus; saliva from the parotid; and the carotid body/sinus reflexes for blood pressure and oxygen.
info.size: About 1.5 mm thick, ~9 cm long
info.notes: It carries the sensory side of the gag reflex (the vagus does the motor side). Glossopharyngeal neuralgia gives stabbing throat and ear pain triggered by swallowing.

info.description: The largest and most superficial gluteal muscle, a thick coarse-fibred quadrilateral sheet that shapes the buttock. It arises from the posterior ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, the back of the sacrum and coccyx and the sacrotuberous ligament, and inserts into the iliotibial tract and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.
info.function: Powerful extensor and lateral rotator of the hip - used to climb stairs, rise from a chair, run and jump; through the iliotibial tract it also steadies the extended knee.
info.size: About 20 x 15 cm and 2-3 cm thick; at roughly 0.8-1 kg the heaviest single muscle.
info.notes: Intramuscular injections go into the upper outer quadrant of the buttock to avoid the sciatic nerve, which runs beneath its lower half.

info.description: Thick fan-shaped muscle on the outer surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines, partly covered by gluteus maximus; its fibres converge on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter.
info.function: Main abductor of the hip; in walking it keeps the pelvis level when the opposite foot is off the ground. Its anterior fibres also rotate the hip medially.
info.size: About 15 cm wide at its origin, 2 cm thick.
info.notes: Weakness or superior gluteal nerve injury gives a positive Trendelenburg sign: the pelvis drops on the unsupported side during single-leg stance.

info.description: Smallest and deepest gluteal muscle, a fan beneath gluteus medius from the outer ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines to the anterior surface of the greater trochanter.
info.function: Abducts and medially rotates the hip and helps keep the pelvis level while walking.
info.size: About 10 cm wide at its origin, 1 cm thick.
info.notes: Tendinopathy or tears of the gluteus minimus and medius tendons ("rotator cuff of the hip") are a major cause of greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

info.description: Long, slender strap along the inner thigh, from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus), between the insertions of sartorius and semitendinosus.
info.function: Adducts the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.
info.size: About 40-45 cm long, 3-4 cm wide at the top.
info.notes: Largely expendable, so it is a favourite free muscle flap in reconstructive surgery and its tendon a graft for ligament reconstruction.

info.description: The longest vein in the body. It starts at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus, climbs the medial side of the leg, passes a hand's breadth behind the patella at the knee, and ascends the medial thigh to join the femoral vein at the saphenous opening just below the groin.
info.function: Drains the skin and superficial tissues of the foot, leg and thigh into the deep system via perforating veins and the saphenofemoral junction.
info.size: ~3–5 mm diameter, ~1 m long; 10–20 valves.
info.notes: Failure of its valves causes varicose veins; it is the vein most often harvested for coronary artery bypass grafts, and its position in front of the medial malleolus makes it reliable for emergency cut-down.

info.description: Wedge-shaped distal-row bone on the little-finger side with a palmar hook (hamulus).
info.function: Distal-row carpal: forms a rigid unit with the metacarpals and transmits grip forces to the forearm.
info.notes: Its hook forms a wall of Guyon's canal and can break in golf or baseball swings.

info.description: Skin of the hand: thick, hair-less, ridged glabrous skin on the palm (facing forward in the anatomical position) with thenar and hypothenar eminences, thin mobile skin on the back, four fingers of three phalanges and an abducted, rotated two-phalanx thumb.
info.function: The body's main tactile organ: fingertips carry the densest touch receptors (Meissner and Merkel), and friction ridges and sweat improve grip.
info.size: Hand length ~19 cm, palm ~8.8 cm wide and ~10 cm long; palmar skin up to ~1.5 mm epidermis
info.notes: Fingerprint ridge patterns are fixed by the 17th week of fetal life and are unique even in identical twins.

info.description: Collects bile from the functional left half of the liver (segments II-IV) and runs along the base of the quadrate lobe to the porta hepatis.
info.function: Drains bile out of the left liver.
info.size: About 2 cm long outside the liver (longer than the right), 3-4 mm wide.
info.notes: Its long horizontal extrahepatic course makes it the preferred site for surgical bile-duct reconstruction.

info.description: Bronchopulmonary nodes packed around the main bronchus and pulmonary vessels at the root (hilum) of each lung, where the airway enters it. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: First filter for lymph draining from the lung tissue and airways, before it passes to the tracheobronchial and mediastinal nodes.
info.size: 5-10 nodes of 5-15 mm per side
info.notes: In adult city-dwellers and smokers these nodes are black with inhaled carbon (anthracosis). Enlargement is seen in tuberculosis, sarcoidosis and lung cancer.

info.description: A curved ridge of rolled-in cortex in the floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, shaped like a seahorse (Greek hippokampos): a knobbly head in front, a body and a tail curving up behind the thalamus into the fornix.
info.function: Turns new experiences into long-term memories and maps places (place cells); essential for remembering facts and events.
info.size: About 4-4.5 cm long and 1 cm wide
info.notes: One of the first areas to shrink in Alzheimer disease; removal of both hippocampi left patient H.M. unable to form new memories.

info.description: Smooth hyaline cartilage covering the articular surface of the humeral head.
info.function: Lets the head glide in the glenoid with almost no friction.
info.size: ≈ 1–2 mm thick
info.notes: The glenoid is only a third as large as the head, so the shoulder is the most commonly dislocated major joint.

info.description: The upper-arm bone: a hemispherical head facing the glenoid, greater and lesser tubercles with the bicipital groove between, a cylindrical shaft with the deltoid tuberosity, and a flattened lower end bearing the trochlea, capitulum and epicondyles.
info.function: Transmits forces between shoulder and elbow and anchors the deltoid, rotator cuff, biceps, brachialis and triceps.
info.size: ≈ 32 cm long; head radius 21 mm; shaft ≈ 22 mm wide
info.notes: The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone"); mid-shaft fractures can injure the radial nerve in its spiral groove.

info.description: A narrow, clear channel running through the vitreous from the optic disc to the back of the lens.
info.function: The remnant of the path of the fetal hyaloid artery, which nourished the developing lens and normally regresses before birth.
info.size: About 1-2 mm wide and ~15 mm long, widening towards the lens.
info.notes: Incomplete regression leaves a tiny dot on the back of the lens (Mittendorf dot) or a tag on the disc (Bergmeister papilla).

info.description: Emerges from the medulla as a line of rootlets between the pyramid and the olive, leaves the skull through the hypoglossal canal, descends lateral to the carotid arteries, then hooks forward just above the hyoid bone into the underside of the tongue.
info.function: Motor to all the muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus - protrusion, retraction and shaping for speech and swallowing.
info.size: About 1.5 mm thick, ~11 cm
info.notes: Ask a patient to stick out the tongue: with a hypoglossal palsy it deviates TOWARD the weak side, because the healthy genioglossus pushes it across.

name: Left hypothenar muscles
latin: Eminentia hypothenaris (mm. abductor, flexor et opponens digiti minimi)

info.description: Muscles forming the little-finger side of the palm: abductor, flexor and opponens digiti minimi, from the pisiform, hamate and flexor retinaculum to the fifth metacarpal and base of the little finger.
info.function: Abducts and flexes the little finger and cups the palm.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 2 cm wide.
info.notes: Supplied by the ulnar nerve; their wasting suggests ulnar nerve damage at the elbow or in Guyon's canal.

info.description: A chain of nodes following the common and external iliac vessels down the side wall of the pelvis to the groin, plus internal iliac nodes deeper in the pelvis around the branches of the internal iliac artery. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: External iliac nodes collect lymph from the inguinal nodes, bladder, prostate/uterus; internal iliac nodes drain the pelvic organs, perineum and buttock; both pass to the common iliac then lumbar nodes.
info.size: 8-12 nodes of 5-15 mm per side
info.notes: Staging cancers of the bladder, prostate, cervix and rectum depends on whether these nodes are involved; they are examined on CT and MRI and often removed at surgery.

info.description: Fan-shaped muscle filling the iliac fossa on the inner surface of the ilium; its fibres converge onto the lateral side of the psoas tendon and insert with it on the lesser trochanter of the femur (together: iliopsoas).
info.function: Flexes the hip and steadies the pelvis on the femur.
info.size: About 15 cm long; fan ~10 cm wide.
info.notes: Bleeding into it (in haemophilia or on anticoagulants) can compress the femoral nerve, weakening the thigh.

info.description: Lateral column of the erector spinae, rising from the sacrum and iliac crest (common erector tendon) along the angles of the ribs to the transverse processes of C4–C6 (lumborum, thoracis and cervicis parts).
info.function: Extends the spine and bends it to its own side; the lumbar part helps depress the lower ribs.
info.size: About 60 cm long; up to 3 cm wide in the loin.
info.notes: Spasm of the lumbar erector spinae is the usual cause of acute "lumbago".

info.description: Twin branches of L1 that emerge from the lateral border of psoas, cross in front of quadratus lumborum behind the kidney, pierce transversus abdominis above the iliac crest and run forward between the abdominal muscle layers; the lower one (ilioinguinal) passes through the inguinal canal.
info.function: Motor to the lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis; sensation from the skin above the pubis, the groin, the upper inner thigh and the front of the scrotum or labia.
info.size: About 2 mm thick; ~25 cm long
info.notes: They can be caught in stitches or mesh during hernia repair or low abdominal incisions, causing chronic burning groin pain; an ilioinguinal block is used for hernia surgery in children.

info.description: Thickened lateral strip of the fascia lata running from the iliac tubercle of the iliac crest down the outside of the thigh to Gerdy's tubercle on the anterolateral tibial condyle. Tensor fasciae latae and about three-quarters of gluteus maximus insert into it.
info.function: Steadies the hip and the extended knee on the lateral side, helping to hold the pelvis level in single-leg stance.
info.size: About 45-50 cm long, 3-5 cm wide in the thigh, 2-3 mm thick.
info.notes: Friction over the lateral femoral epicondyle causes iliotibial band syndrome, a very common cause of lateral knee pain in runners and cyclists.

info.description: The large fan-shaped upper part of the hip bone: a thin wing (ala) with the concave iliac fossa inside, bounded above by the iliac crest from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS).
info.function: Supports the abdominal organs, anchors the abdominal, gluteal and iliacus muscles, and joins the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint.
info.size: Crest ≈ 25 cm long; ASIS to PSIS ≈ 16 cm
info.notes: The iliac crest is a standard donor site for bone grafts and marrow biopsy; the ASIS is a key surface landmark.

info.description: The "anvil": the middle ossicle. Its body articulates with the malleus head, a short process points backwards into the attic, and a long process descends parallel to the malleus handle to end in the knob-like lenticular process that meets the stapes.
info.function: Links malleus to stapes, adding lever action to the chain.
info.size: About 7 mm long, 27 mg.
info.notes: Its long process has the poorest blood supply of the chain and is the part most often eroded by chronic middle-ear disease, breaking the ossicular link.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B5, supplying the inferior lingular bronchopulmonary segment of the left upper lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 2 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: Because each segment has its own airway and blood supply, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).

info.description: Inferior nasal concha (turbinate): a scroll of thin bone covered by thick, vascular mucosa projecting from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
info.function: Increases the mucosal surface and creates turbulent airflow so inhaled air is warmed, humidified and filtered.
info.size: The largest turbinate (a separate bone), about 4–5 cm long and 1 cm high; the nasolacrimal duct opens under it.
info.notes: Its erectile venous tissue swells and shrinks with the nasal cycle; enlargement (turbinate hypertrophy) is a common cause of nasal blockage.

info.description: The only eye muscle that does not start at the orbit apex: it arises from the front of the orbital floor just beside the nasolacrimal canal, runs backward and outward beneath the inferior rectus and inserts on the lower-outer back quarter of the globe, near the macula.
info.function: Rotates the eye outward (extorsion) and elevates and abducts it - chiefly elevation when the eye is turned in.
info.size: ~35 mm long; insertion ~2 mm from the macula projection.
info.notes: Supplied by the inferior division of CN III; overaction of this muscle is common in childhood squint and is treated by weakening surgery.

info.description: A lentil-sized inferior parathyroid gland embedded in the back of the thyroid lobe, one of four. Despite the name it has nothing to do with thyroid hormone; it is the body's calcium sensor.
info.function: Secretes parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium by releasing it from bone, reducing its loss in urine and activating vitamin D.
info.size: 6 × 4 × 2 mm, 30–50 mg each
info.notes: The inferior glands wander: they descend with the thymus in the embryo and may end up anywhere from the lower pole to the chest. About 5–13 % of people have a fifth gland.

info.description: The inferior left pulmonary vein leaves the lower part of the left lung hilum and runs a short course to open into the posterior wall of the left atrium.
info.function: Returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left side of the heart.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm diameter; 1–2 cm long outside the lung.
info.notes: Sleeves of atrial muscle extending into the pulmonary veins trigger most atrial fibrillation, the target of catheter "pulmonary vein isolation".

info.description: A flat strap muscle arising from the common tendinous ring at the orbit apex and running forward along the orbital wall to insert by a thin, broad, white tendon on the sclera in front of the equator.
info.function: Depresses the eye (mainly when it looks outward) and also turns it in and rotates it outward (extorsion).
info.size: ~40 mm long; inserts ~6.5 mm from the limbus.
info.notes: It can be trapped in a blow-out fracture of the orbital floor, preventing upward gaze and causing double vision; enlarged in thyroid eye disease.

info.description: Thick triangular rotator-cuff muscle filling most of the infraspinous fossa below the spine of the scapula and converging on the middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
info.function: The main lateral rotator of the arm; stabilises the humeral head in the glenoid.
info.size: About 15 cm long and ~10 cm wide at its origin.
info.notes: Wastes when the suprascapular nerve is trapped at the spinoglenoid notch, a classic overuse injury of volleyball players.

info.description: The groin nodes: a horizontal row in the fat just below the inguinal ligament and a vertical row along the top of the great saphenous vein, plus a few deep nodes beside the femoral vein (the highest is Cloquet's node, in the femoral canal). Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the whole lower limb, the buttock, the external genitalia, perineum and anus, and the abdominal wall below the navel, sending lymph on to the external iliac nodes.
info.size: 10-15 superficial nodes of 5-20 mm; 1-3 deep nodes
info.notes: The most easily felt nodes in the body; small "shotty" nodes are normal here. Enlarged in leg and foot infections, sexually transmitted infections and melanoma of the leg.

info.description: A hidden lobe of cortex in the depth of the lateral fissure, normally covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula; shown here as the floor of the opened fissure, carrying short and long insular gyri.
info.function: Interoception (awareness of heartbeat, breathing and gut sensations), taste, disgust, pain and emotional awareness, and autonomic control.
info.size: About 5-6 cm long and 3 cm high; in life buried 1.5-2 cm beneath the opercula
info.notes: Branches of the middle cerebral artery run across its surface; damage to the insula has been reported to abolish the urge to smoke.

info.description: The smallest cuneiform, wedged between the medial and lateral cuneiforms at the base of the second metatarsal.
info.function: Locks the second metatarsal base into a mortise that stabilises the midfoot.
info.notes: Lisfranc injuries disrupt the joint between these bones and the metatarsals.

info.description: Rises from the carotid bifurcation without branches in the neck, enters the skull through the carotid canal of the temporal bone, bends forward through the cavernous sinus beside the pituitary (the carotid siphon) and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
info.function: Supplies most of the cerebral hemisphere on its side and, via the ophthalmic artery, the eye.
info.size: ~5 mm diameter at its origin (carotid bulb); ~4 mm intracranially.
info.notes: Narrowing at its origin (carotid stenosis) is treated by endarterectomy or stenting to prevent stroke; transient blindness in one eye (amaurosis fugax) is a warning sign.

info.description: Descends into the pelvis over the pelvic brim and divides at the upper edge of the greater sciatic notch into a posterior division (superior gluteal, iliolumbar and lateral sacral arteries) and an anterior division (to the bladder, rectum, genitals, uterus and buttock).
info.function: Supplies the pelvic organs, perineum, buttocks and medial thigh.
info.size: ~4 cm long, ~7 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its uterine branch crosses above the ureter ("water under the bridge"), a key landmark during hysterectomy.

info.description: Eleven thin sheets deep to the external intercostals with fibres at right angles to them (down and backwards), from the sternum and costal cartilages back to the angles of the ribs, where the internal intercostal membrane takes over.
info.function: Pull the ribs down in forced expiration; their front (interchondral) parts help raise the ribs in inspiration.
info.size: Each space ~1.5–2 cm tall; sheets 2–3 mm thick.
info.notes: The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove between this layer and the innermost intercostals.

info.description: Continues the sigmoid sinus from the jugular foramen at the skull base and descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries, joining the subclavian vein behind the sternoclavicular joint to form the brachiocephalic vein.
info.function: Drains the brain, face and neck.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm wide (widest of the neck veins), with a bulb at each end.
info.notes: Its pulsations reflect right atrial pressure (the jugular venous pressure, JVP); the right one is the standard site for ultrasound-guided central venous catheters.

info.description: Middle flat abdominal muscle, deep to the external oblique with fibres roughly at right angles to it: from the thoracolumbar fascia, anterior two-thirds of the iliac crest and lateral inguinal ligament up and forwards to the lower borders of ribs 10–12 and an aponeurosis that splits around rectus to reach the linea alba.
info.function: Compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and rotates it to the same side (together with the opposite external oblique).
info.size: About 20 cm tall, ~5 mm thick.
info.notes: Its lowest fibres form the cremaster muscle around the spermatic cord and, with transversus, the conjoint tendon.

name: Left interossei of the hand
latin: Musculi interossei dorsales et palmares manus

info.description: Seven small muscles filling the spaces between the metacarpals: four two-headed dorsal interossei and three palmar interossei, inserting on the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions.
info.function: Dorsal interossei spread the fingers (DAB), palmar interossei draw them together (PAD); together they flex the knuckles and straighten the finger joints.
info.size: Each about 5–6 cm long.
info.notes: Supplied by the ulnar nerve; wasting of the first dorsal interosseous hollows the thumb web in ulnar palsy.

info.description: The coloured, contractile diaphragm in front of the lens, part of the uveal tract. Its front surface shows radial fibres, pit-like crypts and a zig-zag collarette; its back is lined by dark pigment epithelium.
info.function: Controls how much light enters the eye: the sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic) narrows the pupil, the dilator pupillae (sympathetic) widens it.
info.size: 12 mm in diameter, 0.3-0.6 mm thick; pupil 2-8 mm.
info.notes: Eye colour depends only on the amount of melanin in the front layers - blue irises have little, brown have much; the crypt pattern is unique enough for biometric iris scans.

info.description: The lower posterior part of the hip bone: a thick body behind the acetabulum, the ischial spine, the rough ischial tuberosity, and a flat ramus that joins the pubis around the obturator foramen.
info.function: Bears the body weight when sitting and anchors the hamstrings and adductor magnus.
info.size: Tuberosity ≈ 5 cm long; inter-tuberous distance ≈ 11 cm
info.notes: The ischial spines mark the narrowest part of the birth canal and guide pudendal nerve blocks.

info.description: Bean-shaped retroperitoneal organ lying on the posterior abdominal wall between T12 and L3, wrapped in a tough fibrous capsule and perirenal fat. Its hilum, facing anteromedially, transmits the renal artery, vein and pelvis.
info.function: Filters about 180 L of plasma a day into 1–2 L of urine, regulating water, salt, potassium, acid–base balance and blood pressure, and secretes renin, erythropoietin and active vitamin D.
info.size: About 11 × 6 × 3 cm, 120–170 g each; ~1 million nephrons per kidney.
info.notes: The right kidney usually sits 1–2 cm lower than the left because the liver lies above it. Both move 2–3 cm with breathing.

info.description: The L1 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between L1 and L2. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which enters the lumbar plexus inside psoas.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the groin and the inguinal region.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Gives the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves; the cremasteric reflex tests L1-L2.

info.description: The L2 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between L2 and L3. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which enters the lumbar plexus inside psoas.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the upper front of the thigh.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: hip flexion (iliopsoas); it contributes to the femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves.

info.description: The L3 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between L3 and L4. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which enters the lumbar plexus inside psoas.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the lower front of the thigh and the inner knee.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: knee extension and hip adduction; an upper lumbar disc or a femoral stretch test provokes L3 pain.

info.description: A swelling on the dorsal (sensory) root of the L4 spinal nerve lying in the intervertebral foramen, just outside the dural sac, where the dorsal and ventral roots join. One of 31 pairs; three levels are shown as representatives.
info.function: Holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that bring touch, pain, temperature and position sense from its dermatome and muscles into the cord.
info.size: About 4-6 mm long
info.notes: The chickenpox virus lies dormant in dorsal root ganglia for decades and can reactivate as shingles, a painful rash confined to one dermatome.

info.description: The L4 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between L4 and L5. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which splits between the lumbar plexus and the lumbosacral trunk.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the medial leg and the medial ankle.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: the knee-jerk reflex and ankle dorsiflexion; compressed by an L3/4 disc or foraminal narrowing.

info.description: The L5 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between L5 and the sacrum. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the sacral plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the lateral leg, top of the foot and the big toe.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: big-toe extension; the L4/5 disc is one of the two commonest sites of sciatica and severe compression causes foot drop.

info.description: Rounded fold of hair-bearing skin over a pad of fat running back from the mons pubis; the two labia majora bound the pudendal cleft.
info.function: Protect the vestibule with the urethral and vaginal openings.
info.size: About 7–8 cm long, 2–3 cm wide and 1–1.5 cm thick.
info.notes: Counterpart of the scrotum; the round ligament of the uterus ends in its fat.

info.description: Thin, hairless fold of skin inside the labium majus bounding the vestibule; in front the two folds split to form the hood (prepuce) and frenulum of the clitoris.
info.function: Enclose the vestibule into which the urethra and vagina open; rich in sebaceous glands and nerve endings.
info.size: About 4–5 cm long; width varies widely (roughly 1–5 cm).
info.notes: They develop from the urogenital folds, which in males fuse to enclose the spongy urethra.

info.description: The small pink, fleshy nodule in the inner corner of the eye, with the crescent-shaped plica semilunaris just lateral to it. It is modified skin carrying fine hairs, sweat and sebaceous glands.
info.function: Collects debris ("sleep") and helps direct tears towards the puncta.
info.size: About 5 mm tall and 3 mm wide.
info.notes: The plica semilunaris beside it is a vestige of the nictitating membrane (third eyelid) of other animals.

info.description: An almond-shaped tear gland lodged in a shallow fossa of the frontal bone at the upper outer corner of the eye socket, above and to the side of the eyeball. A larger orbital part and a smaller palpebral part sit either side of the tendon of the upper-lid muscle.
info.function: Secretes the watery layer of the tear film (with lysozyme and IgA) through 6–12 ducts into the upper outer fornix; blinking spreads it across the eye towards the drainage puncta at the inner corner.
info.size: About 20 × 12 × 5 mm, ~0.8 g
info.notes: Its parasympathetic supply comes from the facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve. Autoimmune damage (Sjögren's syndrome) causes dry, gritty eyes; a very swollen gland gives the upper lid a characteristic S-shaped droop.

info.description: Two tiny openings (puncta) on small elevations near the inner end of each lid margin lead into fine channels that run 2 mm vertically and then 8 mm horizontally, joining as a common canaliculus that enters the lacrimal sac.
info.function: Drain tears from the eye surface; blinking pumps them towards the sac.
info.size: Puncta ~0.3 mm wide, about 6 mm lateral to the inner canthus; canaliculi ~10 mm long, 0.5-1 mm wide.
info.notes: A punctal plug is inserted to keep tears on the eye in dry-eye disease.

info.description: A membranous pouch lying in the lacrimal fossa of the medial orbital wall, behind the medial canthal tendon; its upper end is closed and its lower end continues as the nasolacrimal duct.
info.function: Collects tears from the canaliculi and passes them down to the nose.
info.size: 12-15 mm tall, 4-8 mm across.
info.notes: Infection of a blocked sac (dacryocystitis) gives a tender swelling at the inner corner; dacryocystorhinostomy bypasses the blockage into the nose.

info.description: One duct drains each lobe, converging on the nipple like the spokes of a wheel. Just beneath the areola each widens into a lactiferous sinus, then narrows again to open on the tip of the nipple through its own pore.
info.function: Conduct milk from the lobes to the nipple; the sinuses hold a small reserve that the baby's first sucks release.
info.size: 15–20 ducts, 2–4 mm in diameter, 5–8 mm sinuses; ~4–5 cm long
info.notes: Bloody discharge from a single duct opening is usually a benign intraductal papilloma but always needs investigation; nipple-sparing surgery must preserve these ducts.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B9, supplying the lateral basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lower lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: Because each segment has its own airway and blood supply, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).

info.description: Wedge-shaped cuneiform between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, at the base of the third metatarsal.
info.function: Keystone of the transverse arch of the foot.
info.notes: Together the cuneiforms and cuboid make the foot a flexible, arched lever.

info.description: A sensory branch of L2-L3 that crosses the iliacus muscle toward the anterior superior iliac spine and passes under (sometimes through) the inguinal ligament just medial to it into the outer thigh.
info.function: Sensation from the skin of the front and outer thigh down to the knee.
info.size: About 1.5 mm thick; ~30 cm long
info.notes: Meralgia paraesthetica - burning numbness of the outer thigh - is caused by compression at the inguinal ligament from tight belts, obesity or pregnancy.

info.description: Almost circular (O-shaped) fibrocartilage ring on the lateral tibial plateau.
info.function: Distributes load across the lateral compartment and aids knee stability.
info.size: ≈ 3.5 cm across, 10 mm wide
info.notes: It is more mobile than the medial meniscus, which partly protects it from tearing.

info.description: A flat strap muscle arising from the common tendinous ring at the orbit apex and running forward along the orbital wall to insert by a thin, broad, white tendon on the sclera in front of the equator.
info.function: Rotates the eye outward (abduction), away from the nose.
info.size: ~40 mm long; tendon ~8.8 mm long, inserting ~6.9 mm from the limbus.
info.notes: The only muscle of the abducens nerve (CN VI, "LR6"); a sixth-nerve palsy - often the first sign of raised intracranial pressure - leaves the eye unable to look outward.

info.description: The lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal, tilted about 30 degrees up at the front, bulges into the middle ear above the canal of the facial nerve; its ampulla lies at the anterior end next to the utricle.
info.function: Senses turning the head from side to side (yaw).
info.size: Radius about 3.2-4 mm; the shortest canal, about 15 mm.
info.notes: Caloric testing irrigates the ear canal with warm or cool water to set up convection in this canal and provoke nystagmus.

info.description: The C-shaped CSF cavity inside each hemisphere: an anterior (frontal) horn, a body under the corpus callosum, the atrium, a posterior (occipital) horn and an inferior (temporal) horn curving down and forward into the temporal lobe.
info.function: Its choroid plexus makes most of the cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain, carries away wastes and buoys the brain so it effectively weighs only ~50 g.
info.size: About 7-10 ml each; body 1-1.5 cm wide
info.notes: It drains through the interventricular foramen (of Monro) into the third ventricle; blockage there enlarges it (obstructive hydrocephalus).

info.description: The broadest muscle of the back: a thin triangular sheet arising via the thoracolumbar fascia from the spinous processes of T7–L5 and the sacrum, the posterior iliac crest and the lower ribs. It sweeps up round the side of the chest, forming the posterior axillary fold, to a flat tendon in the floor of the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
info.function: Extends, adducts and medially rotates the arm; pulls the trunk up towards the arms in climbing and helps in forced expiration and coughing.
info.size: Up to ~40 cm across, 2–5 mm thick; tendon about 3 cm wide.
info.notes: A workhorse flap for breast reconstruction; supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.

info.description: Skin of the thigh, knee and leg: the tapering thigh with the quadriceps and the vastus medialis "teardrop", the kneecap, the calf bulge of gastrocnemius at the back, the subcutaneous shin and the ankle malleoli.
info.function: Protective and sensory covering of the lower limb; the calf muscle pump beneath it drives venous blood back up against gravity.
info.size: Hip to ankle ~85 cm; each lower limb ≈ 18 % of body surface (rule of nines)
info.notes: The skin over the shin lies directly on the tibia with little padding, so shin wounds heal slowly; venous leg ulcers occur typically just above the medial malleolus.

info.description: The fatty layer of the thigh and leg above the fascia lata and crural fascia, carrying the great and small saphenous veins and cutaneous nerves.
info.function: Insulation, energy storage and a gliding plane over the muscles.
info.size: 5–25 mm on the thigh (thicker in women), a few mm over the shin
info.notes: The great saphenous vein in this layer is the vessel most often harvested for coronary bypass grafts.

info.description: The thin, elastic, transparent basement membrane that wraps the whole lens; the zonular fibres attach to it around the equator.
info.function: Shapes the lens during accommodation and anchors it to the zonules.
info.size: 4-23 micrometres thick, thickest near the equator in front.
info.notes: In cataract surgery the front of the capsule is opened (capsulorhexis) and the empty bag holds the artificial lens implant.

info.description: The dense central core of the lens, made of the oldest fibre cells, some formed before birth.
info.function: Forms the central, highest-refractive-index part of the lens.
info.size: About 6 x 2.5 mm, growing and hardening with age.
info.notes: A nuclear cataract turns yellow-brown with age and can temporarily improve near vision ("second sight").

info.description: A thin triangular muscle lying above the superior rectus. It arises from the lesser wing of the sphenoid above the optic canal, runs forward to Whitnall's ligament and then becomes a broad aponeurosis that descends into the upper lid to the tarsal plate and skin.
info.function: Raises and holds up the upper eyelid; a small smooth-muscle slip beneath it (Mueller's muscle) adds 1-2 mm of lift.
info.size: Muscle ~40 mm, aponeurosis ~15-20 mm long and ~25 mm wide at the lid.
info.notes: Supplied by CN III (Mueller's muscle by sympathetic fibres); age-related stretching of the aponeurosis is the commonest cause of a drooping lid in adults.

info.description: Strap muscle from the transverse processes of C1–C4 descending along the side and back of the neck to the superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula.
info.function: Elevates the scapula and rotates it so the glenoid tilts downwards; bends the neck to its side.
info.size: About 15 cm long and 2 cm wide.
info.notes: A frequent source of "stiff neck" and trigger-point pain at the angle between neck and shoulder.

info.description: Intermediate and longest column of the erector spinae, from the sacrum and lumbar transverse processes up via the thoracic and cervical transverse processes to the mastoid process (longissimus capitis).
info.function: Extends the vertebral column and head; acting on one side it bends them to that side and turns the head to that side.
info.size: About 70 cm long.
info.notes: It forms most of the rounded paraspinal bulge either side of the lumbar spine.

info.description: Deep prevertebral muscle lying on the front of the vertebral bodies from the atlas (C1) down to T3, made of vertical, superior oblique and inferior oblique parts.
info.function: Flexes the cervical spine and resists hyperextension.
info.size: About 15 cm long, ~1 cm wide and thin.
info.notes: Strained in whiplash injury; calcific tendinitis of longus colli causes sudden painful neck stiffness and pain on swallowing.

info.description: The smaller, less mobile lower fold of skin, orbicularis muscle, tarsal plate and conjunctiva; its margin lies at the lower edge of the cornea.
info.function: Supports the globe, guides tears towards the lower punctum and helps close the eye.
info.size: Palpebral fissure between the two lids ~28-30 mm wide and 9-10 mm high.
info.notes: With age the lower lid can turn out (ectropion, causing watering) or in (entropion, lashes rub the cornea).

info.description: Continues down and back from the left main bronchus, giving a superior segmental bronchus and the basal segmental bronchi.
info.function: Secondary (lobar) bronchus: conducts air to one lobe of the lung.
info.size: About 1–1.5 cm to the basal division, 8–10 mm wide.
info.notes: Lobar bronchi are the level at which the lung is removed in a lobectomy; their walls contain irregular cartilage plates instead of rings.

info.description: The narrower fibrous plate of the lower lid, containing about 20 meibomian glands.
info.function: Stiffens the lower lid and holds its margin against the globe.
info.size: ~29 mm long, 4-5 mm tall, ~1 mm thick.
info.notes: Lower-lid tightening surgery shortens and re-anchors the tarsus to the lateral orbital rim.

info.description: Formed inside the psoas major muscle by the ventral rami of L1-L4. Its branches emerge around psoas: the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves from its lateral border, the femoral nerve lower down, the genitofemoral nerve through its front and the obturator nerve from its medial border; part of L4 joins L5 as the lumbosacral trunk.
info.function: Supplies the lower abdominal wall, hip flexors, knee extensors and thigh adductors, and the skin of the groin, the front and inner thigh and the inner leg.
info.size: Spans ~12 cm inside psoas from L1 to the pelvic brim
info.notes: A psoas haematoma or abscess can compress the whole plexus, causing groin and thigh pain with a weak knee; surgeons approaching the spine through psoas monitor it with electrodes.

info.description: Four slender worm-like muscles arising from the flexor digitorum profundus tendons in the palm and inserting on the radial (thumb) side of the extensor expansions of the fingers.
info.function: Flex the knuckles while straightening the finger joints (the "tabletop" position).
info.size: Each 4–6 cm long and a few mm thick.
info.notes: Unique in arising from tendons; the two lateral ones are supplied by the median nerve, the two medial ones by the ulnar nerve.

info.description: Crescent-shaped bone in the centre of the proximal row, articulating with the radius.
info.function: Proximal-row carpal: adapts its position as the wrist bends so the hand moves smoothly on the forearm.
info.notes: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone; Kienböck disease is its avascular necrosis.

info.description: The left lower lobe lies below and behind the oblique fissure and rests on the left dome of the diaphragm; its medial surface is grooved by the descending aorta.
info.function: Gas exchange; ventilated by the left lower lobe bronchus (superior, anteromedial basal, lateral basal and posterior basal segments).
info.size: About 23% of total lung volume; the left lung as a whole is ~10% smaller than the right because of the heart.
info.notes: Lower-lobe pneumonia irritating the diaphragmatic pleura can refer pain to the shoulder tip (phrenic nerve, C3–C5) or the upper abdomen.

info.description: The upper lobe of the left lung, including the lingula: the tongue-shaped process below the cardiac notch, where the anterior border is pushed aside by the heart.
info.function: Gas exchange; ventilated by the left upper lobe bronchus (apicoposterior and anterior segments, plus superior and inferior lingular segments).
info.size: About 22% of total lung volume; the cardiac notch indents the anterior border by 3–4 cm at the 4th–5th costal cartilages.
info.notes: The lingula is the left-sided counterpart of the right middle lobe; the cardiac notch leaves part of the pericardium uncovered by lung (the area of superficial cardiac dullness).

info.description: The left lymphatic trunks: beaded, valved vessels no wider than a pencil lead that collect tissue fluid from the skin and muscles of the limbs. Superficial trunks run with the cephalic and basilic veins up the arm (via the cubital and axillary nodes) and with the great and small saphenous veins up the leg (via the popliteal and inguinal nodes); a deep trunk follows the femoral vessels, and the lumbar trunk carries everything from the iliac nodes up to the cisterna chyli, while the jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks join the thoracic duct at the root of the neck.
info.function: Return the 2-4 litres of fluid, protein and immune cells that leak out of the capillaries each day, carrying them through the lymph nodes and back to the veins.
info.size: Collecting vessels 0.5-2 mm wide; the lumbar trunk about 3 mm; valves every 6-20 mm giving the beaded look
info.notes: Each segment between two valves (a lymphangion) contracts 6-10 times a minute, helped by the muscle pump. Blocked or removed vessels cause lymphoedema; infection spreading along them shows as red streaks up the limb (lymphangitis).

info.description: An oval, yellowish area at the centre of the back of the retina, on the visual axis, coloured by the carotenoid pigments lutein and zeaxanthin.
info.function: Provides sharp central and colour vision - reading, recognising faces, driving.
info.size: About 5.5 mm across, centred ~3.5-4 mm temporal to the optic disc.
info.notes: Age-related macular degeneration destroys central vision while peripheral vision remains; it is the main cause of sight loss in older adults in wealthy countries.

info.description: The left main bronchus runs more horizontally (about 45°), passing under the aortic arch and in front of the oesophagus and descending aorta to reach the left hilum.
info.function: Carries air into the left lung, dividing at the hilum into the upper and lower lobe bronchi.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 1.2 cm in diameter.
info.notes: An enlarged left atrium or an aortic arch aneurysm can compress it; its length suits left-sided double-lumen tubes used in thoracic surgery.

info.description: The "hammer": the outermost ossicle. Its long handle (manubrium) is embedded in the eardrum down to the umbo, while its rounded head sits up in the attic and articulates with the incus. A small lateral process tents the drum at the top of the handle.
info.function: Transfers eardrum vibrations to the incus.
info.size: About 8 mm long and 25 mg, the largest ossicle.
info.notes: The tensor tympani tendon inserts on its handle. The three ossicles are the only bones that are already adult-sized at birth.

info.description: The milk-producing tissue of the breast: 15–20 lobes arranged like the spokes of a wheel around the nipple, each lobe a cluster of lobules of tiny alveoli, embedded in fat and supported by suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments over the pectoralis major muscle. Shown here as 17 lobes of three lobules each, larger towards the edge of the breast, with one long lobe reaching towards the armpit.
info.function: Under prolactin the alveoli secrete milk; oxytocin makes the muscle-like cells around them contract to eject it. Between pregnancies the gland is mostly quiescent ducts.
info.size: Glandular tissue spread through a breast of ~10–12 cm diameter; adult breast 150–500 g, roughly half of it gland
info.notes: Most glandular tissue — and about half of breast cancers — lies in the upper outer quadrant, which also sends an axillary tail (of Spence) towards the armpit; this is why the axillary lymph nodes are examined.

info.description: The lowest and only mixed division. It drops through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa and splits into the inferior alveolar nerve (which runs inside the jaw bone and exits at the chin as the mental nerve), the lingual nerve to the tongue, the auriculotemporal nerve to the temple, and motor branches to the chewing muscles.
info.function: Sensation from the lower lip, chin, lower teeth, front two-thirds of the tongue, cheek lining and temple; motor to masseter, temporalis, pterygoids and the mylohyoid.
info.size: Trunk about 3-4 mm thick; inferior alveolar nerve ~7 cm
info.notes: The inferior alveolar block at the mandibular foramen is the standard dental anaesthetic for lower teeth; it numbs the lip and chin too, and a misplaced needle can hit the lingual nerve.

info.description: Thick quadrilateral muscle on the side of the jaw, running from the lower border of the zygomatic arch to the lateral surface of the ramus and angle of the mandible.
info.function: Elevates the mandible, closing the jaw with great force; its superficial part also helps protrude it.
info.size: About 5 cm tall, 3 cm wide and up to 1.5 cm thick.
info.notes: Enlarges with habitual clenching or bruxism (masseteric hypertrophy), which is sometimes treated with botulinum toxin.

info.description: The middle, sensory division. It leaves the skull through the foramen rotundum, crosses the pterygopalatine fossa, runs forward in the floor of the orbit as the infraorbital nerve and emerges below the eye at the infraorbital foramen; branches drop to the upper teeth.
info.function: Sensation from the cheek, lower eyelid, side of the nose, upper lip, upper teeth and gums, palate, maxillary sinus and nasal cavity.
info.size: About 2.5 mm thick; ~5 cm from ganglion to cheek
info.notes: A blow-out fracture of the orbit floor bruises the infraorbital nerve, leaving the cheek and upper lip numb. Dentists anaesthetise its alveolar branches for upper-tooth work.

info.description: The largest paranasal sinus: a pyramid-shaped air space in the body of the maxilla, below the orbit and above the upper molar roots, with its base on the lateral nasal wall.
info.function: Lightens the face and warms/humidifies air; it drains into the middle meatus.
info.size: About 3.5 cm high, 2.5 cm wide and 3.5 cm deep (~15 ml).
info.notes: Its opening lies high on the medial wall, so it drains poorly and is the sinus most often infected; upper molar roots can protrude into its floor.

info.description: The largest of the three wedge-shaped cuneiforms, at the base of the first metatarsal.
info.function: Supports the big toe ray and receives tibialis anterior and fibularis longus.
info.notes: Its wedge shape, like the others, helps form the transverse arch of the foot.

info.description: C-shaped wedge of fibrocartilage on the medial tibial plateau, firmly attached to the joint capsule and medial collateral ligament.
info.function: Deepens the tibial socket, spreads load and stabilises the knee.
info.size: ≈ 4.5 cm long, 9–10 mm wide
info.notes: Tears more often than the lateral meniscus because it is less mobile (part of the "unhappy triad").

info.description: A flat strap muscle arising from the common tendinous ring at the orbit apex and running forward along the orbital wall to insert by a thin, broad, white tendon on the sclera in front of the equator.
info.function: Rotates the eye inward (adduction), towards the nose.
info.size: The largest and strongest rectus, ~40 mm long; its tendon inserts ~5.5 mm from the limbus.
info.notes: Supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III); weakness causes an outward-drifting eye. Converging both medial recti lets us look at near objects.

info.description: A short oblique superficial vein crossing the front of the elbow (cubital fossa) from the cephalic vein upward and medially to the basilic vein, lying on the bicipital aponeurosis that shields the brachial artery beneath.
info.function: Links the two main superficial veins of the upper limb.
info.size: ~3–4 mm diameter; ~2.5 cm long.
info.notes: The most common site for drawing blood (venepuncture) because it is large, fixed and superficial.

info.description: Formed by the lateral and medial cords in front of the axillary artery, it runs down the medial side of the arm with the brachial artery, enters the forearm between the heads of pronator teres, descends in the middle of the forearm between the superficial and deep finger flexors and passes through the carpal tunnel into the palm.
info.function: Motor to most forearm flexors and both pronators, the thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals; sensation from the palm side of the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger.
info.size: About 4 mm thick in the arm; ~60 cm from the axilla to the fingertips
info.notes: Carpal tunnel syndrome - compression under the flexor retinaculum - causes night-time tingling in the thumb-to-ring fingers and wasting of the thumb ball; a supracondylar fracture in a child can injure it higher up.

info.description: The tympanic cavity: an air-filled, mucosa-lined space in the temporal bone between the eardrum and the inner ear, bridged by the three ossicles. Its upper extension (the epitympanic recess or attic) holds the malleus head and incus body; behind, it opens into the mastoid air cells and in front into the Eustachian tube.
info.function: Houses the ossicular chain and keeps air at atmospheric pressure on the inner side of the eardrum.
info.size: About 15 mm high and 15 mm front-to-back but only 2-6 mm wide; volume 1-2 ml.
info.notes: Otitis media is infection of this space. The facial nerve runs in a thin bony canal along its medial wall, so it is at risk in ear surgery.

info.description: Middle nasal concha (turbinate): a scroll of thin bone covered by thick, vascular mucosa projecting from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
info.function: Increases the mucosal surface and creates turbulent airflow so inhaled air is warmed, humidified and filtered.
info.size: Part of the ethmoid bone, about 4 cm long; the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain beneath it into the middle meatus.
info.notes: The middle meatus (ostiomeatal complex) is the key drainage pathway targeted by functional endoscopic sinus surgery.

name: Left middle phalanx of the fourth toe

info.description: Middle phalanx of the fourth toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 10 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left middle phalanx of the index finger

info.description: Middle phalanx of the index finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 20 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left middle phalanx of the little finger

info.description: Middle phalanx of the little finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 16 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left middle phalanx of the little toe

info.description: Middle phalanx of the little toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 8 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left middle phalanx of the middle finger

info.description: Middle phalanx of the middle finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 22 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left middle phalanx of the ring finger

info.description: Middle phalanx of the ring finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 20 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left middle phalanx of the second toe

info.description: Middle phalanx of the second toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 12 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left middle phalanx of the third toe

info.description: Middle phalanx of the third toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 11 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

info.description: The bony central pillar of the cochlea, perforated by tiny canals for the fibres of the cochlear nerve. The spiral ganglion, holding the cell bodies of the hearing neurons, lies in a spiral canal around its base.
info.function: Anchors the bony spiral lamina and channels nerve fibres from the organ of Corti to the internal acoustic meatus.
info.size: About 4-5 mm high; the spiral ganglion holds roughly 30,000 neurons.
info.notes: Loss of spiral ganglion cells limits how well a cochlear implant can work, because the implant stimulates these neurons directly.

info.description: A branch of the lateral cord that pierces coracobrachialis, runs down between biceps and brachialis and emerges lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow, where it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
info.function: Motor to the three front-of-arm muscles (coracobrachialis, biceps, brachialis); sensation from the lateral side of the forearm.
info.size: About 3 mm thick; ~20 cm in the arm plus ~20 cm of cutaneous branch
info.notes: Rarely injured on its own; its loss weakens elbow flexion and supination and abolishes the biceps reflex. Heavy lifting can pinch its cutaneous branch under the biceps aponeurosis.

info.description: Small oblong bone forming, with its partner, the bony bridge of the nose; the lower edge carries the nasal cartilages.
info.function: Supports the upper nose and protects the nasal cavity.
info.size: ≈ 2.5 cm long, 1 cm wide
info.notes: The most commonly fractured facial bones.

info.description: A membranous canal running down from the lacrimal sac through a bony canal in the maxilla to open under the inferior nasal concha, guarded by a mucosal fold (valve of Hasner).
info.function: Carries tears into the nose - which is why crying makes the nose run.
info.size: 12-18 mm long, 3-4 mm wide.
info.notes: In ~5% of newborns the lower end is still closed, causing a watery, sticky eye that usually opens by itself within the first year.

info.description: Boat-shaped bone on the medial side of the midfoot between the talar head and the three cuneiforms, with a palpable medial tuberosity.
info.function: Keystone of the medial longitudinal arch; receives the tibialis posterior tendon.
info.notes: Stress fractures occur in sprinters and jumpers.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the ninth rib to the cartilage above, forming the costal margin.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 5 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The ninth rib, a false (vertebrochondral) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T9 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T9 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 25 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: The nipple (mammary papilla) surrounded by the pigmented areola, which carries small raised areolar (Montgomery) glands. In men it lies over the 4th intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line.
info.function: Rudimentary in males; sensitive erogenous skin with smooth muscle but no functioning gland.
info.size: Areola ~2.5 cm diameter, nipple ~5 mm
info.notes: Extra (supernumerary) nipples along the embryonic milk line from axilla to groin occur in 1–5 % of people.

info.description: Flat triangular muscle covering the outer surface of the obturator membrane; its tendon winds below and behind the neck of the femur to the trochanteric fossa.
info.function: Laterally rotates the hip and steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum.
info.size: About 8-10 cm long.
info.notes: Unlike the other short lateral rotators it is supplied by the obturator nerve; an obturator hernia can compress that nerve and cause medial thigh pain.

info.description: Fan-shaped muscle lining the inner surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding pelvic bone. Its tendon turns a right angle around the lesser sciatic notch and runs laterally, flanked by the two gemelli, to the medial surface of the greater trochanter.
info.function: Laterally rotates the extended hip, abducts the flexed hip and stabilises the femoral head.
info.size: About 10 cm long; its intrapelvic fan is about 5 cm across.
info.notes: Its fascia forms the pudendal (Alcock's) canal carrying the pudendal nerve and vessels along the side wall of the ischioanal fossa.

info.description: Leaves the medial border of psoas at the pelvic brim, runs along the side wall of the pelvis and leaves through the obturator canal at the top of the obturator foramen, then splits into anterior and posterior branches around adductor brevis.
info.function: Motor to the adductor muscles of the thigh (adductor longus, brevis and part of magnus, gracilis, obturator externus); sensation from a patch of skin on the inner thigh.
info.size: About 3 mm thick; ~25 cm long
info.notes: A pelvic tumour or hernia through the obturator canal pressing on it causes pain referred to the inner knee (Howship-Romberg sign); it is blocked during bladder surgery to stop the leg jerking.

info.description: The smallest lobe, forming the pointed back of each hemisphere behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and resting on the tentorium above the cerebellum; the calcarine sulcus runs along its medial face.
info.function: Vision: the primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus receives the optic radiation, and surrounding areas analyse shape, colour and motion.
info.size: About 4-5 cm from the occipital pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus
info.notes: Each occipital lobe sees the opposite half of the visual field; a posterior cerebral artery stroke causes a homonymous hemianopia, often sparing central (macular) vision.

info.description: Leaves the front of the midbrain between the cerebral peduncles, runs forward in the roof and lateral wall of the cavernous sinus beside the pituitary and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
info.function: Moves the eye up, down and inward (superior, inferior and medial recti, inferior oblique), lifts the upper lid (levator palpebrae) and constricts the pupil and focuses the lens via parasympathetic fibres.
info.size: About 3 mm thick, 2.5 cm from midbrain to orbit
info.notes: A complete third-nerve palsy gives a drooping lid and an eye that sits "down and out"; a dilated pupil with it suggests compression by an aneurysm or a herniating temporal lobe - a neurosurgical emergency.

info.description: The nerve of smell. About twenty tiny bundles (fila) rise from the roof of the nasal cavity through the sieve-like cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb, which lies under the frontal lobe; the olfactory tract then runs back to the brain.
info.function: Carries smell from the olfactory mucosa to the olfactory cortex; it is the only sense that bypasses the thalamus.
info.size: Bulb 10-12 x 4 mm; tract about 3.5 cm long
info.notes: Fila are torn in head injuries that shear the cribriform plate, causing loss of smell (anosmia); a fracture there can also leak cerebrospinal fluid into the nose.

info.description: The upper, purely sensory division of the trigeminal nerve. It passes through the superior orbital fissure and splits into frontal, lacrimal and nasociliary nerves; the frontal nerve runs along the orbit roof and emerges at the supraorbital notch onto the forehead.
info.function: Sensation from the forehead and scalp back to the vertex, upper eyelid, cornea and conjunctiva, bridge of the nose and the frontal and ethmoid sinuses.
info.size: About 2.5 mm thick, 2.5 cm to the fissure
info.notes: The corneal reflex tests V1 (the blink is via the facial nerve). Shingles in V1 (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) threatens the cornea; a lesion on the nose tip warns of eye involvement.

info.description: The pale, round head of the optic nerve, where about 1.2 million ganglion-cell axons leave the eye and the central retinal vessels enter; it has a central depression, the optic cup.
info.function: Carries all visual signals out of the eye; having no photoreceptors, it forms the physiological blind spot.
info.size: 1.5-1.8 mm in diameter, about 3-4 mm nasal to the fovea and slightly above it; normal cup-to-disc ratio < 0.5.
info.notes: An enlarging cup signals glaucoma; a swollen disc (papilloedema) signals raised intracranial pressure.

name: Left optic nerve (CN II), intracranial part

info.description: The intracanalicular and intracranial part of the optic nerve, from the apex of the orbit through the optic canal to the optic chiasm. The part inside the orbit is built with the eye. It is really a tract of the brain, wrapped in all three meninges.
info.function: Carries about 1.2 million retinal ganglion-cell axons - the entire visual signal of one eye - toward the chiasm.
info.size: 4 mm in diameter with its sheath; intracranial part ~10 mm, canal ~6 mm
info.notes: Because it is bathed in cerebrospinal fluid, raised intracranial pressure swells the nerve head (papilloedema), visible with an ophthalmoscope.

info.description: Cranial nerve II, a bundle of about 1.2 million retinal ganglion-cell axons. Its orbital part runs in a gentle S-curve from the back of the eyeball to the optic canal at the orbit apex; beyond the apex it continues to the optic chiasm.
info.function: Carries visual information from the retina to the brain.
info.size: Orbital part ~25 mm long (slack allows eye movement), 3-4 mm thick; whole nerve ~45-50 mm.
info.notes: It is a tract of the central nervous system, so it does not regenerate; inflammation (optic neuritis) is often the first sign of multiple sclerosis.

info.description: The three meningeal layers (dura, arachnoid, pia) that wrap the optic nerve from the brain to the eyeball, where the dura blends with the sclera. The subarachnoid space inside it contains cerebrospinal fluid.
info.function: Protects the nerve and carries CSF pressure forward to the back of the eye.
info.size: Outer diameter ~4.5-5 mm.
info.notes: An optic nerve sheath diameter above ~5-6 mm on ultrasound suggests raised intracranial pressure.

info.description: The band of visual fibres running back from the chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate body of the thalamus, with a small branch to the midbrain for pupil reflexes.
info.function: Delivers the opposite half of the visual field of both eyes to the thalamus, which relays it to the visual cortex.
info.size: About 3 cm long, 3-4 mm wide
info.notes: Damage to one tract causes loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia), the opposite side to the lesion.

info.description: Concentric sphincter around the eye: an orbital part lying on the bony orbital margin and a thin palpebral part within the eyelids, anchored medially to the medial palpebral ligament and lacrimal bone.
info.function: Closes the eyelids — gently in blinking (palpebral part) or tightly when squeezing the eyes shut (orbital part) — and helps pump tears into the lacrimal sac.
info.size: Ring about 5 cm across and ~1 cm wide, 1–2 mm thick.
info.notes: Facial nerve palsy prevents eye closure and risks corneal drying; "crow's feet" wrinkles run at right angles to its lateral fibres.

info.description: Soft, lobulated fat divided by fine septa that fills the orbit around the globe, muscles, nerves and vessels, both inside and outside the cone of the recti.
info.function: Cushions the eye, lets it rotate smoothly and supports it in the orbit.
info.size: Orbit volume ~30 ml, of which the globe is ~7 ml; fat makes up much of the rest.
info.notes: Swelling of orbital fat and muscles in thyroid eye disease pushes the eyes forward (proptosis); fat prolapsing through a weak septum forms "eye bags".

info.description: The fenestra vestibuli: an oval opening in the bony wall between the middle ear and the vestibule of the inner ear, sealed by the stapes footplate and its annular ligament.
info.function: Entry point for sound energy into the perilymph of the scala vestibuli.
info.size: About 3 x 1.5 mm.
info.notes: The eardrum is about 17 times larger than the footplate; this area ratio plus the ossicular lever boosts pressure some 22-fold, matching air to fluid.

info.description: Almond-shaped gonad lying in the ovarian fossa on the side wall of the pelvis, hung from the broad ligament and tethered to the uterus by the ovarian ligament; its surface bulges with follicles.
info.function: Matures egg cells in follicles, releasing usually one each cycle (ovulation), and secretes oestrogen and progesterone.
info.size: About 3 × 2 × 1.5 cm; shrinks after menopause.
info.notes: Born with about 1–2 million primordial follicles, of which only about 400 ever ovulate.

info.description: An almond-shaped mass of lymphoid tissue in the side wall of the throat, sitting in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Its surface is pitted with 10-20 deep crypts. These are the "tonsils" seen at the back of the mouth.
info.function: Samples swallowed and inhaled antigens at the entrance of the throat and starts antibody responses, as part of Waldeyer's ring.
info.size: About 20-25 x 15 x 10 mm in a child; they shrink in adults
info.notes: Tonsillitis is usually viral or due to group A streptococcus. Tonsillectomy is one of the commonest childhood operations. A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) pushes the uvula toward the opposite side.

info.description: Fibro-fatty pad of the palm, divided into small chambers by vertical fibrous bands that tie the skin to the palmar aponeurosis; thin and loose on the back of the hand.
info.function: Cushions grip while stopping the palmar skin from sliding.
info.size: ~3–8 mm under the palm, 1–2 mm on the dorsum
info.notes: Because the palmar skin is tethered, infections of the palm spread to the looser dorsal tissues, so a palm infection often shows as swelling on the back of the hand.

info.description: Small spindle-shaped muscle from the medial epicondyle with a long slender tendon passing superficial to the flexor retinaculum into the palmar aponeurosis.
info.function: Weakly flexes the wrist and tenses the palmar aponeurosis.
info.size: Belly ~6 cm, tendon ~15 cm.
info.notes: Absent in about 15% of people; its tendon is a favourite graft for tendon and ligament reconstruction.

info.description: Left parietal bone: a large, gently curved square plate forming the side and roof of the cranium, meeting its partner at the sagittal suture.
info.function: Protects the parietal lobes and gives attachment to the temporalis fascia.
info.size: ≈ 12 × 12 cm, 5–7 mm thick
info.notes: The parietal eminence is the widest point of the skull; the fontanelles of the newborn lie at its corners.

info.description: Lies behind the central sulcus and above the lateral fissure, reaching back to the parieto-occipital sulcus under the parietal bone.
info.function: Receives touch, pain, temperature and limb position (primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus) and builds the spatial map used for reaching, attention and reading.
info.size: About 5-6 cm front to back at the vertex
info.notes: Right parietal strokes often cause hemispatial neglect: the patient ignores the left side of space, e.g. eats only from the right half of the plate.

info.description: The outer pleural layer lining the inner chest wall, diaphragm and mediastinum; below the lung edge it forms the costodiaphragmatic recess.
info.function: Seals the pleural cavity, a potential space with 10–20 ml of fluid under negative pressure that keeps the lungs expanded.
info.size: The recess extends about two rib spaces (≈5 cm) below the lower lung border in the mid-axillary line.
info.notes: Effusions collect first in the costodiaphragmatic recess and blunt the costophrenic angle on an upright chest X-ray; the parietal pleura is richly supplied by pain-sensitive intercostal and phrenic nerves.

info.description: The parotid (Stensen's) duct leaves the front edge of the gland, runs forward over the masseter muscle a finger-breadth below the cheekbone, turns sharply inward through the buccinator muscle and opens inside the cheek opposite the upper second molar.
info.function: Carries parotid saliva into the mouth; the buccinator acts as a valve so the duct is not inflated when you blow.
info.size: About 5 cm long, 3 mm in diameter
info.notes: A small papilla marks its opening inside the cheek — press the gland and saliva squirts from it. Stones are rarer here than in the submandibular duct because parotid saliva is thin.

info.description: The largest salivary gland, a lobulated wedge of tissue in front of and below the ear, wrapped around the back edge of the jaw bone and reaching down to the angle of the jaw. The facial nerve fans out through the middle of it on its way to the face muscles.
info.function: Produces thin, watery (serous) saliva rich in amylase, which starts starch digestion; it contributes ~25 % of saliva, most of it during meals.
info.size: About 5.8 × 3.4 cm, 1–2 cm thick, 20–30 g
info.notes: Mumps swells the parotids painfully in front of the ears. Because the facial nerve runs through the gland, parotid surgery carries a risk of facial palsy, and parotid tumours (mostly benign pleomorphic adenomas) must be removed carefully.

info.description: The kneecap: a triangular sesamoid bone, apex down, embedded in the quadriceps tendon, with a ridged cartilage-covered back that runs in the femoral groove.
info.function: Increases the leverage of the quadriceps by about 30% and protects the front of the knee.
info.size: ≈ 4.5 cm tall, 4.5 cm wide, 2–2.5 cm thick
info.notes: Its posterior cartilage is the thickest in the body (up to 5 mm); anterior knee pain often arises here.

info.description: Thick hyaline cartilage on the back of the patella, divided by a vertical ridge into medial and lateral facets.
info.function: Glides in the femoral trochlear groove as the knee bends.
info.size: Up to 5 mm thick
info.notes: Softening of this cartilage (chondromalacia patellae) causes pain on stairs.

info.description: Strong flat band running from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity - the continuation of the quadriceps tendon below the patella (strictly a ligament, as it joins two bones).
info.function: Transfers the quadriceps pull to the tibia to extend the knee; tapping it elicits the knee-jerk reflex (L3-L4).
info.size: About 4-5 cm long, 2.5-3 cm wide and 5 mm thick.
info.notes: Its central third, with bone blocks, is a classic graft for ACL reconstruction; overload causes patellar tendinopathy ("jumper's knee").
