info.description: Flat quadrangular muscle from the pectineal line (pecten) of the superior pubic ramus to the pectineal line of the femur just below the lesser trochanter; it forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle.
info.function: Adducts and flexes the hip.
info.size: About 10-12 cm long and 4-5 cm wide.
info.notes: Often has a dual nerve supply (femoral and obturator); it lies directly behind the femoral vessels and femoral canal, the site of femoral hernias.

info.description: Large fan-shaped chest muscle arising from the medial half of the clavicle, the front of the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages; its fibres converge on a folded flat tendon inserting on the lateral lip of the intertubercular groove (crest of the greater tubercle) of the humerus.
info.function: Adducts and medially rotates the arm; the clavicular head flexes it, the sternocostal head pulls the raised arm down and forwards.
info.size: About 20 cm across, 1–1.5 cm thick; insertion tendon ~5 cm wide.
info.notes: Congenital absence of its sternocostal head is Poland syndrome; the muscle is often used as a pedicled flap in head-and-neck reconstruction.

info.description: Thin triangular muscle deep to pectoralis major, from the outer surfaces of ribs 3–5 near their costal cartilages up to the coracoid process of the scapula.
info.function: Draws the scapula forwards and downwards and steadies it; helps raise the ribs in forced inspiration.
info.size: About 12 cm long and 5 cm wide at its origin.
info.notes: A key surgical landmark: it divides the axillary artery into three parts and the axillary lymph nodes into levels I–III in breast-cancer surgery.

info.description: Arises mainly from C4 (with C3 and C5) in the neck, runs straight down on the front of the anterior scalene muscle, enters the chest between the subclavian artery and vein and descends over the fibrous pericardium in front of the lung root to the diaphragm. The left nerve crosses the aortic arch and runs over the left ventricle, piercing the diaphragm near the heart apex.
info.function: The only motor nerve to its half of the diaphragm (the main breathing muscle); also carries sensation from the central diaphragm, pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
info.size: About 2 mm thick; ~33 cm long
info.notes: Irritation under the diaphragm is felt as shoulder-tip pain (C4 dermatome). A paralysed phrenic nerve - after heart surgery, from a lung tumour or after an interscalene block - leaves one hemidiaphragm high on the chest X-ray.

info.description: Pear-shaped muscle arising from the front (pelvic) surface of the sacrum; it leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and inserts on the upper border of the greater trochanter.
info.function: Laterally rotates the extended hip, abducts the flexed hip and helps hold the femoral head in the acetabulum.
info.size: About 12 cm long, 3-4 cm wide at its origin.
info.notes: Landmark of the buttock: vessels and nerves are described as above or below it. The sciatic nerve passes beneath it (or through it in ~10-15 % of people) - the anatomical basis of "piriformis syndrome".

info.description: Pea-shaped sesamoid bone lying on the palmar face of the triquetrum within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.
info.function: Proximal-row carpal: adapts its position as the wrist bends so the hand moves smoothly on the forearm.
info.notes: Palpable at the base of the hypothenar eminence.

name: Left plantar arteries
latin: Arteriae plantares medialis et lateralis; arcus plantaris profundus

info.description: The terminal branches of the posterior tibial artery: the small medial plantar artery runs along the inner sole towards the big toe; the larger lateral plantar artery crosses the sole and curves medially as the deep plantar arch, which joins the dorsalis pedis.
info.function: Supply the muscles, skin and toes of the sole via plantar metatarsal and digital arteries.
info.size: Lateral plantar ~2 mm, medial ~1.5 mm diameter.
info.notes: The plantar arch lies deep between muscle layers, well protected from weight-bearing pressure.

info.description: The plantar aponeurosis: a thick, pearly fibrous sheet under the sole, from the medial tubercle of the calcaneus fanning out into five slips that attach to the toes via the plantar plates and flexor sheaths.
info.function: Ties the heel to the toes like a bowstring, supporting the longitudinal arch; it tightens when the toes extend at push-off (windlass mechanism).
info.size: About 20 cm long; 2-4 mm thick at the heel.
info.notes: Plantar fasciitis - heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning - is the commonest cause of heel pain in adults.

info.description: Small muscle with a 7-10 cm belly arising from the lateral supracondylar line of the femur just above the lateral head of gastrocnemius, continuing as a very long thin tendon.
info.function: Weakly assists knee flexion and plantarflexion; its many muscle spindles suggest a proprioceptive role.
info.size: Belly 7-10 cm long; tendon about 30 cm long and 3 mm wide.
info.notes: Absent in roughly one person in ten; because it is expendable its tendon is harvested as a free tendon graft.

info.description: The long, ribbon-like tendon of plantaris running down between gastrocnemius and soleus, along the medial edge of the calcaneal tendon, to the posterior calcaneus.
info.function: Transmits the small plantaris force to the heel.
info.size: About 30 cm long, 2-3 mm wide.
info.notes: A sudden "snap" felt in the calf was once blamed on plantaris rupture; ultrasound shows most such injuries are gastrocnemius tears.

info.description: Very thin broad muscle sheet in the superficial fascia of the neck, running from the fascia over the upper pectoralis major and deltoid, across the clavicle, up to the lower border of the mandible and the skin of the lower face.
info.function: Tenses the skin of the neck and pulls the corners of the mouth and the lower lip downwards (grimace of horror or strain).
info.size: About 15 cm long and under 2 mm thick.
info.notes: With age its medial edges separate into visible vertical "platysmal bands"; it is closed as a separate layer when suturing neck incisions.

info.description: Continues the femoral artery from the adductor hiatus through the diamond-shaped popliteal fossa behind the knee, lying deepest of the neurovascular structures, and divides at the lower border of popliteus into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
info.function: Supplies the knee joint (genicular arteries) and the calf muscles, and carries all blood to the leg and foot.
info.size: ~6–7 mm diameter; ~15–20 cm long.
info.notes: The popliteal pulse is hard to feel because the artery is deep; popliteal aneurysm is the commonest peripheral aneurysm, and knee dislocation can tear the artery.

info.description: Five to seven small nodes buried in the fat of the hollow behind the knee, around the popliteal vessels and at the end of the small saphenous vein. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the outer side of the foot and the calf (the small saphenous territory) and the deep tissues of the leg, sending lymph up along the femoral vessels to the deep inguinal nodes.
info.size: 5-7 nodes of 3-8 mm
info.notes: Rarely palpable; they enlarge with infections of the heel and lateral foot and with melanoma of the lower leg.

info.description: Formed at the lower border of popliteus by the venae comitantes of the tibial arteries; it ascends through the popliteal fossa between the popliteal artery and the tibial nerve, receives the small saphenous vein and becomes the femoral vein at the adductor hiatus.
info.function: Drains the leg, knee and foot.
info.size: ~7–10 mm diameter.
info.notes: A common site of deep vein thrombosis, checked by compression ultrasound behind the knee.

info.description: Thin triangular muscle forming the floor of the popliteal fossa: from a groove on the lateral femoral condyle (and the lateral meniscus) obliquely down to the back of the tibia above the soleal line.
info.function: "Unlocks" the fully extended knee by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia at the start of flexion, and pulls the lateral meniscus backwards.
info.size: About 8-10 cm long, triangular.
info.notes: Its tendon runs inside the knee joint capsule; popliteus tendon injuries are part of posterolateral corner knee injuries.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B10, supplying the posterior basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lower lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 3 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: Because each segment has its own airway and blood supply, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).

info.description: The posterior semicircular canal lies in a vertical plane parallel to the long axis of the petrous bone, the most posterior of the three, with its ampulla at the lower end.
info.function: Senses rotation in its plane: tilting the head toward the shoulder combined with pitch.
info.size: Radius about 3.2-4 mm; the longest canal, about 20 mm.
info.notes: The canal most often affected by benign positional vertigo, because loose otoconia settle into its lowest point.

info.description: The larger terminal branch of the popliteal artery; it descends in the deep posterior compartment of the calf and curves behind the medial malleolus (with tibialis posterior and the long flexor tendons and the tibial nerve) to divide under the flexor retinaculum into the medial and lateral plantar arteries. Shown with its fibular (peroneal) branch.
info.function: Supplies the calf muscles, the fibula (via the fibular artery) and the sole of the foot.
info.size: ~4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its pulse is felt midway between the medial malleolus and the heel; weak foot pulses are an early sign of peripheral arterial disease.

info.description: Flat square muscle deep in the lower forearm, stretching across from the lower quarter of the front of the ulna to that of the radius.
info.function: The prime mover of pronation; also binds the lower ends of radius and ulna together.
info.size: About 4–5 cm square and ~5 mm thick.
info.notes: It is lifted off the radius in the standard volar approach for plating distal radius fractures.

info.description: Two-headed muscle from the medial epicondyle (humeral head) and coronoid process (ulnar head) crossing the front of the forearm obliquely to the middle of the lateral surface of the radius.
info.function: Pronates the forearm and assists elbow flexion.
info.size: About 13 cm long.
info.notes: The median nerve passes between its two heads, where it can be compressed (pronator syndrome).

name: Left proximal phalanx of the big toe (hallux)

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the big toe (hallux): a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 33 mm long
info.notes: The big toe has only two phalanges and bears most push-off force; gout classically attacks its first joint.

name: Left proximal phalanx of the fourth toe

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the fourth toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 20 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left proximal phalanx of the index finger

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the index finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 31 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left proximal phalanx of the little finger

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the little finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 24 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left proximal phalanx of the little toe

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the little toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 17 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left proximal phalanx of the middle finger

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 34 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left proximal phalanx of the ring finger

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 31 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

name: Left proximal phalanx of the second toe

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the second toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 25 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left proximal phalanx of the third toe

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the third toe: a short tubular bone.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 23 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Left proximal phalanx of the thumb

info.description: Proximal phalanx of the thumb, a short long bone with a concave base and a pulley-shaped head.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 25 mm long
info.notes: Each finger has three phalanges but the thumb only two (14 per hand).

info.description: Long spindle-shaped muscle beside the lumbar spine, from the sides of the T12–L5 vertebral bodies, their discs and transverse processes, running down along the pelvic brim and under the inguinal ligament to join iliacus on the lesser trochanter of the femur.
info.function: The main flexor of the hip; also flexes the trunk on the thigh (sitting up) and bends the lumbar spine sideways.
info.size: About 30 cm long and up to 5 cm thick at the lower lumbar spine.
info.notes: A spinal abscess can track down its sheath to the groin; pain on hip extension ("psoas sign") suggests an inflamed retrocaecal appendix.

info.description: The anterior part of the hip bone: a body meeting its partner at the pubic symphysis, with superior and inferior rami framing the obturator foramen and a pubic tubercle for the inguinal ligament.
info.function: Completes the pelvic ring in front and anchors the adductors, rectus abdominis and inguinal ligament.
info.size: Body ≈ 3 × 2 cm; symphysis ≈ 4 cm tall
info.notes: The subpubic angle is wider in females (≈ 80–85°) than in males (≈ 50–60°).

info.description: Arises from S2-S4, leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine, re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen and runs forward in the pudendal (Alcock) canal on the wall of the ischioanal fossa, giving the inferior rectal, perineal and dorsal penile nerves.
info.function: Motor to the external anal and urethral sphincters and the perineal muscles; sensation from the anus, perineum and external genitalia - the nerve of continence and sexual sensation.
info.size: About 3 mm thick; ~15 cm long
info.notes: A pudendal block at the ischial spine is used in childbirth and perineal repairs; long-distance cyclists can compress it on the saddle, causing genital numbness.

info.description: The shorter branch: passes to the left in front of the descending aorta and arches over the left main bronchus into the hilum of the left lung; the ligamentum arteriosum links its origin to the aortic arch.
info.function: Carries deoxygenated blood to the left lung.
info.size: ~3 cm long before dividing, ~2 cm diameter.
info.notes: In the fetus the ductus arteriosus shunted blood from here into the aorta, bypassing the unexpanded lungs; it closes within days of birth.

info.description: The round opening in the centre of the iris. It looks black because light entering it is absorbed inside the eye.
info.function: Admits light to the lens and retina; its size adjusts to brightness, focusing distance and emotion.
info.size: 2-4 mm in daylight, up to 8 mm in darkness; shown here at 4 mm.
info.notes: Unequal or unreactive pupils are an urgent neurological sign (e.g. a third-nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure).

info.description: The outer, lens-shaped part of the lentiform nucleus, lying lateral to the globus pallidus and internal capsule and deep to the insula; strands of grey matter link it to the caudate across the capsule (the "striatum").
info.function: Receives motor and sensory cortex input and, with the caudate, shapes the scaling and smoothness of learned movements.
info.size: About 3 cm long, 2 cm high and 1 cm wide
info.notes: The lenticulostriate arteries supplying it are the commonest site of hypertensive brain haemorrhage.

info.description: Quadrilateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall between the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament below and the 12th rib and transverse processes of L1–L4 above, lateral to psoas and in front of erector spinae.
info.function: Bends the trunk to its own side, extends the lumbar spine and anchors the 12th rib during deep inspiration.
info.size: About 12 cm tall, 5–6 cm wide, 1–2 cm thick.
info.notes: A common hidden source of low-back pain; the kidney lies directly in front of it.

info.description: Common tendon of the four quadriceps heads, attaching to the base (upper border) of the patella; its superficial fibres continue over the patella into the patellar ligament.
info.function: Transmits the pull of the quadriceps across the knee via the patella, which acts as a pulley that increases its leverage.
info.size: About 3 cm wide, 7-8 mm thick and 4-5 cm long above the patella.
info.notes: Ruptures mainly in people over 40, often with diabetes, kidney disease or steroid use; the patient cannot straighten the knee against gravity.

info.description: The smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery, running down the lateral (thumb) side of the forearm under brachioradialis to the wrist, where it lies on the distal radius, then winds through the anatomical snuffbox into the palm to form the deep palmar arch.
info.function: Supplies the lateral forearm, the thumb and the deep palmar arch of the hand.
info.size: ~2–3 mm diameter; ~20 cm long.
info.notes: The radial pulse is felt just lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon; it is the usual route for coronary angiography and for arterial blood-gas samples.

info.description: The largest branch of the posterior cord. It winds around the back of the humerus in the spiral groove between the heads of triceps, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to reach the front of the lateral elbow, and there splits into a superficial sensory branch running down the lateral forearm to the back of the hand, and a deep branch that turns through supinator into the back of the forearm as the posterior interosseous nerve.
info.function: Motor to triceps, brachioradialis, supinator and every extensor of the wrist, fingers and thumb; sensation from the back of the arm and forearm and the thumb side of the back of the hand.
info.size: About 4 mm thick; ~55 cm long
info.notes: A mid-shaft humeral fracture, or sleeping with the arm hung over a chair ("Saturday night palsy"), damages it in the spiral groove and causes wrist drop; the triceps is usually spared because its branches arise higher.

info.description: The lateral (thumb-side) forearm bone: a disc-shaped head that spins against the capitulum and ulna, a bowed shaft, and a broad lower end that forms most of the wrist joint, ending in the styloid process.
info.function: Rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down (supination and pronation) and carries the hand.
info.size: ≈ 24 cm long; head ≈ 22 mm across
info.notes: The distal radius (Colles' fracture) is the most common fracture in adults, typically from a fall on an outstretched hand.

info.description: The only quadriceps head that crosses the hip: a spindle-shaped, bipennate muscle running straight down the front of the thigh from the anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head) and the rim above the acetabulum (reflected head) to the quadriceps tendon, patella and, via the patellar ligament, the tibial tuberosity.
info.function: Extends the knee and flexes the hip - the main kicking muscle.
info.size: About 35-40 cm long; belly up to 5 cm wide and 3 cm thick.
info.notes: The most frequently strained quadriceps muscle (sprinting, kicking) because it crosses two joints; in adolescents its origin can avulse from the AIIS.

info.description: Leaves the left vagus as it crosses the aortic arch, hooks under the arch behind the ligamentum arteriosum and climbs back up in the groove between the trachea and oesophagus to enter the larynx behind the thyroid gland.
info.function: Motor to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, and sensation below the vocal folds - it opens and closes the vocal cords.
info.size: About 1 mm thick, ~15 cm on the left (the right is ~5 cm shorter)
info.notes: Its detour into the chest lets a lung cancer or enlarged left atrium paralyse the left vocal cord, causing a hoarse voice; it is also the nerve thyroid surgeons must protect.

info.description: Leaves the side of the aorta at L1–L2 just below the superior mesenteric artery and runs to the left, behind the left renal vein, dividing near the hilum into segmental arteries.
info.function: Supplies the kidney (plus the adrenal gland and ureter); the kidneys receive ~20% of the cardiac output.
info.size: ~5–6 mm diameter; ~4–6 cm long.
info.notes: About 25–30% of people have an extra (accessory) renal artery; renal artery narrowing is a curable cause of high blood pressure.

info.description: Leaves the left kidney in front of the renal artery and crosses in front of the aorta, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, to enter the inferior vena cava. It receives the left gonadal and left adrenal veins.
info.function: Drains the left kidney, adrenal gland and gonad.
info.size: ~7.5 cm long (three times the right), ~1 cm diameter.
info.notes: Compression between the aorta and SMA ("nutcracker syndrome") can cause blood in the urine and, in men, a left-sided varicocele.

info.description: The thin light-sensitive neural layer lining the back of the eye from the optic disc to the scalloped ora serrata. It has ten layers, with rods and cones at the back and the ganglion cells whose axons form the optic nerve on the inner surface.
info.function: Converts the focused image into nerve signals and begins processing them (contrast, colour, motion) before sending them to the brain.
info.size: About 0.25 mm thick (0.1 mm at the fovea); ~120 million rods and 6 million cones; surface ~1100 mm2.
info.notes: A retinal detachment (flashes, floaters, a curtain over the vision) is an emergency; diabetes and high blood pressure can be seen directly in the retinal vessels.

info.description: Parallelogram-shaped sheet deep to trapezius, from the spinous processes of T2–T5 running down and laterally to the medial border of the scapula between the root of the spine and the inferior angle.
info.function: Retracts (braces back) the scapula, rotates the glenoid downwards and holds the scapula against the chest wall.
info.size: About 10 cm long, 5–6 cm wide, a few mm thick.
info.notes: Weakness (dorsal scapular nerve injury) lets the medial border of the scapula drift away from the ribs.

info.description: Small band above rhomboid major, from the lower ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7 and T1 to the medial border of the scapula at the root of its spine.
info.function: Retracts and elevates the scapula together with rhomboid major.
info.size: About 2 cm wide and 8 cm long.
info.notes: Often fused with rhomboid major; both are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve (C5).

info.description: The fenestra cochleae: a round opening at the base of the scala tympani, closed by a thin, flexible secondary tympanic membrane, lying below and behind the oval window in a small niche.
info.function: Bulges outward when the stapes pushes in, letting the incompressible inner-ear fluid move so the basilar membrane can vibrate.
info.size: About 2 mm in diameter; membrane about 70 micrometres thick.
info.notes: A route for delivering drugs to the inner ear and the usual entry point for cochlear-implant electrodes.

info.description: The S1 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the first sacral foramina. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the sacral plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the lateral border and sole of the foot and the little toe.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: the ankle-jerk reflex and standing on tiptoe; the L5/S1 disc is the other classic sciatica level.

info.description: The S2 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the second sacral foramina. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the sacral plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the back of the thigh and calf.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: S2-S4 carry the pelvic parasympathetic outflow for bladder emptying and erection ("S2, 3, 4 keeps the penis off the floor").

info.description: The S3 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the third sacral foramina. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the sacral plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the buttock crease and inner buttock.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Part of the saddle area; saddle numbness with urinary retention signals cauda equina syndrome - a surgical emergency.

info.description: The S4 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the fourth sacral foramina. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the sacral plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the skin around the anus.
info.size: About 1 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Supplies the pelvic floor and external anal sphincter; the anal wink reflex tests S2-S4.

info.description: The S5 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the sacral hiatus and the coccyx. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the small coccygeal plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the skin immediately around the anus.
info.size: About 1 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: A tiny nerve that joins S4 and the coccygeal nerve in the coccygeal plexus.

info.description: A smaller, rounded membranous sac in the front lower part of the vestibule, joined to the cochlear duct by the tiny ductus reuniens; its macula stands vertically on its medial wall.
info.function: Senses vertical linear acceleration (as in a lift) and head tilt in the sagittal plane.
info.size: About 2-3 mm across; macula about 2 mm.
info.notes: Its response to loud clicks is the basis of the cervical VEMP test of vestibular function.

info.description: A triangular sheet on the front of the piriformis muscle on the back wall of the pelvis, formed by the lumbosacral trunk (L4-L5) and the ventral rami of S1-S4. Its roots converge on the greater sciatic foramen, where the sciatic, gluteal, posterior femoral cutaneous and pudendal nerves leave the pelvis.
info.function: Supplies the buttock muscles, the back of the thigh, everything below the knee, the pelvic floor and perineum, and the S2-S4 parasympathetic outflow to the pelvic organs.
info.size: About 10 cm across; the roots converge into a band ~2 cm wide
info.notes: Pelvic fractures, sacral tumours or a difficult childbirth can stretch it; the S2-S4 parasympathetic branches that control bladder emptying and erection are protected during rectal-cancer surgery.

info.description: The longest muscle in the body: a narrow strap that spirals across the front of the thigh from the anterior superior iliac spine, down the inner side of the knee, to the upper medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
info.function: Flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip and flexes the knee - together producing the cross-legged "tailor's" position (sartor = tailor).
info.size: About 50 cm long, 4 cm wide and 1 cm thick.
info.notes: Forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal; the ASIS origin can be avulsed in adolescent sprinters.

info.description: The lower perilymph-filled channel of the cochlea, running from the apex (helicotrema) back to the round window, beneath the basilar membrane.
info.function: Returns the pressure wave to the round window; the pressure difference across the basilar membrane between the two scalae makes it vibrate.
info.size: Follows all 2.5 turns; widest (about 1 mm) at the base.
info.notes: The preferred channel for inserting a cochlear-implant electrode, entered through the round window.

info.description: The upper perilymph-filled channel of the cochlea, running from the oval window to the apex above the cochlear duct, from which it is separated by the very thin Reissner's (vestibular) membrane.
info.function: Carries the pressure wave from the stapes footplate toward the apex.
info.size: Follows all 2.5 turns; joins the scala tympani through the helicotrema at the apex.
info.notes: Perilymph resembles cerebrospinal fluid (sodium-rich) and communicates with the subarachnoid space through the cochlear aqueduct.

info.description: Lies deep to sternocleidomastoid, running from the anterior tubercles of the C3–C6 transverse processes to the scalene tubercle on the inner border of the first rib.
info.function: Elevates the first rib in forced inspiration and flexes and bends the neck to its side.
info.size: About 6 cm long and 1 cm wide.
info.notes: The phrenic nerve descends on its front; the subclavian artery and brachial plexus pass behind it, between it and scalenus medius — a narrow gap here causes thoracic outlet syndrome.

info.description: The largest scalene, from the posterior tubercles of the C2–C7 transverse processes to the upper surface of the first rib behind the groove for the subclavian artery.
info.function: Elevates the first rib and bends the neck to its own side.
info.size: About 8 cm long.
info.notes: The dorsal scapular nerve and roots of the long thoracic nerve pierce it.

info.description: The smallest and deepest scalene, from the posterior tubercles of the C4–C6 transverse processes to the outer surface of the second rib.
info.function: Elevates the second rib and bends the neck to its side.
info.size: About 6 cm long.
info.notes: Often fused with scalenus medius; it is the only scalene to reach the second rib.

info.description: Boat-shaped bone of the proximal row on the thumb side, bridging both carpal rows.
info.function: Proximal-row carpal: adapts its position as the wrist bends so the hand moves smoothly on the forearm.
info.notes: The most frequently fractured carpal bone; its blood supply enters distally, so the proximal pole can die (avascular necrosis).

info.description: The shoulder blade: a thin triangular plate over ribs 2–7 with a posterior spine ending in the acromion, a hook-like coracoid process in front and the shallow glenoid cavity for the humeral head.
info.function: Provides the socket of the shoulder joint and attachment for 17 muscles, gliding over the chest wall to extend the arm's reach.
info.size: ≈ 15–17 cm tall, 10 cm wide; glenoid ≈ 35 × 25 mm
info.notes: Winging of the scapula signals paralysis of serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve injury).

info.description: A circular channel running around the eye in the limbal sclera, just outside the trabecular meshwork of the drainage angle.
info.function: Collects aqueous humour filtered through the trabecular meshwork and passes it to the episcleral veins.
info.size: Ring ~12 mm across; channel ~0.2-0.3 mm wide.
info.notes: Resistance to outflow here raises eye pressure in open-angle glaucoma; minimally invasive glaucoma stents are placed into the canal.

info.description: The thickest and longest nerve in the body (L4-S3). It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, curves down under gluteus maximus between the greater trochanter and the ischial tuberosity, and descends in the middle of the back of the thigh deep to the hamstrings, dividing above the knee into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
info.function: Motor to the hamstrings and part of adductor magnus, and through its two divisions to every muscle below the knee; sensation from nearly all of the leg below the knee and the foot.
info.size: Up to 2 cm wide at its origin; ~50 cm from the pelvis to the knee
info.notes: Sciatica - pain shooting down the back of the leg - is usually caused by a disc pressing on its L5 or S1 root. Buttock injections go in the upper outer quadrant to avoid it.

info.description: The tough white outer coat of the eyeball, made of dense interwoven collagen. It covers the posterior five-sixths of the globe and is continuous in front with the cornea at the limbus and behind with the dural sheath of the optic nerve.
info.function: Protects the eye and keeps its shape against the intraocular pressure; the six extraocular muscles pull on it.
info.size: Globe 24 mm in diameter; sclera about 1 mm thick at the back, thinnest (0.3 mm) just behind the rectus insertions; anterior opening ~11-12 mm wide.
info.notes: A bluish sclera is seen in osteogenesis imperfecta (thin collagen lets the choroid show through); a yellow sclera is the first sign of jaundice.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the second rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 7 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: Long bone of the palm behind the index finger, with a base at the carpus, a slender shaft and a rounded head forming the knuckle.
info.function: Forms the skeleton of the palm and the knuckle joint of its finger.
info.size: ≈ 56 mm long
info.notes: The metacarpal heads are the knuckles seen when making a fist.

info.description: Long bone of the forefoot behind the second toe, with a wedge-shaped base, slender shaft and rounded head at the ball of the foot.
info.function: Forms a spoke of the foot's arches and a lever for walking.
info.size: ≈ 81 mm long
info.notes: The second metatarsal is the longest and the commonest site of "march" stress fractures.

info.description: The second rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T2 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T2 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 24 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: Deep medial hamstring with a flat, membrane-like upper tendon and a thick lower belly. It runs from the ischial tuberosity to the posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle, sending an expansion that forms the oblique popliteal ligament.
info.function: Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the leg.
info.size: About 40 cm long; belly about 6 cm wide in the lower thigh.
info.notes: The bursa between it and the medial head of gastrocnemius can distend into a Baker's (popliteal) cyst behind the knee.

info.description: Lobulated sac behind the bladder base, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens; it is really a single tube about 15 cm long folded on itself. Its duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct.
info.function: Secretes 60–70% of the semen volume: a thick, alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that fuels sperm.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 1–2 cm wide.
info.notes: Its secretion contains semenogelin, which makes semen clot briefly after ejaculation.

info.description: Superficial medial hamstring with a fleshy upper half and a long cord-like tendon. It arises from the ischial tuberosity with the biceps long head and inserts on the upper medial tibia (pes anserinus) behind gracilis.
info.function: Extends the hip, flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed knee.
info.size: About 45 cm long including a tendon of roughly 20 cm.
info.notes: Its tendon (often with gracilis) is the commonest graft used to reconstruct a torn anterior cruciate ligament.

info.description: Broad sheet on the side of the chest whose saw-toothed digitations arise from the outer surfaces of ribs 1–8; it wraps backwards around the chest wall, deep to the scapula, to the costal surface of its medial border, most fibres converging on the inferior angle.
info.function: Protracts the scapula (punching, pushing) and rotates it upwards so the arm can be raised above the head; holds the scapula flat against the ribs.
info.size: About 15 cm tall; each digitation 1–2 cm wide.
info.notes: Injury to its long thoracic nerve (for example during axillary surgery) produces a "winged scapula" when pushing against a wall.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the seventh rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 11 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The seventh rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T7 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T7 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 29 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the sixth rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 10 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The sixth rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T6 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T6 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 30 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: Begins at the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, passes behind the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve, ascends the middle of the back of the calf and pierces the deep fascia to drain into the popliteal vein behind the knee.
info.function: Drains the lateral foot and the back of the leg.
info.size: ~2–4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its close companion, the sural nerve, can be injured when it is stripped for varicose veins.

info.description: Broad flat muscle deep to gastrocnemius, named after the sole fish. It arises from the back of the fibular head and upper fibula, the soleal line of the tibia and a tendinous arch between them, and joins the calcaneal tendon; its fleshy fibres reach almost to the ankle and bulge on both sides of the tendon.
info.function: Plantarflexes the ankle; a tireless postural muscle that stops the body toppling forward at the ankle while standing.
info.size: About 30 cm long, 8-9 cm wide.
info.notes: Its large venous sinuses are emptied by contraction - the "calf muscle pump" or second heart; calf immobility is a major risk factor for deep vein thrombosis.

info.description: Medial and smallest column of the erector spinae, running between spinous processes from the upper lumbar to the upper thoracic and lower cervical spine.
info.function: Extends the thoracic and cervical spine.
info.size: About 30 cm long and ~1 cm wide.
info.notes: Lies against the spinous processes, where the paraspinal muscles are stripped in posterior spinal surgery.

info.description: The smallest skeletal muscle in the body, hidden inside the pyramidal eminence on the back wall of the middle ear; only its tendon emerges, to attach to the neck of the stapes.
info.function: Tilts the stapes to stiffen the ossicular chain: the acoustic reflex that protects the inner ear from loud sounds.
info.size: About 6 mm long and 1 mm wide.
info.notes: Paralysed in Bell's palsy (facial nerve, CN VII), causing hyperacusis: ordinary sounds seem uncomfortably loud.

info.description: The "stirrup": the innermost and smallest ossicle. Its head receives the incus; two slender crura (anterior and posterior) run down to an oval footplate that sits in the oval window, held by the annular ligament.
info.function: Pistons in the oval window, driving pressure waves into the perilymph of the inner ear.
info.size: About 3.3 mm long; footplate 3 x 1.4 mm; weight 3 mg, the smallest bone in the body.
info.notes: In otosclerosis new bone fixes the footplate, causing conductive hearing loss; a stapedectomy replaces it with a tiny piston prosthesis.

info.description: Strap muscle crossing the side of the neck obliquely, from the mastoid process and superior nuchal line down to two heads: a rounded tendinous sternal head on the manubrium and a flat fleshy clavicular head on the medial third of the clavicle.
info.function: Acting alone it turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head to the same side; both together flex the neck and help lift the thorax in forced inspiration.
info.size: About 16 cm long and 3–4 cm wide at mid-neck.
info.notes: Fibrosis of it in infancy causes congenital torticollis (wry neck); it divides the neck into the anterior and posterior triangles.

info.description: Arises directly from the aortic arch and arches laterally over the dome of the pleura and the first rib, passing behind the anterior scalene muscle; at the outer border of the first rib it becomes the axillary artery.
info.function: Supplies the arm and, through the vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical branches, the brain, chest wall and neck.
info.size: ~9 mm diameter; ~6–9 cm long.
info.notes: Narrowing near its origin can make the vertebral artery flow backwards when the arm is exercised ("subclavian steal").

info.description: Continues the axillary vein from the outer border of the first rib and runs medially over the rib in front of the anterior scalene muscle, beneath the clavicle, to join the internal jugular vein at the venous angle.
info.function: Drains the upper limb, and on the left receives lymph from the thoracic duct at its junction with the internal jugular vein.
info.size: ~1–2 cm diameter, ~3–4 cm long.
info.notes: Held open by fascial attachments, it is a classic site for central venous catheters placed just below the clavicle; repetitive overhead arm use can cause its thrombosis (Paget–Schroetter syndrome).

info.description: The smallest major salivary gland, an almond-shaped body lying in the floor of the mouth just under the mucosa, between the tongue and the inner surface of the jaw bone; the two glands almost touch behind the chin.
info.function: Secretes mainly thick mucous saliva through 8–20 tiny ducts (of Rivinus) that open along a ridge under the tongue, lubricating food and speech.
info.size: About 3.5–4 cm long, 1.5 cm tall, 3–4 g
info.notes: A blocked sublingual duct produces a ranula — a bluish, frog-belly swelling under the tongue.

info.description: A walnut-sized gland tucked under the jaw bone in the submandibular triangle of the neck, hooking around the back edge of the mylohyoid muscle. Its duct runs forward under the tongue to open beside the frenulum.
info.function: Supplies about 70 % of resting saliva — a mixed watery and mucous secretion that keeps the mouth wet between meals.
info.notes: Because its saliva is thick and its duct (Wharton's duct, ~5 cm) runs uphill, 80 % of salivary stones form here, causing painful swelling under the jaw at mealtimes.

info.description: Three to six nodes lying just under the lower border of the jaw, on and around the submandibular salivary gland. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the cheeks, nose, lips, gums, teeth, the front of the tongue and the floor of the mouth, sending their lymph on to the deep cervical chain.
info.size: 3-6 nodes of 5-10 mm
info.notes: The nodes most often felt as tender lumps under the jaw in dental abscesses, mouth ulcers and lip infections.

info.description: The largest rotator-cuff muscle: a triangular sheet filling the subscapular fossa on the rib-facing surface of the scapula, converging onto the lesser tubercle of the humerus in front of the shoulder joint.
info.function: Medially rotates the arm and prevents forward dislocation of the humeral head.
info.size: About 15 cm long; fan ~10 cm wide.
info.notes: Tested with the "lift-off" and "belly-press" tests; it glides on serratus anterior across the scapulothoracic space.

name: Left superficial palmar arch and digital arteries
latin: Arcus palmaris superficialis; arteriae digitales palmares

info.description: An arterial arcade in the palm, level with the outstretched thumb's web, formed mainly by the ulnar artery and completed by a branch of the radial artery; common palmar digital arteries run from it to the finger webs and divide into proper digital arteries along each finger.
info.function: Supplies the palm and the fingers (with the deep palmar arch as a parallel back-up).
info.size: Arch ~1.5 mm diameter; digital arteries ~1 mm.
info.notes: Lies just beneath the palmar aponeurosis, so deep palm cuts can bleed briskly from both ends because of the double supply.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B4, supplying the superior lingular bronchopulmonary segment of the left upper lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 2 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: The lingular segments correspond to the right middle lobe.

info.description: Superior nasal concha (turbinate): a scroll of thin bone covered by thick, vascular mucosa projecting from the lateral wall of the nasal cavity.
info.function: Increases the mucosal surface and creates turbulent airflow so inhaled air is warmed, humidified and filtered.
info.size: The smallest turbinate, part of the ethmoid, about 2 cm long; the posterior ethmoid cells drain beneath it and the sphenoid sinus opens above and behind it.
info.notes: Olfactory epithelium covers its upper surface, next to the cribriform plate.

info.description: The longest, thinnest eye muscle. Its belly runs forward along the upper inner orbital wall; its round tendon passes through a cartilage pulley (the trochlea) and turns back and outward under the superior rectus to fan out on the upper-outer back quarter of the globe.
info.function: Rotates the top of the eye inward (intorsion) and depresses and abducts it - most effective at looking down when the eye is turned in, as in reading or walking downstairs.
info.size: Belly ~40 mm, reflected tendon ~20 mm; the reflected part runs ~54 degrees to the visual axis.
info.notes: Its nerve, the trochlear (CN IV), is the thinnest and longest intracranial cranial nerve; a palsy gives vertical double vision that patients reduce by tilting the head away from the affected side.

info.description: A lentil-sized superior parathyroid gland embedded in the back of the thyroid lobe, one of four. Despite the name it has nothing to do with thyroid hormone; it is the body's calcium sensor.
info.function: Secretes parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium by releasing it from bone, reducing its loss in urine and activating vitamin D.
info.size: 6 × 4 × 2 mm, 30–50 mg each
info.notes: The superior glands are the more constant in position (behind the upper-middle lobe, near where the inferior thyroid artery crosses the recurrent laryngeal nerve). Removing all four during thyroid surgery causes tetany from low calcium within a day or two.

info.description: The superior left pulmonary vein leaves the upper part of the left lung hilum and runs a short course to open into the posterior wall of the left atrium.
info.function: Returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left side of the heart.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm diameter; 1–2 cm long outside the lung.
info.notes: Sleeves of atrial muscle extending into the pulmonary veins trigger most atrial fibrillation, the target of catheter "pulmonary vein isolation".

info.description: A flat strap muscle arising from the common tendinous ring at the orbit apex and running forward along the orbital wall to insert by a thin, broad, white tendon on the sclera in front of the equator.
info.function: Elevates the eye (mainly when it looks outward) and also turns it in and rotates it inward (intorsion).
info.size: ~42 mm long; inserts ~7.7 mm from the limbus, obliquely.
info.notes: Supplied by the superior division of CN III; it is tied to the levator by fascia, so the lid rises when we look up.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B6, supplying the superior bronchopulmonary segment of the left lower lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 3 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: The superior segment of the lower lobe is the commonest site of aspiration pneumonia in a patient lying on the back.

info.description: Deep curved sheet wrapping around the upper third of the radius, from the lateral epicondyle, radial collateral and annular ligaments and the supinator crest of the ulna.
info.function: Supinates the forearm (turns the palm up), especially with the elbow straight.
info.size: About 6 cm long.
info.notes: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes through it beneath the arcade of Frohse, a site of nerve entrapment.

info.description: Rotator-cuff muscle filling the supraspinous fossa above the spine of the scapula; its tendon runs under the acromion and over the top of the shoulder joint to the superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
info.function: Initiates abduction of the arm (first ~15°) and holds the humeral head in the glenoid.
info.size: About 12 cm long, up to 3 cm thick in the fossa; tendon ~2.5 cm wide.
info.notes: The most commonly torn rotator-cuff tendon; pinched under the acromion in impingement, giving a "painful arc" between about 60° and 120° of abduction.

info.description: A cutaneous nerve formed by the medial sural branch of the tibial nerve and a communicating branch from the common fibular nerve. It descends just under the skin down the back of the calf beside the small saphenous vein, passes behind the lateral malleolus and runs along the outer edge of the foot to the little toe.
info.function: Sensation from the lower back of the calf, the outer ankle and the lateral border of the foot.
info.size: About 2 mm thick; ~40 cm long
info.notes: Losing it only numbs a strip of the foot, so it is the standard donor for nerve grafts and the nerve biopsied to diagnose peripheral neuropathy.

info.description: A beaded nerve cord running the whole length of the spine beside the vertebral bodies, from the base of the skull to the coccyx, where the two trunks meet. Each bead is a sympathetic ganglion: three in the neck (superior, middle and cervicothoracic or stellate), eleven thoracic, four lumbar and four sacral; thin white and grey rami link them to the spinal nerves.
info.function: Distributes the "fight or flight" outflow: preganglionic fibres from cord segments T1-L2 enter through white rami, relay in the ganglia, and postganglionic fibres return through grey rami to every spinal nerve (sweat glands, blood vessels, hair muscles) or go directly to the head, heart and lungs.
info.size: About 45 cm long; ganglia 3-6 mm, the superior cervical ganglion 2.5-3 cm, the stellate ganglion ~1.5 cm
info.notes: Interrupting the cervical chain (apical lung tumour, carotid dissection, neck surgery) causes Horner syndrome - a drooping lid, small pupil and dry skin on that side of the face. Cutting the T2-T3 ganglia cures severe hand sweating.

info.description: The T1 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T1 and T2. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the brachial plexus (a small part forms the first intercostal nerve).
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the medial side of the arm and forearm.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Supplies the small muscles of the hand. An apical lung (Pancoast) tumour invading T1 and the sympathetic chain gives hand wasting with a Horner syndrome.

info.description: The T10 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T10 and T11. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 10th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin around the waist at the umbilicus.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: T10 at the umbilicus is a key sensory landmark; early appendicitis pain is felt here because the appendix shares T10 visceral afferents.

info.description: The T11 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T11 and T12. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 11th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin across the lower abdomen.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: With T12 it supplies the lower abdominal muscles; weakness pulls the umbilicus upward when the patient lifts the head (Beevor sign).

info.description: The T12 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T12 and L1. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the subcostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the lower abdomen and the skin above the pubis and the hip.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Its ventral ramus runs under the twelfth rib as the subcostal nerve, which can be irritated in kidney surgery through the flank.

info.description: The T2 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T2 and T3. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 2nd intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the armpit and inner upper arm.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Its intercostobrachial branch supplies the armpit and is often cut in axillary breast surgery, leaving the inner arm numb.

info.description: The T3 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T3 and T4. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 3rd intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin across the upper chest.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Shingles (herpes zoster) reactivates in a thoracic dorsal root ganglion more often than anywhere else, giving a painful blistering stripe along one dermatome.

info.description: The T4 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T4 and T5. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 4th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin around the chest at the level of the nipples.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: T4 at the nipple is the classic landmark for mapping the sensory level of a spinal cord injury.

info.description: The T5 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T5 and T6. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 5th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin around the chest below the nipples.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Its ventral ramus is the fifth intercostal nerve; the fourth to sixth are blocked for breast and chest-drain surgery.

info.description: A swelling on the dorsal (sensory) root of the T6 spinal nerve lying in the intervertebral foramen, just outside the dural sac, where the dorsal and ventral roots join. One of 31 pairs; three levels are shown as representatives.
info.function: Holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that bring touch, pain, temperature and position sense from its dermatome and muscles into the cord.
info.size: About 4-6 mm long
info.notes: The chickenpox virus lies dormant in dorsal root ganglia for decades and can reactivate as shingles, a painful rash confined to one dermatome.

info.description: The T6 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T6 and T7. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 6th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin around the lower chest.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Cord injuries at or above T6 risk autonomic dysreflexia - dangerous surges of blood pressure triggered by a full bladder or bowel.

info.description: The T7 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T7 and T8. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 7th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin at the level of the xiphoid process.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: T7 marks the xiphoid; lower intercostal nerves also supply the abdominal wall, so chest disease can mimic abdominal pain.

info.description: The T8 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T8 and T9. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 8th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin just below the rib margin.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: T7-T9 supply the upper abdominal wall; the upper abdominal reflex tests these segments.

info.description: The T9 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between T9 and T10. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which becomes the 9th intercostal nerve.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a band of skin across the upper abdomen.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: A T9 dermatome band crosses the upper abdomen halfway between xiphoid and umbilicus.

info.description: The ankle bone: a domed trochlea gripped by the malleoli above, a neck and a rounded head that fits the navicular.
info.function: Transmits the entire body weight from the tibia to the foot; no muscles attach to it.
info.size: ≈ 5.5 cm long
info.notes: Most of its surface is cartilage, so its blood supply is fragile and neck fractures risk avascular necrosis.

info.description: Left temporal bone: a thin squama on the side of the skull, the zygomatic process forming the back of the cheek arch, the mastoid process behind the ear, the styloid process and the dense petrous part housing the middle and inner ear.
info.function: Houses the organs of hearing and balance, forms the socket of the jaw joint and anchors the temporalis, masseter and sternocleidomastoid.
info.size: Squama ≈ 6 × 5 cm; mastoid ≈ 2.5 cm
info.notes: The pterion, where it meets the frontal, parietal and sphenoid, overlies the middle meningeal artery — a blow here can cause an epidural haematoma.

info.description: Lies below the lateral (Sylvian) fissure in the middle cranial fossa; its rounded temporal pole projects forward beneath the frontal lobe, and its medial part hides the hippocampus and amygdala.
info.function: Hearing (primary auditory cortex on the transverse temporal gyri), understanding language (Wernicke area, usually left), recognising objects and faces, and laying down new memories.
info.size: About 9-10 cm long from the temporal pole back to the occipital lobe
info.notes: The commonest source of focal epilepsy (mesial temporal sclerosis); seizures often begin with a rising stomach sensation, deja vu or a strange smell.

info.description: Fan-shaped muscle filling the temporal fossa on the side of the skull. Its fibres converge deep to the zygomatic arch onto a strong tendon inserting on the coronoid process and anterior border of the mandibular ramus.
info.function: Elevates the mandible (closes the jaw); its horizontal posterior fibres retract the jaw.
info.size: Fan about 10 cm across, up to 1.5 cm thick near the arch.
info.notes: Tension-type headache is often felt over it; it can be felt hardening at the temple when the teeth are clenched.

info.description: A thin fibrous sheath enveloping the globe from the optic nerve to just behind the limbus, separated from the sclera by the episcleral space and pierced by the tendons of the eye muscles.
info.function: Forms a socket in which the eye rotates smoothly, and gives rise to check ligaments and the suspensory ligament of Lockwood.
info.size: About 0.5-1 mm thick; fuses with the conjunctiva ~1.5 mm behind the limbus.
info.notes: Anaesthetic injected into the space beneath it (sub-Tenon block) numbs the eye for cataract surgery.

info.description: Short flat muscle enclosed between two layers of the fascia lata, running from the anterior iliac crest and ASIS to the iliotibial tract about a third of the way down the thigh.
info.function: Abducts, flexes and medially rotates the hip and tenses the iliotibial band to steady the extended knee.
info.size: About 15 cm long, 2-4 cm wide.
info.notes: Supplied by the superior gluteal nerve; a tight TFL/iliotibial band contributes to lateral hip and knee pain.

info.description: A small pennate muscle lying in a bony semicanal just above the Eustachian tube; its tendon turns sharply laterally around the cochleariform process to insert on the upper part of the malleus handle.
info.function: Pulls the malleus inward, tensing the eardrum and damping loud low-frequency sound and the noise of chewing.
info.size: About 20-25 mm long and 1.5 mm wide.
info.notes: Supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), unlike the stapedius, which is a facial-nerve muscle.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the tenth rib to the cartilage above, forming the costal margin.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 4 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The tenth rib, a false (vertebrochondral) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T10, its tubercle with the T10 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 24 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: Thick rounded muscle from the dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula, running up and laterally with latissimus dorsi to the medial lip of the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
info.function: Adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm.
info.size: About 12 cm long and 3–4 cm wide.
info.notes: Nicknamed "lat's little helper"; with teres minor and the long head of triceps it bounds the quadrangular and triangular spaces through which axillary vessels and nerves pass.

info.description: Narrow rotator-cuff muscle from the upper two-thirds of the lateral border of the scapula to the lowest facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.
info.function: Laterally rotates the arm and holds the humeral head in place.
info.size: About 10 cm long and 2 cm wide.
info.notes: Unlike the other posterior cuff muscles it is supplied by the axillary nerve.

info.description: A long, slender artery arising from the aorta just below the renal arteries; it descends on psoas behind the peritoneum, crosses the ureter, and passes through the inguinal canal in the spermatic cord to the testis.
info.function: Supplies the testis and epididymis.
info.size: ~1–2 mm diameter; very long (up to ~30 cm in men).
info.notes: The gonads develop high in the abdomen next to the kidneys and descend, dragging their arteries with them — hence the high origin from the aorta.

info.description: Ascends beside the gonadal artery on psoas, formed from the pampiniform plexus of the spermatic cord, and drains into the left renal vein at a right angle.
info.function: Drains the testis.
info.size: ~3–4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its right-angled entry into the left renal vein is one reason varicoceles are far more common on the left.

info.description: Oval gonad hanging in the scrotum on the spermatic cord, enclosed in the white fibrous tunica albuginea and divided into about 250 lobules packed with seminiferous tubules.
info.function: Produces sperm (about 100 million a day) and the hormone testosterone from its interstitial Leydig cells.
info.notes: Kept 2–3 °C below core temperature; the left usually hangs a little lower. An undescended testis raises the risk of infertility and cancer.

info.description: An egg-shaped mass of grey matter on each side of the third ventricle, with a swollen back end (pulvinar) and the lateral and medial geniculate bodies beneath it.
info.function: The relay and gatekeeper for almost all sensory information (except smell) and for motor loops on the way to the cortex; also important for arousal and attention.
info.size: About 3 cm long, 1.5-2 cm wide and 2 cm high
info.notes: A small thalamic stroke can cause loss of all sensation on the opposite side of the body, sometimes followed by severe burning pain (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome).

name: Left thenar muscles
latin: Eminentia thenaris (mm. abductor et flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis)

info.description: The fleshy ball of the thumb: abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis (with adductor pollicis deeper), from the flexor retinaculum, scaphoid and trapezium to the first metacarpal and base of the thumb's proximal phalanx.
info.function: Moves the thumb, above all in opposition — bringing the thumb pad onto the finger pads.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 3 cm wide.
info.notes: Wasting of the thenar eminence is a late sign of carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression).

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the third rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 8 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: Long bone of the palm behind the middle finger, with a base at the carpus, a slender shaft and a rounded head forming the knuckle.
info.function: Forms the skeleton of the palm and the knuckle joint of its finger.
info.size: ≈ 59 mm long
info.notes: The metacarpal heads are the knuckles seen when making a fist.

info.description: Long bone of the forefoot behind the third toe, with a wedge-shaped base, slender shaft and rounded head at the ball of the foot.
info.function: Forms a spoke of the foot's arches and a lever for walking.
info.size: ≈ 73 mm long
info.notes: Bunions (hallux valgus) develop at the first metatarsal head.

info.description: The third rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T3 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T3 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 27 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: The paler inner zone of each thymic lobule, surrounded by the dark, lymphocyte-packed cortex. It holds mature T cells, epithelial cells and Hassall's corpuscles, whorled keratinised bodies found nowhere else.
info.function: Site of negative selection: T cells that react against the body's own proteins are deleted here before release into the blood.
info.size: Each lobule 0.5-2 mm across; the medulla is continuous from lobule to lobule
info.notes: Medullary epithelial cells use the AIRE gene to display tissue-specific proteins (insulin, thyroglobulin...) to developing T cells; AIRE mutations cause autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1.

info.description: One of the two lobes of the butterfly-shaped thyroid, lying against the side of the windpipe just below the voice box. Its pointed upper pole rests on the thyroid cartilage and its rounded lower pole reaches the 5th–6th tracheal ring. It is packed with hormone-filled follicles.
info.function: Makes thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which set the metabolic rate of nearly every cell, plus calcitonin from its C cells, which lowers blood calcium.
info.size: Each lobe about 5 × 2.5 × 2 cm; whole gland 15–25 g
info.notes: The gland is bound to the larynx by fascia, so a thyroid lump moves up and down when the patient swallows — the classic bedside test. Enlargement (goitre) is usually due to iodine deficiency worldwide.

info.description: The shin bone: a broad upper end with two flat condyles (the tibial plateau) and the tibial tuberosity, a triangular shaft with a sharp anterior border just under the skin, and a lower end forming the medial malleolus.
info.function: Carries almost all the body weight from knee to ankle and forms the roof and inner wall of the ankle joint.
info.size: ≈ 41 cm long; plateau ≈ 7.5 cm wide
info.notes: Because its front lies directly under the skin, the tibia is the long bone most often broken open (compound fracture).

info.description: The larger division of the sciatic nerve. It runs straight down the middle of the popliteal fossa, passes under the fibrous arch of soleus, descends deep in the calf with the posterior tibial artery, curves behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves of the sole.
info.function: Motor to the calf muscles (pointing the foot and toes, inversion) and all the small muscles of the sole; sensation from the heel and the sole.
info.size: About 4 mm thick; ~45 cm from the knee to the ankle
info.notes: Tarsal tunnel syndrome - compression behind the medial malleolus - causes burning pain in the sole. Tibial nerve loss prevents standing on tiptoe and abolishes the ankle jerk.

info.description: The fleshy muscle just lateral to the shin, arising from the lateral tibial condyle, the upper two-thirds of the lateral tibia and the interosseous membrane.
info.function: Dorsiflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; lifts the forefoot clear of the ground during the swing phase of walking.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm long, 3-4 cm wide.
info.notes: Paralysis (e.g. common fibular nerve palsy) causes foot drop with a high-stepping gait; it is often involved in anterior "shin splints" and compartment syndrome.

info.description: Thick tendon crossing the front of the ankle, the most medial under the extensor retinacula, to the medial surface of the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.
info.function: Transmits dorsiflexion and inversion to the medial foot.
info.size: About 15 cm long, 6-7 mm diameter.
info.notes: Easily seen and felt in front of the ankle when the foot is dorsiflexed and inverted; spontaneous rupture occurs in older adults.

info.description: The deepest muscle of the back of the leg, arising from the interosseous membrane and adjoining tibia and fibula between flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus.
info.function: Inverts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle; the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm; total length with tendon about 35 cm.
info.notes: Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction is the commonest cause of adult-acquired flatfoot.

info.description: Tendon of tibialis posterior: it grooves the back of the medial malleolus, then runs forward under the spring ligament to the tuberosity of the navicular, with slips to the cuneiforms, cuboid and bases of metatarsals 2-4.
info.function: Pulls the foot into inversion and supports the arch from below.
info.size: About 15 cm long, 6 mm diameter.
info.notes: Degeneration where it rounds the medial malleolus (a zone of poor blood supply) leads to progressive collapse of the arch.

info.description: Keratin plates on the dorsal tips of the five toes; the big-toe nail is by far the largest.
info.function: Protect the tips of the toes and give counter-pressure to the toe pulp.
info.size: Big-toe nail ~15–18 mm wide; toenails grow only ~1–1.5 mm per month (12–18 months to regrow)
info.notes: Ingrown toenail (onychocryptosis) usually affects the big toe, promoted by tight shoes and cutting the nail edges too short.

info.description: Deepest flat abdominal muscle, with horizontal fibres running from the inner surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, the thoracolumbar fascia, the iliac crest and the lateral inguinal ligament forwards into an aponeurosis that ends in the linea alba.
