info.function: Acts like a corset, compressing the abdominal contents and stiffening the lumbar spine just before limb movements.
info.size: About 20 cm tall, 2–4 mm thick.
info.notes: The TAP (transversus abdominis plane) block places local anaesthetic between it and the internal oblique, where the lower intercostal nerves run.

info.description: Distal-row bone at the base of the thumb with a saddle-shaped joint for the first metacarpal.
info.function: Distal-row carpal: forms a rigid unit with the metacarpals and transmits grip forces to the forearm.
info.notes: Its saddle joint gives the thumb opposition; it is a common site of osteoarthritis.

info.description: Large flat kite-shaped muscle of the upper back and neck (the pair together forms a trapezium). It arises from the external occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line, the ligamentum nuchae and the spinous processes of C7–T12, and inserts on the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula.
info.function: Upper fibres elevate the shoulder (shrug) and extend the neck, middle fibres retract the scapula, lower fibres depress it; upper and lower parts together rotate the glenoid upwards for overhead reaching.
info.size: About 45 cm tall along the spine, up to ~1 cm thick in the neck.
info.notes: Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI), which can be injured in surgery of the posterior triangle of the neck, leaving a drooping shoulder; note the tendinous "diamond" at the neck–back junction.

info.description: Small wedge-shaped distal-row bone at the base of the index metacarpal.
info.function: Distal-row carpal: forms a rigid unit with the metacarpals and transmits grip forces to the forearm.
info.notes: The least commonly fractured carpal bone.

info.description: The only muscle on the back of the arm, with three heads: the long head from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, the lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial groove and the deep medial head from below it. They join a broad flat tendon on the olecranon of the ulna.
info.function: The main extensor of the elbow; the long head also extends and adducts the shoulder.
info.size: About 30 cm long; the bulkiest muscle of the arm.
info.notes: The radial nerve spirals between its lateral and medial heads in the radial groove, where humeral shaft fractures injure it (wrist drop); the triceps reflex tests C7.

info.description: A crescent-shaped sensory ganglion the size of a fingernail, lodged in a dural pocket (Meckel's cave) on the tip of the petrous temporal bone. It holds the cell bodies of the facial sensory neurons; its convex front edge gives off the three divisions.
info.function: Relay station equivalent to a dorsal root ganglion for the face: the first-order sensory neurons of touch, pain and temperature sit here.
info.size: About 15-20 x 5 mm
info.notes: The ganglion can be reached with a needle through the foramen ovale to inject or heat it for intractable trigeminal neuralgia; it is also where the chickenpox virus hides before shingles of the face.

info.description: The largest cranial nerve. Its thick sensory root and small motor root leave the side of the pons and run forward over the petrous ridge to the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion in Meckel's cave.
info.function: Sensation for the whole face, scalp to the vertex, cornea, teeth, mouth and the front two-thirds of the tongue; motor to the chewing muscles.
info.size: Sensory root about 4-5 mm wide; 1.5 cm to the ganglion
info.notes: Trigeminal neuralgia - lightning stabs of facial pain - is usually caused by a looping artery pressing on this root where it enters the pons.

info.description: Pyramidal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row.
info.function: Proximal-row carpal: adapts its position as the wrist bends so the hand moves smoothly on the forearm.
info.notes: Second most commonly fractured carpal, often as a dorsal chip.

name: Left trochlea of the superior oblique

info.description: A small U-shaped loop of fibrocartilage attached to the trochlear fossa of the frontal bone, just inside the upper inner orbital rim, lined by a synovial sheath.
info.function: Acts as a pulley that redirects the pull of the superior oblique tendon backward and outward.
info.size: ~4-6 mm long; lies about 17 mm medial and 17 mm above the eye centre, just behind the rim.
info.notes: Inflammation here (trochleitis) causes pain at the inner upper corner of the orbit on looking up; the Brown syndrome is a tight tendon-trochlea complex that limits elevation in adduction.

info.description: The thinnest cranial nerve and the only one to leave the back of the brainstem. It winds around the midbrain, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit to reach the superior oblique muscle.
info.function: Supplies the superior oblique, which turns the eye down and in and rotates it inward (intorsion) - essential for looking down stairs.
info.size: About 1 mm thick; the longest intracranial course (~7.5 cm)
info.notes: Its long, thin course makes it the cranial nerve most often damaged by closed head injury; patients tilt the head away from the weak side to fuse double images.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the twelfth rib (a short free tip).
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 1 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The twelfth rib, a floating rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T12, its tubercle with the T12 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 17 cm
info.notes: Floating ribs end free in the flank muscles and have no anterior attachment.

info.description: The medial (little-finger-side) forearm bone: a large hooked upper end (olecranon and coronoid process around the trochlear notch) that grips the humeral trochlea, tapering to a small head and styloid process at the wrist.
info.function: Forms the hinge of the elbow and the stable axis around which the radius rotates.
info.size: ≈ 25 cm long
info.notes: The olecranon is the point of the elbow; it is fractured by falls directly onto the elbow.

info.description: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery; it passes deep to the flexor muscles, descends along the medial (little-finger) side of the forearm with the ulnar nerve and crosses the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum beside the pisiform bone.
info.function: Supplies the medial forearm (including the common interosseous artery) and forms most of the superficial palmar arch.
info.size: ~3 mm diameter; ~23 cm long.
info.notes: The Allen test checks that the ulnar artery alone can supply the hand before the radial artery is cannulated or harvested for bypass grafts.

info.description: The main continuation of the medial cord. It runs down the medial arm, passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus (the "funny bone"), enters the forearm through flexor carpi ulnaris, runs under that muscle to the wrist and enters the hand through Guyon's canal beside the pisiform bone.
info.function: Motor to flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus and most small muscles of the hand (interossei, hypothenar muscles, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis); sensation from the little finger and half of the ring finger.
info.size: About 4 mm thick; ~65 cm from the axilla to the little finger
info.notes: Knocking the funny bone jolts this nerve against the epicondyle. Chronic compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist gives tingling in the little finger, a weak pinch (Froment sign) and eventually a claw hand.

info.description: A mobile fold of very thin skin over a layer of orbicularis muscle, a stiff tarsal plate and the palpebral conjunctiva. Its margin carries the lashes in front and the openings of the meibomian glands behind; a skin crease marks where the levator aponeurosis inserts.
info.function: Protects the cornea, spreads the tear film with every blink (15-20 per minute) and shuts out light during sleep.
info.size: Covers the top 1-2 mm of the cornea; crease ~8-10 mm above the margin; lid skin <1 mm thick, the thinnest in the body.
info.notes: A drooping upper lid (ptosis) can come from a stretched levator aponeurosis, a third-nerve palsy, Horner syndrome or myasthenia gravis.

info.description: Leaves the left main bronchus at the hilum and divides into an upper division (apicoposterior and anterior) and a lingular division.
info.function: Secondary (lobar) bronchus: conducts air to one lobe of the lung.
info.size: About 1–1.5 cm long, 8–10 mm wide.
info.notes: Lobar bronchi are the level at which the lung is removed in a lobectomy; their walls contain irregular cartilage plates instead of rings.

info.description: A plate of dense fibrous tissue that forms the skeleton of the upper lid, D-shaped and tallest in the middle. About 25-30 tall meibomian glands lie embedded in it vertically.
info.function: Keeps the lid stiff and curved to fit the globe; its glands secrete the oily layer of the tear film.
info.size: ~29 mm long, 10 mm tall centrally, 1 mm thick.
info.notes: A blocked meibomian gland forms a chalazion, a painless lump in the tarsus; everting the upper lid over the tarsus is how foreign bodies are found.

info.description: Muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis down along the front of psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, runs down the pelvic side wall and pierces the bladder base obliquely.
info.function: Moves urine to the bladder by peristaltic waves (1–5 per minute); its oblique course through the bladder wall acts as a one-way valve against reflux.
info.size: 25–30 cm long, 3–5 mm in diameter.
info.notes: Stones lodge at three narrowings: the pelviureteric junction, the pelvic brim and the vesicoureteric junction.

info.description: Slender muscular tube in the upper edge of the broad ligament running from the uterine corner (intramural part) through the narrow isthmus and the wide, curving ampulla to the funnel-shaped infundibulum over the ovary.
info.function: Catches the ovulated egg, is the usual site of fertilisation (ampulla) and carries the early embryo to the uterus over 3–4 days by cilia and peristalsis.
info.size: 10–12 cm long; lumen about 1 mm at the isthmus and up to 1 cm in the ampulla.
info.notes: The ampulla is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy; tying or removing the tubes gives permanent contraception.

info.description: An oblong membranous sac in the upper back part of the vestibule into which all three semicircular ducts open. On its floor lies a horizontal sensory patch (macula) covered by a gelatinous membrane studded with calcium-carbonate crystals, the otoconia.
info.function: Senses horizontal linear acceleration and tilt of the head relative to gravity.
info.size: About 3-4 mm long and 2 mm across.
info.notes: Otoconia that break loose and fall into the posterior semicircular canal cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), treated with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre.

info.description: The "wandering" nerve. From the jugular foramen it runs down the neck inside the carotid sheath behind the carotid artery and jugular vein, crosses the left side of the aortic arch (where it gives off the recurrent laryngeal nerve), passes behind the root of the left lung, spreads over the front of the oesophagus and enters the abdomen as the anterior vagal trunk onto the stomach.
info.function: Parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs and gut as far as the transverse colon; sensation from the larynx, airways and viscera; motor to the palate, pharynx and larynx (via the recurrent laryngeal).
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick in the neck; ~60 cm long
info.notes: Vagal stimulation slows the heart - the basis of carotid sinus massage and of fainting at the sight of blood. Its anterior gastric branches were once cut (vagotomy) to treat peptic ulcers.

info.description: Thick-walled muscular duct that continues from the tail of the epididymis, climbs in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal, hooks over the ureter and widens into the ampulla behind the bladder.
info.function: Propels sperm toward the ejaculatory duct by powerful peristalsis during ejaculation.
info.size: About 30–45 cm long and 2–3 mm thick, with a narrow lumen.
info.notes: It is the cord cut and tied in a vasectomy; it feels like a firm string in the upper scrotum.

info.description: Deepest head of the quadriceps, wrapped directly around the front and outer side of the femoral shaft beneath rectus femoris. It arises from the upper two-thirds of the anterior and lateral femur and inserts through the deep layer of the quadriceps tendon.
info.function: Extends the knee.
info.size: About 30 cm long, 1.5-2 cm thick.
info.notes: A small slip (articularis genus) lifts the suprapatellar bursa during extension; a "dead leg" contusion crushes it against the femur and can lead to myositis ossificans.

info.description: Largest head of the quadriceps, forming the bulk of the outer thigh. It arises from the greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the linea aspera, and inserts through the quadriceps tendon on the lateral border of the patella.
info.function: Extends the knee.
info.size: About 40 cm long and up to 8 cm wide; roughly 3 cm thick at mid-thigh.
info.notes: Common site for intramuscular injections in infants and for muscle biopsies; its lateral pull on the patella is balanced by vastus medialis.

info.description: The teardrop-shaped bulge above and inside the knee. It arises from the intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera; its lowest, almost horizontal fibres (vastus medialis obliquus) insert on the medial border of the patella and the quadriceps tendon.
info.function: Extends the knee and holds the patella medially in its groove during the last degrees of extension.
info.size: About 30 cm long; the teardrop is about 7 cm wide and 3 cm thick above the knee.
info.notes: Wastes quickly after knee injury or surgery; weakness of its oblique fibres is linked to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar maltracking.

info.description: The thick-walled, cone-shaped lower-left chamber of the heart. It forms the apex, the left border and most of the diaphragmatic (inferior) surface of the heart.
info.function: Pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and the entire systemic circulation.
info.size: Wall 8–12 mm thick (about three times the right ventricle); cavity ~120–150 mL at end-diastole; ejects ~70 mL per beat at rest.
info.notes: Generates systolic pressures of ~120 mmHg; its wall thickens with long-standing high blood pressure, and its ejection fraction (normally 55–70%) is the key measure of heart failure.

info.description: The first branch of the subclavian artery. It climbs through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1, winds backwards over the arch of the atlas, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and joins its partner at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
info.function: Supplies the spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum and the back of the cerebrum (posterior circulation).
info.size: ~3–4 mm diameter; the left is often larger.
info.notes: Can be torn (dissected) by sudden neck twisting, a cause of stroke in young adults; about 20% of brain blood flow comes through the two vertebral arteries.

info.description: The balance part of CN VIII: a superior division from the utricle and the anterior and lateral ampullae, and an inferior division from the saccule and the posterior ampulla. The cell bodies form Scarpa's ganglion in the internal acoustic meatus, where it joins the cochlear nerve.
info.function: Carries signals of head rotation, tilt and acceleration to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.
info.size: About 20,000 fibres.
info.notes: Vestibular neuritis, a viral inflammation of this nerve, causes days of severe spinning vertigo without hearing loss.

info.description: The central chamber of the bony labyrinth, between the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind, with the oval window in its lateral wall. It contains the two otolith organs, the utricle and the saccule.
info.function: Houses the gravity and linear-acceleration sensors and connects the cochlea to the semicircular canals.
info.size: About 4 mm wide, 5 mm long and 3 mm deep.
info.notes: Its medial wall borders the internal acoustic meatus, through which the vestibular nerves leave for the brainstem.

info.description: A short, thick sensory nerve that crosses the cerebellopontine angle from the brainstem to the internal acoustic meatus together with the facial nerve. Inside the temporal bone it splits into the cochlear nerve (hearing) and the vestibular nerve (balance).
info.function: Hearing from the cochlea and head position and motion from the utricle, saccule and semicircular canals.
info.size: About 3 mm thick, 2 cm from brainstem to meatus
info.notes: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) grows on its vestibular part in the meatus, causing slowly progressive one-sided deafness and tinnitus before it presses on the facial nerve and cerebellum.

info.description: A thin, glistening serous membrane that tightly covers the lung surface and dips into the fissures between the lobes.
info.function: Secretes and spreads pleural fluid so the lung glides smoothly against the chest wall during breathing.
info.size: A single layer of mesothelial cells on connective tissue, roughly 30–80 µm thick.
info.notes: The visceral pleura has no pain fibres; chest pain in pneumonia (pleurisy) starts only when inflammation reaches the parietal pleura.

info.description: The clear gel that fills the large cavity behind the lens (about 80% of the eye's volume). It is 99% water held in a mesh of collagen fibrils and hyaluronic acid, attached firmly at the ora serrata and optic disc.
info.function: Keeps the globe inflated, holds the retina in place and transmits light to it.
info.size: Volume ~4 ml; about 16-17 mm from lens to retina.
info.notes: With age it liquefies and can peel off the retina (posterior vitreous detachment), causing floaters; vitreous samples are used in forensic medicine.

info.description: The true vocal cord: a fold of mucosa over the vocal ligament and vocalis muscle, running from the inside of the thyroid angle to the arytenoid vocal process; the two folds bound the V-shaped rima glottidis.
info.function: Vibrates in the exhaled airstream to produce voice, and closes tightly to protect the airway and build pressure for a cough.
info.size: About 17–23 mm long in men and 12–17 mm in women; vibrates at ~100–150 Hz (men) and ~180–250 Hz (women) in speech.
info.notes: Swelling of its loose superficial layer (Reinke's oedema) in smokers deepens the voice; hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks warrants laryngoscopy.

name: Left zonular fibres (suspensory ligament of the lens)

info.description: Hundreds of fine, transparent fibrillin threads running from the ciliary processes and pars plana to the capsule in front of, at, and behind the lens equator.
info.function: Hold the lens centred behind the pupil and transmit the pull of the ciliary body: taut zonules flatten the lens for distance vision.
info.size: Each fibre 5-30 micrometres thick; the zonular gap spans ~0.5-2 mm.
info.notes: In Marfan syndrome (fibrillin defect) the zonules are weak and the lens often dislocates upward (ectopia lentis).

info.description: The cheekbone: a four-sided body forming the prominence of the cheek, with a frontal process up the lateral orbital rim and a temporal process joining the temporal bone to complete the zygomatic arch.
info.function: Shapes the cheek, forms the lateral wall and floor of the orbit and anchors the masseter.
info.size: ≈ 5 cm wide, 4 cm tall
info.notes: A "tripod" fracture separates it at its three sutures after a blow to the cheek.

info.description: Slender strap from the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone running down and forwards to the modiolus at the corner of the mouth.
info.function: Draws the angle of the mouth upwards and outwards — the principal smiling muscle.
info.size: About 6 cm long and 1 cm wide.
info.notes: A bifid zygomaticus major is thought to cause cheek dimples; a genuine (Duchenne) smile combines it with orbicularis oculi.

info.description: Tendinous midline seam from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis where the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles interlace; the umbilical ring lies in it.
info.function: Anchors the abdominal aponeuroses so the left and right muscles pull against each other.
info.size: About 1–2 cm wide above the umbilicus, only a few mm below it; ~31 cm long.
info.notes: Being nearly bloodless it is the classic route of midline laparotomy; defects in it cause epigastric and umbilical hernias.

info.description: A collection of lymphoid nodules covering the back third of the tongue (behind the V-shaped sulcus terminalis), giving it a cobblestone surface. Each nodule has a single crypt.
info.function: Forms the lower part of Waldeyer's ring of lymphoid tissue that guards the throat.
info.size: Spread over about 3 x 2 cm; individual nodules 1-3 mm
info.notes: It can enlarge and cause a sensation of a lump in the throat, or make intubation difficult; it is a rare site of carcinoma and lymphoma.

info.description: Small lobe on the posterior visceral surface, between the groove for the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum; its lower end forms the papillary process.
info.function: Hepatocytes make bile, process nutrients arriving in the portal vein, store glycogen and vitamins, build plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, and detoxify drugs and ammonia.
info.size: About 6 cm high and 3 cm wide (segment I).
info.notes: It drains straight into the IVC by its own short hepatic veins, so in Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein blockage) it is spared and enlarges.

info.description: Thinner, flattened lobe to the left of the falciform ligament, lying over the front of the stomach and reaching into the left upper abdomen under the heart.
info.function: Hepatocytes make bile, process nutrients arriving in the portal vein, store glycogen and vitamins, build plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, and detoxify drugs and ammonia.
info.size: About 2-3 cm thick, reaching about 8 cm left of the midline.
info.notes: Its left lateral segments (II and III) are the part most often donated by a living adult for a liver transplant into a child.

info.description: Rectangular area of the visceral surface in front of the porta hepatis, between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres.
info.function: Hepatocytes make bile, process nutrients arriving in the portal vein, store glycogen and vitamins, build plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, and detoxify drugs and ammonia.
info.size: About 5 cm long and 3 cm wide (segment IVb).
info.notes: Although classically counted with the right lobe, its blood supply and bile drainage come from the left branches, so functionally it belongs to the left liver.

info.description: Largest lobe of the liver, filling the right upper abdomen under the right dome of the diaphragm. Its smooth diaphragmatic surface is domed; below, it ends in a sharp inferior border, and its concave visceral surface carries impressions of the colon, right kidney, duodenum and the gallbladder fossa.
info.function: Hepatocytes make bile, process nutrients arriving in the portal vein, store glycogen and vitamins, build plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, and detoxify drugs and ammonia.
info.size: The whole liver weighs 1.4-1.6 kg and measures about 21-22 cm across and up to 15-17 cm front-to-back; the anatomical right lobe is about six times larger than the left.
info.notes: Surgeons divide the liver along Cantlie's line (gallbladder fossa to IVC) into functional right and left halves and 8 Couinaud segments, each with its own portal and biliary supply.

info.description: Hairpin loop dipping into the medulla: a thin descending limb, a thin ascending limb and a thick ascending limb that climbs back to touch its own glomerulus (macula densa).
info.function: Builds the salty medullary gradient by countercurrent multiplication: the descending limb lets water out, while the water-tight thick ascending limb pumps out NaCl (NKCC2 transporter).
info.size: Reaches up to ~1 cm into the medulla in juxtamedullary nephrons.
info.notes: Loop diuretics such as furosemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb and cause a large diuresis.

info.description: The longest tooth, with one pointed cusp and a single very long root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grips and tears food and guides the jaw in side-to-side movements.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 7.5 mm, 11.0 mm tall; root ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Canine roots can reach 17 mm; upper canines are often called eye teeth.

info.description: Chisel-shaped tooth with a thin cutting edge and a single conical root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 5.3 × 6.0 mm, 9.0 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: Central incisors erupt at about 7 years (lower first) and are the teeth most often chipped in falls.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and two roots (mesial and distal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 11.0 × 10.5 mm, 7.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: The first molar erupts at about 6 years (the "six-year molar") and is the key to the bite.

info.description: Transitional tooth with two cusps (buccal and lingual) on its biting surface and a single root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 7.7 mm, 8.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: First premolars are the teeth most often extracted to make space in orthodontics.

info.description: Chisel-shaped tooth with a thin cutting edge and a single conical root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 5.9 × 6.3 mm, 9.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: Upper lateral incisors are the most often congenitally missing teeth after wisdom teeth.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and two roots (mesial and distal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 10.5 × 10.0 mm, 7.0 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: The second molar erupts at about 12 years.

info.description: Transitional tooth with two cusps (buccal and lingual) on its biting surface and a single root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 8.0 mm, 8.0 mm tall; root ≈ 15 mm
info.notes: Premolars replace the deciduous molars at 10–12 years.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and two roots (mesial and distal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 10.0 × 9.5 mm, 7.0 mm tall; root ≈ 11 mm
info.notes: The wisdom tooth erupts at 17–25 years, if at all, and is often impacted.

info.description: The lower lip vermilion, fuller than the upper lip, resting on the lower incisors. The red colour comes from blood in capillaries seen through a thin, non-keratinised, hair-less epithelium.
info.function: Closes the mouth, seals around food and drink, shapes speech sounds and is one of the most touch-sensitive areas of the body.
info.size: Vermilion ~5 cm wide, ~10 mm high
info.notes: The lips lack sweat and sebaceous glands and so dry and crack easily; the vermilion border must be realigned exactly when repairing a cut lip or cleft lip.

info.description: The longest tooth, with one pointed cusp and a single very long root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grips and tears food and guides the jaw in side-to-side movements.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 7.5 mm, 11.0 mm tall; root ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Canine roots can reach 17 mm; upper canines are often called eye teeth.

info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 5.3 × 6.0 mm, 9.0 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: Central incisors erupt at about 7 years (lower first) and are the teeth most often chipped in falls.

info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 11.0 × 10.5 mm, 7.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: The first molar erupts at about 6 years (the "six-year molar") and is the key to the bite.

info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 7.7 mm, 8.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: First premolars are the teeth most often extracted to make space in orthodontics.

info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 5.9 × 6.3 mm, 9.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: Upper lateral incisors are the most often congenitally missing teeth after wisdom teeth.

info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 10.5 × 10.0 mm, 7.0 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: The second molar erupts at about 12 years.

info.description: Transitional tooth with two cusps (buccal and lingual) on its biting surface and a single root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 8.0 mm, 8.0 mm tall; root ≈ 15 mm
info.notes: Premolars replace the deciduous molars at 10–12 years.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and two roots (mesial and distal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 10.0 × 9.5 mm, 7.0 mm tall; root ≈ 11 mm
info.notes: The wisdom tooth erupts at 17–25 years, if at all, and is often impacted.

info.description: Main duct running the length of the pancreas from tail to head, collecting from side branches like a herringbone, then joining the common bile duct in the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater).
info.function: Carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum through the major duodenal papilla.
info.size: About 2 mm wide in the tail widening to 3-4 mm in the head.
info.notes: A gallstone stuck at the shared ampulla can block it and trigger acute pancreatitis.

info.description: S-shaped tube about 20 cm long running from the bladder neck through the prostate (prostatic part), the pelvic floor (membranous part, with the external sphincter) and the corpus spongiosum (spongy part) to the external meatus on the glans.
info.function: Carries urine from the bladder and semen from the ejaculatory ducts to the outside.
info.size: About 18–22 cm: prostatic ~3 cm, membranous ~1–2 cm, spongy ~15 cm.
info.notes: Its double curve and narrow membranous part make catheterisation harder in men; the prostatic part is squeezed by benign prostatic enlargement.

info.description: The lower jaw, the only freely movable skull bone: a U-shaped body carrying the 16 lower teeth and the chin, and two vertical rami ending in the coronoid process (for temporalis) and the condyle that sits in the temporomandibular joint in front of the ear.
info.function: Opens and closes the mouth for chewing and speech, driven by the masseter, temporalis and pterygoid muscles.
info.size: ≈ 10 cm between the angles; ramus ≈ 5–6 cm tall
info.notes: The strongest facial bone, yet often fractured in two places at once because it forms a ring with the skull base.

info.description: The broad upper part of the breastbone, with the jugular notch on top and notches for the clavicles and first ribs.
info.function: Anchors the clavicles (sternoclavicular joints) and the first two pairs of costal cartilages.
info.size: ≈ 50 mm wide, 60 mm tall, 12 mm thick
info.notes: Its joint with the sternal body forms the sternal angle (of Louis), the landmark for the 2nd rib and the tracheal bifurcation.

info.description: The upper jaw, formed by two maxillae fused in the midline: the alveolar arch holding the 16 upper teeth, the hard palate, the walls of the pear-shaped nasal aperture, the orbital floors and frontal processes beside the nose.
info.function: Holds the upper teeth, separates the mouth from the nose and forms the central face; it contains the large maxillary sinuses.
info.size: Dental arch ≈ 5.5 cm wide, 5 cm deep; alveolar process ≈ 2 cm tall
info.notes: Failure of the maxillary processes to fuse in the embryo causes cleft lip and palate.

info.description: Nodes clustered around the windpipe and its fork in the middle of the chest: right and left paratracheal chains, tracheobronchial nodes at the carina, subcarinal nodes beneath it and prevascular nodes in front of the great vessels behind the thymus. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Receive lymph from the lungs (via the hilar nodes), heart, oesophagus and thymus and pass it to the bronchomediastinal trunks.
info.size: About 20-40 nodes of 5-15 mm
info.notes: Spread of lung cancer to these nodes (N2 disease) usually rules out simple surgery. Symmetrical enlargement of hilar and mediastinal nodes on a chest X-ray is the classic picture of sarcoidosis.

info.description: The lowest part of the brainstem, tapering from the pons down to the foramen magnum where it becomes the spinal cord. Its front shows the two pyramids either side of the anterior median fissure and the oval olives lateral to them.
info.function: Vital centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure; reflexes of swallowing, coughing and vomiting; nuclei of cranial nerves IX-XII; and the crossing of the motor pyramids.
info.size: About 3 cm long; 1 cm wide below, 2 cm wide at the pons
info.notes: Most motor fibres cross here (decussation of the pyramids), so each side of the brain moves the opposite side of the body; tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and stops breathing.

info.description: A hundred or more nodes strung along the branches of the superior mesenteric artery inside the fan-shaped mesentery that suspends the small intestine, densest along its root, which runs obliquely from the upper left to the lower right of the abdomen. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Filter lymph from the small intestine, including fat-laden chyle absorbed after a meal, and pass it to the intestinal trunk and cisterna chyli.
info.size: 100-150 nodes of 3-10 mm
info.notes: Viral or Yersinia infection makes them swell and ache (mesenteric adenitis), the commonest mimic of appendicitis in children. They are a favoured site of lymphoma and of spread from bowel cancer.

info.description: Fan-shaped double fold of peritoneum suspending the jejunum and ileum from an oblique root on the posterior abdominal wall; its free border is pleated to match the full length of the intestine.
info.function: Carries the superior mesenteric vessels, lymphatics, lymph nodes and nerves to the small intestine while letting it move freely.
info.size: Root about 15 cm long, from the duodenojejunal flexure (left of L2) to the right sacroiliac joint; about 20 cm from root to gut edge.
info.notes: Reclassified as a single continuous organ in 2016; twisting of the gut around its narrow root (volvulus) cuts off the intestinal blood supply.

info.description: The top of the brainstem, passing through the notch of the tentorium. In front, two cerebral peduncles diverge upward with the interpeduncular fossa between them; behind, the tectum carries four bumps, the superior and inferior colliculi, and the cerebral aqueduct runs through its centre.
info.function: Carries the motor tracts from cortex to spinal cord, controls eye movements and pupil reflexes (oculomotor and trochlear nuclei), orients the eyes and head to sights and sounds, and contains the substantia nigra.
info.size: About 2 cm long and 2.5-3 cm wide across the peduncles
info.notes: Parkinson disease results from loss of the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra; a swollen temporal lobe herniating through the tentorial notch compresses the midbrain.

info.description: The left atrioventricular valve, with a large anterior leaflet (continuous with the aortic valve) and a long, narrow posterior leaflet, tethered by chordae tendineae to two papillary muscles.
info.function: Lets blood flow from the left atrium into the left ventricle and seals during systole so blood is ejected only into the aorta.
info.size: Annulus ~3 cm diameter (circumference ~9–10 cm); opening area 4–6 cm².
info.notes: Named for its resemblance to a bishop's mitre; mitral valve prolapse affects 2–3% of people, and rheumatic fever classically causes mitral stenosis.

info.description: Segments of fatty insulation wrapped around the axon in dozens of tight spiral layers - made by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves and by oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord.
info.function: Insulates the axon so the impulse jumps from gap to gap (saltatory conduction), raising conduction speed from about 1 m/s to as much as 120 m/s.
info.size: Each internode 0.2-2 mm long; sheath up to ~2 micrometres thick
info.notes: Multiple sclerosis strips myelin in the brain and cord; Guillain-Barre syndrome attacks peripheral myelin, causing rapidly ascending weakness.

info.description: The flexible lower two-thirds of the external nose: the midline septal cartilage, paired upper lateral cartilages under the dorsum, and paired U-shaped major alar cartilages that shape the tip and nostrils.
info.function: Give the nose its shape while keeping the nostrils open yet pliable; the alar cartilages stiffen the nasal valve against collapse when breathing in.
info.size: Septal cartilage about 3 × 3.5 cm and 2–4 mm thick; the alar domes lie ~4 mm under the skin of the tip.
info.notes: Rhinoplasty mainly reshapes these cartilages; a septal haematoma after injury can cut off the cartilage's blood supply and cause a "saddle nose".

info.description: The air passage from the nostrils (nares) to the choanae at the back of the nose, divided by the septum into two halves whose side walls carry the turbinates.
info.function: Warms, humidifies and filters inhaled air; the olfactory mucosa in its roof detects smell.
info.size: About 7–8 cm long and 5 cm high; each half is only 1–1.5 cm wide at the floor and a few mm at the roof.
info.notes: Air flows mainly through the middle meatus; the nasal cycle alternately congests each side every few hours.

info.description: The midline wall dividing the nasal cavity, formed by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above, the vomer below and the septal cartilage in front, all covered by vascular mucosa.
info.function: Separates the two nasal passages and supports the nasal dorsum.
info.size: About 7 cm long and 2–4 mm thick; most adults have a slight deviation to one side.
info.notes: Kiesselbach's plexus on the front of the septum (Little's area) is the source of about 90% of nosebleeds.

info.description: The upper part of the pharynx, behind the choanae and above the soft palate; the adenoid lies on its roof and the Eustachian tubes open on its side walls.
info.function: Air passage from the nose to the lower airway; the soft palate seals it off during swallowing.
info.size: About 2 cm high, 3–4 cm wide and 2 cm deep.
info.notes: Enlarged adenoids block nasal breathing and the Eustachian tubes in children; nasopharyngeal cancer often first shows as one-sided glue ear.

info.description: Short narrowed part joining the head to the body, lying in front of the portal vein and superior mesenteric vessels.
info.function: Its acinar cells secrete about 1.5 L a day of enzyme-rich alkaline juice into the duodenum; scattered islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
info.size: About 2 cm long.
info.notes: The portal vein forms right behind it (superior mesenteric + splenic veins), making it the key landmark in pancreatic surgery.

info.description: Schematic enlargement of one juxtamedullary nephron, the kidney's filtering unit: the renal corpuscle and convoluted tubules sit in the cortex (above the line), the loop of Henle and collecting duct run down into the medulla (below it).
info.function: Each nephron filters blood and then reabsorbs or secretes water and solutes along its tubule to produce urine.
info.size: About 1 million per kidney; a nephron tubule is 3–5 cm long but only ~50 µm wide (not drawn to one scale).
info.notes: About 85% of nephrons are cortical with short loops; the 15% juxtamedullary nephrons with long loops make concentrated urine possible.

info.description: Magnified model (about 1000x) of a multipolar neuron such as a spinal motor neuron. The cell body holds the nucleus, stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum (Nissl bodies) and the machinery that makes the proteins for the whole cell.
info.function: Keeps the entire neuron alive and integrates the signals arriving on its dendrites before firing an impulse from the axon hillock.
info.size: Real soma 20-100 micrometres across; shown ~16 mm
info.notes: Neurons do not divide, so a lost cell body is not replaced; motor neurone disease (ALS) destroys exactly these cells.

info.description: A large, round, pale nucleus with a prominent nucleolus sitting in the middle of the soma - the sign of a cell making proteins at a very high rate.
info.function: Stores the DNA and directs protein synthesis for the soma, dendrites and the whole length of the axon.
info.size: About 10-20 micrometres in reality
info.notes: When an axon is cut, the nucleus moves to the edge of the soma and the Nissl bodies dissolve (chromatolysis) as the cell switches to repair mode.

info.description: Short bare gaps between neighbouring myelin segments, where the axon membrane is exposed and densely packed with voltage-gated sodium channels.
info.function: Regenerate the action potential at each gap so the signal leaps from node to node instead of creeping along the whole membrane.
info.size: About 1 micrometre long, spaced 0.2-2 mm apart
info.notes: Local anaesthetics work by blocking the sodium channels at the nodes; blocking about three nodes in a row stops conduction completely.

info.description: The back and base of the skull: a curved squama with the external occipital protuberance, cupping the cerebellum, and a base pierced by the foramen magnum with the occipital condyles on either side.
info.function: Protects the occipital lobes and cerebellum and articulates with the atlas to carry the head.
info.size: Foramen magnum ≈ 35 × 30 mm at y 1.578
info.notes: The spinal cord becomes the medulla oblongata as it passes up through the foramen magnum.

info.description: Emerges from the interpeduncular fossa on the medial side of the cerebral peduncle, between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to four extraocular muscles and the eyelid levator; parasympathetic to the pupil.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 2.8 mm thick
info.notes: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses it here, giving a painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.

info.description: Oval opening in the muscular part of the diaphragm at about T10, formed by a sling of right-crus fibres, transmitting the oesophagus and the vagal trunks.
info.function: Its muscular sling acts as an external lower oesophageal sphincter, helping to prevent acid reflux.
info.size: About 2.5 × 1.5 cm.
info.notes: Widening of the hiatus lets the top of the stomach slide into the chest — a sliding hiatus hernia, a common cause of heartburn.

info.description: Where the olfactory tract, running back from the olfactory bulb under the frontal lobe, joins the brain at the olfactory trigone and splits into lateral and medial olfactory striae at the anterior perforated substance. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Carries smell to the olfactory cortex (uncus, amygdala) without a thalamic relay.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 2.2 mm thick
info.notes: Frontal meningiomas of the olfactory groove often present with a lost sense of smell on one side.

info.description: The X-shaped crossing of the two optic nerves on the floor of the brain, just above the pituitary gland and in front of the pituitary stalk.
info.function: Fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross here so that each optic tract carries the opposite visual field.
info.size: About 12 mm wide, 8 mm long, 4 mm thick
info.notes: A pituitary tumour growing upward presses on the crossing fibres first, producing loss of both outer (temporal) visual fields - bitemporal hemianopia.

info.description: The start of each optic tract at the back corner of the optic chiasm, where fibres from both eyes regroup before sweeping round the cerebral peduncle toward the lateral geniculate body. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Carries the opposite half of the visual field from both eyes.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 3.8 mm thick
info.notes: A pituitary tumour pressing up on the chiasm from below classically causes bitemporal hemianopia.

info.description: Sphincter of the mouth made of fibres encircling the lips; many are continuations of buccinator and the other lip muscles converging at the modioli, with small incisive slips to the maxilla and mandible.
info.function: Closes, purses and protrudes the lips (whistling, kissing) and keeps food in the mouth while chewing.
info.size: Ring about 6 cm wide and 3.5 cm tall around the oral fissure.
info.notes: Its fibres must be re-joined precisely in cleft-lip repair for normal lip movement and speech.

info.description: A slice through the cochlear duct magnified about 500 times, floating beside the left ear. The faint frame shows the boundaries of the scala media: the floor, the outer wall (stria vascularis) and the sloping Reissner's membrane above. On the basilar membrane sits the organ of Corti with its inner and outer hair cells, pillar cells, the tectorial membrane and the nerve fibres leaving toward the modiolus.
info.function: The site where mechanical vibration is converted into nerve impulses.
info.size: Real organ of Corti about 0.1-0.2 mm wide and 35 mm long along the spiral; here about 50 mm wide.
info.notes: Alfonso Corti described it in 1851; the hair cells number only about 15,500 per ear and do not regenerate in mammals.

info.description: The middle part of the pharynx, behind the mouth from the soft palate down to the tip of the epiglottis, containing the palatine and lingual tonsils.
info.function: Shared passage for air and food, where the breathing and swallowing pathways cross.
info.size: About 4–5 cm high and 4 cm wide.
info.notes: Loss of muscle tone here during sleep causes snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea; HPV now causes most oropharyngeal cancers in many countries.

info.description: Three rows of cylindrical cells, about 12,000 per ear, each topped by a V- or W-shaped bundle of stereocilia in three rows of graded height, the tallest embedded in the tectorial membrane.
info.function: The cochlear amplifier: the motor protein prestin makes them shorten and lengthen with each sound cycle, boosting basilar-membrane vibration up to a thousand-fold and sharpening frequency tuning.
info.size: Real length 25-70 micrometres (longer toward the apex), diameter about 8 micrometres.
info.notes: Their motion produces otoacoustic emissions, used to screen newborns for hearing. They are the first cells destroyed by loud noise and by ototoxic drugs such as gentamicin and cisplatin.

info.description: The islets of Langerhans: roughly a million microscopic clusters of hormone cells scattered through the pancreas, shown here as 42 exaggerated markers running from the head to the tail (where they are most numerous). They make up only 1–2 % of the organ, the rest being digestive-enzyme tissue.
info.function: Beta cells secrete insulin (lowers blood glucose), alpha cells glucagon (raises it), delta cells somatostatin and PP cells pancreatic polypeptide.
info.size: Each islet 0.1–0.2 mm across (markers here are ~2.5 mm); about 1–1.5 g of islet tissue in total
info.notes: Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of the beta cells; the islets are transplanted into the liver's portal vein in islet-cell transplantation.

info.description: Finger-like muscles projecting from the ventricular walls (two in the left ventricle, three in the right) whose tips send fine tendinous cords to the edges of the mitral and tricuspid leaflets.
info.function: Contract with the ventricle and keep the leaflets from turning inside-out (prolapsing) into the atria during systole.
info.size: Papillary muscles 1.5–3 cm long; chordae tendineae ~0.5–1 mm thick, 1–2 cm long.
info.notes: Rupture of a papillary muscle after a heart attack causes sudden severe mitral regurgitation; the chordae are nicknamed the "heart strings".

info.description: Lumbar nodes lying on the back wall of the abdomen on either side of the aorta and in front of and between the aorta and inferior vena cava, from the diaphragm down to where the aorta divides. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the kidneys, adrenals, ovaries and testes, the posterior abdominal wall and all the lymph arriving from the pelvis and legs via the iliac nodes; their efferents form the lumbar trunks.
info.size: 20-30 nodes of 5-15 mm
info.notes: Because the testes descend from the abdomen, testicular cancer spreads first to these nodes at the level of the kidneys, not to the groin.

info.description: A tough two-layered sac enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels: an outer fibrous layer fused to the diaphragm below and the great vessels above, lined by a serous layer that also covers the heart surface (epicardium).
info.function: Anchors the heart in the mediastinum, limits sudden over-filling and lets the heart beat almost frictionlessly on a film of fluid.
info.size: Wall ~1–2 mm thick; contains ~15–50 mL of serous fluid.
info.notes: Fluid or blood accumulating in the sac can compress the heart (cardiac tamponade); inflammation (pericarditis) causes sharp chest pain eased by leaning forward.

info.description: Oval, slightly raised plaques of lymphoid follicles in the wall of the last part of the small intestine (ileum), on the side away from the mesentery. Shown here as representative plaques on a loop of ileum in the lower right abdomen; the real gut carries 30-40 of them.
info.function: Sample the contents of the gut through specialised M cells and generate IgA-secreting plasma cells that protect the whole intestinal lining.
info.size: Each 2-5 cm long and 1-2 cm wide; 30-40 patches, most numerous in the terminal ileum
info.notes: Typhoid fever ulcerates the patches and can perforate the bowel; they are also the entry point for polio virus and for prions in variant CJD.

info.description: A ridged pad of lymphoid tissue in the roof and back wall of the nasopharynx, behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. Its free surface has 5-6 sagittal folds. It is prominent in children and normally regresses by the teenage years.
info.function: Traps and responds to antigens in the air breathed through the nose.
info.size: About 2-3 cm wide and 1-1.5 cm thick in a child
info.notes: Enlarged adenoids block the nose and the openings of the Eustachian tubes, causing mouth-breathing, snoring and "glue ear", the usual reasons for adenoidectomy.

info.description: Inner and outer pillar cells lean against each other to form the triangular tunnel of Corti between the inner and outer hair cells; with Deiters' cells they make up the stiff scaffold of the organ.
info.function: Give the organ of Corti its rigidity and form the reticular lamina at its surface through which the stereocilia project.
info.size: Real height about 50 micrometres.
info.notes: The tunnel is crossed by thin efferent nerve fibres running from the brainstem to the outer hair cells.

info.description: A tiny pine-cone-shaped gland in the exact midline of the brain, tucked behind the third ventricle above the midbrain. It receives light information from the eyes by a roundabout nerve route via the neck.
info.function: Secretes melatonin during darkness, setting the body's day–night (circadian) rhythm and, in childhood, restraining puberty.
info.size: 5–8 mm long, ~5 mm wide, 100–150 mg
info.notes: It calcifies with age ("brain sand"), so it shows up on skull X-rays and CT scans as a midline marker — a shifted pineal was once a classic sign of a mass pushing the brain sideways.

info.description: A thin funnel of nerve fibres and portal blood vessels that hangs the pituitary from the floor of the hypothalamus (the median eminence), passing through a hole in the diaphragma sellae.
info.function: Carries hypothalamic axons to the posterior lobe and the hypophyseal portal veins that deliver releasing hormones to the anterior lobe.
info.size: About 8–10 mm long, 2–3 mm in diameter
info.notes: Anything that compresses the stalk (tumour, surgery, head injury) interrupts the dopamine brake on prolactin: prolactin rises while every other anterior hormone falls — the "stalk effect".

info.description: The bulging middle part of the brainstem, lying on the clivus in front of the cerebellum. Transverse fibres wrap its front and sweep back on each side as the thick middle cerebellar peduncles; the basilar artery runs in the groove down its midline.
info.function: Relays signals from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum, houses the nuclei of cranial nerves V-VIII and helps control breathing rhythm and sleep (REM).
info.size: About 2.5 cm long, 3-3.5 cm wide
info.notes: A stroke in the ventral pons can cause locked-in syndrome: complete paralysis with consciousness and vertical eye movements preserved.

info.description: The rear quarter of the pituitary. It is not a gland in its own right but a bundle of nerve endings: axons of hypothalamic neurons run down the stalk and end here beside capillaries.
info.function: Stores and releases oxytocin (uterine contraction, milk let-down) and vasopressin/ADH (water retention by the kidney), both made in the hypothalamus.
info.size: About 4–6 mm across, ~20 % of the gland
info.notes: Damage to the posterior lobe or stalk causes central diabetes insipidus — the kidneys cannot concentrate urine and the patient may pass 10–15 litres a day.

name: Postsynaptic dendrite of the next neuron

info.description: A segment of a dendrite belonging to the next neuron in the chain, with small spines; a receptor-rich postsynaptic density lies under each bouton.
info.function: Receives the neurotransmitter and turns it back into an electrical signal - an excitatory or inhibitory postsynaptic potential.
info.size: About 1-2 micrometres thick in reality
info.notes: A single cortical neuron receives around 10 000 synapses; strengthening or weakening individual synapses (synaptic plasticity) is the cellular basis of memory.

info.description: Walnut-sized fibromuscular gland just below the bladder neck that encircles the first part of the urethra; it has transition, central and peripheral zones and is pierced by the two ejaculatory ducts.
info.function: Adds a thin, slightly acidic fluid rich in PSA and zinc that makes up about 20–30% of semen and helps liquefy it.
info.size: About 4 × 3 × 2.5 cm, 20–25 g in a young adult.
info.notes: Benign enlargement of the transition zone squeezes the urethra in older men; most cancers arise in the peripheral zone, which can be felt through the rectum.

info.description: Longest part of the tubule: a coiled segment near its own corpuscle, then a straight part heading into the medulla, lined by cube-shaped cells with a dense brush border of microvilli.
info.function: Reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered salt and water and almost all glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate, and secretes drugs and organic acids.
info.size: About 14 mm long, 50–60 µm across.
info.notes: Glucose spills into the urine once its transporters saturate (blood glucose ~10 mmol/L); SGLT2-inhibitor drugs block glucose uptake here.

info.description: Fibrocartilaginous disc joining the two pubic bones in the midline.
info.function: Allows slight movement and absorbs stress in the pelvic ring.
info.size: ≈ 4 cm tall, 4 mm wide
info.notes: Pregnancy hormones (relaxin) loosen it, widening the pelvis slightly for childbirth.

info.description: Branch of the pulmonary artery that runs beside the bronchiole and divides with it to feed the alveolar capillaries; shown blue because it carries deoxygenated blood.
info.function: Delivers blood from the right ventricle to the gas-exchange surface.
info.size: Real pulmonary arterioles are ~15–100 µm in diameter.
info.notes: Unlike systemic arterioles, pulmonary arterioles constrict when alveolar oxygen is low (hypoxic vasoconstriction), diverting blood to well-ventilated lung.

info.description: A short, wide trunk rising from the conus arteriosus of the right ventricle, in front of and then to the left of the ascending aorta, dividing under the aortic arch into right and left pulmonary arteries.
info.function: Carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
info.size: ~5 cm long, ~2.5–3 cm diameter (normally under 2.9 cm on CT).
info.notes: With its branches it is the only adult artery carrying deoxygenated blood; a clot straddling the bifurcation is a "saddle" pulmonary embolus.

info.description: Three thin semilunar cusps (anterior, left and right) at the top of the right ventricular outflow tract, the most anterior and superior of the four valves.
info.function: Lets the right ventricle eject into the pulmonary trunk and prevents back-flow during diastole.
info.size: Annulus ~20–25 mm; cusps thinner than the aortic ones because pulmonary pressures are ~1/5 of systemic.
info.notes: Heard best in the left 2nd intercostal space; the pulmonary component of S2 normally splits from the aortic one on inspiration.

info.description: Thick ring of circular smooth muscle at the outlet of the stomach, felt as a firm ridge between the antrum and the duodenum.
info.function: Meters chyme into the duodenum a few millilitres at a time and limits reflux of bile back into the stomach.
info.size: Ring about 2-3 cm across; the muscle is about 0.5 cm thick.
info.notes: In infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis the muscle thickens, causing projectile vomiting at 2-8 weeks of age; it is cured by splitting the muscle (pyloromyotomy).

info.description: Final segment of the large intestine, following the curve of the sacrum and widening below into the rectal ampulla; it has no haustra because the taeniae spread into a continuous muscle coat.
info.function: Holds faeces before defecation; stretch receptors in its wall trigger the urge to defecate.
info.size: About 12-15 cm long; the ampulla can widen to about 5 cm.
info.notes: Three transverse rectal folds (Houston's valves) project into it; a finger in the rectum can feel the prostate or cervix through its front wall.

info.description: Paired vertical strap muscles either side of the linea alba, running from the pubic crest and symphysis up to the xiphoid process and costal cartilages 5–7. Three tendinous intersections divide each strap into the segments of the "six-pack".
info.function: Flexes the lumbar spine (sit-up), tenses the abdominal wall and raises intra-abdominal pressure.
info.size: About 30 cm long; each strap ~8 cm wide above, ~3 cm at the pubis, ~1 cm thick.
info.notes: Rectus diastasis (separation at the linea alba) is common after pregnancy; the anterior rectus sheath is omitted here to show the muscle.

info.description: Minor calyces are cups that clasp each renal papilla; two or three of them join into each of two or three major calyces, which unite to form the renal pelvis.
info.function: Collect urine dripping from the papillary ducts and start the peristaltic waves that drive it toward the ureter.
info.size: 7–14 minor calyces (8 shown) and 2–3 major calyces per kidney.
info.notes: A "staghorn" calculus is a branched stone that fills the pelvis and calyces like a cast.

info.description: Outer granular zone of the kidney, about 1 cm thick, containing the glomeruli and convoluted tubules; it dips between the pyramids as the renal columns (of Bertin).
info.function: Site of blood filtration in the renal corpuscles and of most tubular reabsorption; receives about 90% of renal blood flow.
info.size: About 1 cm thick beneath the capsule.
info.notes: Shown as the posterior half of a coronal section so the medulla and collecting system are visible.

info.description: Funnel-shaped expansion of the upper ureter lying in the renal sinus, formed by the union of the major calyces and emerging through the hilum behind the renal vessels.
info.function: Gathers urine from the calyces and funnels it into the ureter.
info.size: Holds about 5–10 mL; narrows to 2–3 mm at the pelviureteric junction.
info.notes: The pelviureteric junction is the first of the three narrowings where kidney stones tend to lodge.

info.description: Cone-shaped masses of the renal medulla with their bases toward the cortex and their apices (papillae) pointing into the minor calyces at the hilum; their striped look comes from parallel tubules and vessels.
info.function: Contain the loops of Henle, vasa recta and collecting ducts that build the medullary salt gradient and concentrate the urine.
info.size: 8–18 per kidney (8 shown), each about 2.5 cm tall.
info.notes: Renal papillary necrosis (analgesic abuse, diabetes, sickle-cell disease) kills the papillary tips.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 10th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 10th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: The tenth thoracic dermatome encircles the body at the umbilicus.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 11th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 11th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 30-35 cm long
info.notes: The last intercostal nerve; below it runs the subcostal nerve (T12). Transverse abdominal incisions spare these segmental nerves better than vertical ones.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 1st thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 1st rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 17-22 cm long
info.notes: The first intercostal nerve is tiny because most of T1 goes up into the brachial plexus; it has no anterior cutaneous branch.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 2nd thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 2nd rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 22-27 cm long
info.notes: Its lateral cutaneous branch, the intercostobrachial nerve, crosses the armpit to the inner arm and is commonly cut during axillary lymph-node surgery.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 3rd thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 3rd rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 25-30 cm long
info.notes: An intercostal nerve block is given just below the lower edge of the rib, where the nerve lies under the intercostal vein and artery.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 4th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 4th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 27-32 cm long
info.notes: Supplies the skin at the nipple (T4 dermatome) - the landmark used to map the level of a spinal-cord injury.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 5th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 5th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 29-34 cm long
info.notes: Chest drains are pushed in just ABOVE a rib so that the needle misses this nerve and its vessels in the groove below the rib above.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 6th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 6th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, ending beside the sternum as an anterior cutaneous branch.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 30-35 cm long
info.notes: Shingles most often erupts along a mid-thoracic intercostal nerve as a one-sided painful band of blisters that stops at the midline.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 7th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 7th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: The seventh to eleventh nerves continue into the abdominal wall (thoracoabdominal nerves), so lower-lobe pneumonia can present as abdominal pain.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 8th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 8th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: Supplies the upper rectus abdominis; cutting it in an upper abdominal incision weakens the muscle segment below.

info.description: The ventral ramus of the 9th thoracic nerve. It runs round the chest in the costal groove on the underside of the 9th rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and below the intercostal vein and artery, then leaves the costal margin to run forward between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis to the rectus sheath.
info.function: Motor to the intercostal muscles and the anterior abdominal wall; sensation from a band of skin (lateral and anterior cutaneous branches) and from the parietal pleura and peritoneum.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; 31-36 cm long
info.notes: Anterior cutaneous branches can become trapped where they pierce the rectus sheath (ACNES), a cause of chronic abdominal-wall pain.

info.description: A slender nerve that leaves the junction of the pons and medulla, climbs the clivus inside the dura, bends sharply over the petrous apex and runs through the middle of the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery to the orbit.
info.function: Supplies only the lateral rectus, which turns the eye outward (abduction).
info.size: About 1-1.5 mm thick; ~4 cm intracranial course
info.notes: Its long climb up the clivus makes it vulnerable to any rise in intracranial pressure: a sixth-nerve palsy (eye cannot look outward, horizontal double vision) is a classic "false localising sign".

info.description: Forms the soft medial border of the sole, from the medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and flexor retinaculum to the medial side of the base of the great toe's proximal phalanx.
info.function: Abducts and flexes the great toe and helps support the medial arch.
info.size: About 12-14 cm long.
info.notes: The plantar nerves and vessels pass deep to it - it can compress them in tarsal tunnel syndrome; it is often weak in hallux valgus (bunions).

info.description: Formed mainly by a spinal root that rises from the upper five cervical cord segments, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and leaves again through the jugular foramen. It then runs down and back across the side of the neck, piercing the sternocleidomastoid and crossing the posterior triangle to the trapezius.
info.function: Motor to the sternocleidomastoid (turns the head) and trapezius (shrugs the shoulder and rotates the shoulder blade).
info.size: About 1.5 mm thick; ~12 cm from foramen magnum to trapezius
info.notes: Its superficial course through the posterior triangle makes it the nerve most often injured in lymph-node biopsies of the neck, leaving a dropped shoulder and difficulty lifting the arm.

info.description: Deep cup-shaped socket on the outer hip bone, formed where the ilium, ischium and pubis fuse (the triradiate cartilage in children).
info.function: Holds the femoral head in the hip joint, facing outward, downward and forward.
info.size: ≈ 5–5.5 cm across, 2.5–3 cm deep
info.notes: Shallow acetabula (developmental dysplasia of the hip) are screened for in newborns.

info.description: The calcaneal tendon, thickest and strongest tendon in the body, formed by the union of gastrocnemius and soleus and inserting on the middle of the back of the calcaneus.
info.function: Transmits the force of the triceps surae to plantarflex the foot in walking, running and jumping - loads of several times body weight.
info.size: About 15 cm long; about 1.5 cm wide and 6 mm thick at its narrowest.
info.notes: Usually ruptures 2-6 cm above its insertion where the blood supply is poorest; the Thompson (calf-squeeze) test detects a complete tear.

info.description: Short triangular adductor lying behind pectineus and adductor longus, from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis to the upper third of the linea aspera.
info.function: Adducts the hip and helps flex it.
info.size: About 12-15 cm long.
info.notes: The obturator nerve divides around it - the anterior division runs in front of it and the posterior division behind it.

info.description: Triangular fan arising by a narrow tendon from the body of the pubis just below the pubic tubercle and widening to insert on the middle third of the linea aspera. The most anterior adductor; its medial border bounds the femoral triangle.
info.function: Adducts and flexes the hip and assists medial rotation.
info.size: About 20-25 cm long and up to 6 cm wide.
info.notes: Its tendinous origin is the usual site of a "groin strain" in football, ice hockey and other kicking or cutting sports.

info.description: The largest adductor: a huge triangular sheet from the inferior pubic ramus, ischial ramus and ischial tuberosity to the whole length of the linea aspera (adductor part) and the adductor tubercle above the medial femoral condyle (hamstring part).
info.function: Adducts the hip; its adductor part also flexes and its hamstring part extends the hip.
info.size: About 30 cm long and up to 15 cm wide.
info.notes: The adductor hiatus in its lower tendon lets the femoral vessels pass to the back of the knee, where they become the popliteal vessels; dual nerve supply (obturator and tibial).

info.description: The thick yellow outer layer of the adrenal, about nine-tenths of the gland by weight. It has three zones from outside in: glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis, each making a different class of steroid from cholesterol.
info.function: Aldosterone (zona glomerulosa), cortisol (zona fasciculata) and DHEA/androgens (zona reticularis).
info.size: 1–2 mm thick shell around the medulla
info.notes: Too much cortisol (Cushing's syndrome) gives a moon face, central obesity, thin skin and diabetes; too much aldosterone (Conn's syndrome) is a common curable cause of high blood pressure.

info.description: A pyramid-shaped gland perched on the top of the right kidney, wedged between the liver, the inferior vena cava and the diaphragm. Shown with a wedge cut away to reveal its outer cortex and inner medulla. Its thin fibrous capsule is what you see here.
info.function: The capsule binds the cortex and medulla into one organ and carries the dozens of small arteries that pierce it from the aorta, phrenic and renal arteries.
info.size: About 3 × 3.5 × 1 cm, 4–5 g
info.notes: The right adrenal vein is only a few millimetres long and enters the vena cava directly, which makes right adrenal surgery bloodier than the left.

info.description: The dark red-brown core of the adrenal, a modified sympathetic ganglion whose chromaffin cells pour hormones straight into the blood instead of onto a nerve target.
info.function: Releases adrenaline (≈80 %) and noradrenaline within seconds of sympathetic stimulation — faster heart, dilated airways, mobilised glucose.
info.size: A central plate a few millimetres thick, ~10 % of the gland
info.notes: A phaeochromocytoma is a tumour of the medulla that causes episodic pounding headache, sweating and dangerous blood-pressure surges; ~10 % are outside the adrenal, bilateral or malignant.

info.description: An almond-shaped cluster of nuclei in the front of the medial temporal lobe (the uncus), just in front of the hippocampal head and the tip of the temporal horn.
info.function: Detects threat and emotional significance, triggers fear responses and tags memories with emotion.
info.size: About 1.5-2 cm across; roughly 1.2-1.7 cm3
info.notes: Rare bilateral amygdala damage (Urbach-Wiethe disease) leaves people unable to feel or recognise fear.

info.description: Small triangular muscle behind the elbow, from the back of the lateral epicondyle to the lateral surface of the olecranon and upper posterior ulna.
info.function: Assists triceps in extending the elbow and steadies the ulna during pronation.
info.size: About 4 cm long.
info.notes: Often regarded as a continuation of triceps; the Kocher approach to the radial head passes between it and extensor carpi ulnaris.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B8, supplying the anterior basal bronchopulmonary segment of the right lower lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 4 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: Because each segment has its own airway and blood supply, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).

info.description: The fluid-filled space between the back of the cornea and the front of the iris and lens, filled with clear aqueous humour made by the ciliary body.
info.function: Aqueous humour nourishes the lens and cornea and maintains the intraocular pressure (10-21 mmHg).
info.size: About 3 mm deep centrally, volume ~0.25 ml; aqueous is replaced roughly every 100 minutes.
info.notes: If drainage at the angle is blocked, pressure rises (glaucoma) and slowly damages the optic nerve; a shallow chamber predisposes to acute angle-closure.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B3, supplying the anterior bronchopulmonary segment of the right upper lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 4 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: Because each segment has its own airway and blood supply, a diseased segment can be removed on its own (segmentectomy).

info.description: The anterior (superior) semicircular canal arches upward in a vertical plane set at about 45 degrees to the midline, at right angles to the long axis of the petrous bone. Its dilated ampulla lies at the anterolateral end; its other limb joins the posterior canal in a common crus.
info.function: Senses rotation of the head in its own plane, such as nodding forward and down.
info.size: Radius of curvature about 3.2-4 mm; bony lumen about 1 mm, membranous duct 0.3 mm; ampulla about 2 mm.
