info.notes: Its summit raises the arcuate eminence on the floor of the middle cranial fossa; a thinned roof (superior canal dehiscence) lets patients hear their own eye movements.

info.description: Passes forward above the interosseous membrane into the front compartment of the leg and descends on the membrane between tibialis anterior and the long toe extensors, becoming the dorsalis pedis artery in front of the ankle.
info.function: Supplies the anterior (extensor) compartment of the leg and the front of the ankle.
info.size: ~4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Swelling in the tight anterior compartment (anterior compartment syndrome) can compress it and its nerve.

info.description: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus B1, supplying the apical bronchopulmonary segment of the right upper lobe.
info.function: Conducts air to one bronchopulmonary segment, a pyramidal unit of lung with its own bronchus and segmental artery.
info.size: About 4 cm long and 4–6 mm in diameter; its wall holds irregular cartilage plates.
info.notes: The apical segments of the upper lobes are the classic site of post-primary (reactivation) tuberculosis.

info.description: Skin of the upper arm, elbow and forearm, showing the biceps and triceps bulges, the olecranon and epicondyles at the elbow and the fleshy forearm muscle masses tapering to the flattened wrist.
info.function: Protective, sensory and thermoregulatory covering of the arm; the skin over the olecranon is loose and wrinkled so the elbow can flex fully.
info.size: Shoulder to wrist ~57 cm; each arm ≈ 9 % of body surface (rule of nines)
info.notes: The cubital fossa at the front of the elbow is the usual site for drawing blood, because the median cubital vein lies just under the thin skin there.

info.description: The layer of fat between the arm skin and the deep (brachial and antebrachial) fascia, carrying the cephalic and basilic veins and cutaneous nerves.
info.function: Insulation, energy storage and a gliding layer over the muscles.
info.size: Usually 4–15 mm; thickest over the back of the upper arm
info.notes: Triceps skinfold thickness, pinched over the back of the upper arm, is a classic field measure of body fat.

info.description: A small pyramid-shaped cartilage sitting on the upper border of the cricoid lamina, with a vocal process pointing forward and a muscular process pointing sideways.
info.function: Rotates and glides to open (abduct) and close (adduct) the vocal folds for breathing, speaking and coughing.
info.size: About 15–18 mm tall.
info.notes: Only the posterior cricoarytenoid muscles open the glottis; injury to both recurrent laryngeal nerves can therefore obstruct breathing.

info.description: Thin-walled chamber forming the right border of the heart. It receives the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus; its ear-shaped right auricle overlaps the root of the aorta.
info.function: Collects deoxygenated blood from the body and the heart wall and passes it through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle.
info.size: About 4–5 cm across; wall ~2 mm; auricle lined with comb-like pectinate muscles.
info.notes: Contains the sinoatrial node (the natural pacemaker) near the superior vena cava; the fossa ovalis on its septal wall marks the fetal foramen ovale, which stays probe-patent in about 25% of adults.

info.description: The visible outer ear: a plate of elastic cartilage covered by thin skin and folded into the curled helix rim, the inner antihelix ridge, the deep concha bowl that funnels into the ear canal, the small tragus flap in front and the soft, cartilage-free lobule below.
info.function: Collects sound and, through its folds, filters it in a direction-dependent way that helps locate sounds above, below and behind the head.
info.size: About 62 mm tall and 35 mm wide; stands off the head at 20-30 degrees; cartilage 0.5-1 mm thick.
info.notes: The auricle keeps growing slowly throughout life (about 0.2 mm a year), which is why ears look larger in old age. A blow that strips the perichondrium off the cartilage causes a haematoma that scars into a "cauliflower ear".

info.description: Continues the subclavian artery from the outer border of the first rib through the axilla, behind pectoralis minor and surrounded by the cords of the brachial plexus, to the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery.
info.function: Supplies the shoulder, lateral chest wall and axilla (thoracoacromial, lateral thoracic, subscapular and circumflex humeral branches) and carries blood on to the arm.
info.size: ~8–9 mm diameter; ~10 cm long.
info.notes: Its rich anastomosis around the scapula can keep the arm alive if the artery is tied off above the subscapular branch.

info.description: Twenty to thirty nodes embedded in the fat of the armpit, arranged in five groups: pectoral (anterior, along the chest wall), subscapular (posterior), humeral (lateral, beside the axillary vein), central and apical, the last passing lymph to the subclavian trunk. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the whole upper limb, the breast and the chest and upper back wall down to the navel.
info.size: 20-30 nodes of 5-15 mm
info.notes: About 75 % of breast lymph drains here, so a "sentinel node" biopsy of the first axillary node is used to stage breast cancer; clearing all the nodes can cause chronic swelling of the arm (lymphoedema).

info.description: A short branch of the posterior cord that leaves the armpit backwards through the quadrangular space, with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus beneath the deltoid.
info.function: Motor to deltoid and teres minor; sensation from the "regimental badge" patch of skin over the lower deltoid.
info.size: About 3 mm thick; ~10 cm long
info.notes: Injured by a dislocated shoulder or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus: the deltoid wastes, lifting the arm sideways is weak and the badge area goes numb.

info.description: Formed at the lower border of teres major by the basilic vein joining the brachial veins; it ascends through the axilla on the medial side of the axillary artery and becomes the subclavian vein at the outer border of the first rib.
info.function: Drains the whole upper limb and part of the chest wall, receiving the cephalic vein.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm diameter.
info.notes: Lymph nodes cluster along it, so it is carefully dissected during axillary clearance for breast cancer.

info.description: A superficial vein arising from the little-finger side of the dorsal venous network of the hand; it ascends along the medial forearm, receives the median cubital vein in front of the elbow, pierces the deep fascia halfway up the arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
info.function: Drains superficial tissues of the medial hand, forearm and arm.
info.size: ~4–6 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its large size and deep course make it a common choice for PICC lines and for dialysis fistulas.

info.description: Two-headed muscle on the front of the arm. The long head's tendon arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and arches through the shoulder joint into the intertubercular groove; the short head arises from the coracoid process. The united belly ends in a tendon on the radial tuberosity plus the bicipital aponeurosis fanning over the forearm flexors.
info.function: The strongest supinator of the forearm and a powerful elbow flexor; weakly flexes the shoulder.
info.size: About 30 cm from origin to insertion; belly ~4 cm wide.
info.notes: Rupture of the long-head tendon gives a "Popeye" bulge; the biceps reflex tests the C5–C6 nerve roots.

info.description: The lateral hamstring. Its long head arises from the ischial tuberosity (common tendon with semitendinosus) and runs obliquely down the back of the thigh, joining the short head to insert on the head of the fibula.
info.function: Extends the hip, flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed knee.
info.size: About 35 cm long; belly 4-5 cm wide.
info.notes: The most frequently injured hamstring in sprinting; the common fibular nerve runs along its medial border at the knee.

info.description: Arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur, deep to the long head, and joins it in the common tendon to the fibular head.
info.function: Flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg.
info.size: About 15-20 cm long.
info.notes: The only part of the hamstrings that does not cross the hip; it is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve.

info.description: The main artery of the arm: runs down the medial side of the arm in the groove between biceps and triceps with the median nerve, then crosses to the front of the elbow (cubital fossa), dividing about 1 cm below the elbow crease into the radial and ulnar arteries.
info.function: Supplies the arm muscles and the humerus (via the profunda brachii) and feeds the forearm and hand.
info.size: ~6 mm diameter; ~20 cm long.
info.notes: It is the artery used for measuring blood pressure with a cuff and stethoscope; supracondylar fractures of the humerus in children can compress it.

info.description: The nerve network of the upper limb, formed by the ventral rami of C5-T1. The five roots emerge between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, merge into upper, middle and lower trunks in the base of the neck, split into divisions behind the clavicle and regroup as lateral, posterior and medial cords around the axillary artery in the armpit.
info.function: Mixes fibres from five spinal segments so that each arm nerve carries several segments; supplies every muscle of the shoulder girdle and limb and all the skin of the arm except the armpit.
info.size: About 15 cm from the spine to the armpit; roots and trunks 3-6 mm thick
info.notes: Birth or motorbike traction injuries damage the upper roots (Erb palsy, "waiter's tip") or the lower roots (Klumpke palsy, claw hand). Anaesthetists block the plexus above or below the clavicle to operate on the arm.

info.description: Broad flat muscle deep to biceps, from the lower half of the anterior humerus across the front of the elbow joint to the coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna.
info.function: The main flexor of the elbow, whatever the position of the forearm.
info.size: About 15 cm long and 4–5 cm wide.
info.notes: Bleeding into it after elbow injury can ossify (myositis ossificans), limiting movement.

info.description: Formed behind the right sternoclavicular joint by the right internal jugular and subclavian veins; descends almost vertically to unite with the left brachiocephalic vein as the superior vena cava.
info.function: Drains the right side of the head, neck and right arm; receives the right lymphatic duct.
info.size: ~2.5 cm long, ~1.2 cm wide.
info.notes: Its straight line into the SVC makes the right internal jugular the preferred route for central lines and pacing wires.

info.description: Superficial muscle along the radial (thumb) border of the forearm, from the upper lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the base of the radial styloid process.
info.function: Flexes the elbow, most strongly with the forearm half-pronated (thumb up, as when drinking).
info.size: About 25 cm long; belly 3–4 cm wide.
info.notes: Although it lies in the extensor compartment and is supplied by the radial nerve, it flexes the elbow; its reflex tests C6.

info.description: The skin-covered mound of the female breast over pectoralis major between the 2nd and 6th ribs, sternum to mid-axillary line, with an axillary tail. Inside lie the mammary gland lobes, ducts and fat (glands module).
info.function: Houses the mammary gland, which produces and delivers milk to the nipple during lactation.
info.size: ~12 cm wide, ~11 cm high, projecting ~3–4 cm here; size varies greatly
info.notes: About three-quarters of lymph from the breast drains to the axillary nodes, which is why the axilla is examined and sampled in breast cancer; most cancers arise in the upper outer quadrant.

info.description: The subcutaneous and retromammary fat that makes up most of the volume of the non-lactating breast, divided by suspensory (Cooper) ligaments.
info.function: Gives the breast its shape and cushions the glandular tissue.
info.size: Majority of breast volume (typically 200–500 ml per breast)
info.notes: Cooper ligament shortening by a tumour dimples the overlying skin — a warning sign on examination.

info.description: The subsegmental bronchi and bronchioles branch repeatedly (about 23 generations in all) from each segmental bronchus into the lung tissue; four further generations are shown here.
info.function: Distributes inspired air evenly through the lung and warms, humidifies and filters it on the way to the alveoli.
info.size: Airways shrink from ~4 mm (subsegmental) to ~1 mm (bronchioles, which lack cartilage) and 0.5 mm (terminal bronchioles).
info.notes: Bronchioles have no cartilage, so their smooth muscle can close them almost completely during an asthma attack.

info.description: Thin quadrilateral muscle forming the wall of the cheek, from the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible opposite the molars and the pterygomandibular raphe, running forwards into the modiolus and orbicularis oris.
info.function: Presses the cheek against the teeth to keep food between the molars and expels air from the mouth (blowing, playing a trumpet).
info.size: About 5 cm long, 2–3 cm tall, 2–3 mm thick.
info.notes: Pierced by the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar; although named after the trumpeter, it is supplied by the facial nerve.

info.description: A thin, transparent mucous membrane covering the white of the eye up to the limbus; at the fornices it folds back to line the inner surface of both lids (palpebral conjunctiva).
info.function: Lubricates the eye with mucus and tears, lets the lids glide over the globe and forms a barrier against infection.
info.size: Epithelium only a few cell layers thick; upper fornix ~10 mm and lower ~8 mm from the limbus.
info.notes: Its fine vessels dilate in conjunctivitis ("pink eye"); a painless bright-red subconjunctival haemorrhage looks alarming but is usually harmless.

info.description: Pea-sized gland (Cowper's gland) in the deep perineal pouch beside the membranous urethra; its 2–3 cm duct opens into the spongy urethra in the bulb.
info.function: Releases clear mucus (pre-ejaculate) on arousal that lubricates the urethra and neutralises traces of acidic urine.
info.size: About 1 cm across.
info.notes: The female counterpart is the greater vestibular (Bartholin's) gland.

info.description: The C1 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the occipital bone and the atlas. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the cervical plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the suboccipital muscles (it usually has no skin territory).
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: C1 is almost purely motor; some of its fibres travel with the hypoglossal nerve to reach the infrahyoid strap muscles via the ansa cervicalis.

info.description: The C2 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C1 and C2. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the cervical plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the back of the scalp (via the greater occipital nerve).
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Its dorsal ramus becomes the greater occipital nerve; irritation causes occipital neuralgia - shooting pain from the nape over the back of the head.

info.description: The C3 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C2 and C3. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the cervical plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the upper neck and the skin over the angle of the jaw.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: "C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive": a spinal-cord injury above C3 stops breathing because the phrenic nerve is cut off.

info.description: The C4 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C3 and C4. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the cervical plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the base of the neck and the top of the shoulder.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: The main root of the phrenic nerve, which is why diaphragm irritation (e.g. a ruptured spleen) is felt as shoulder-tip pain.

info.description: The C5 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C4 and C5. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the brachial plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the skin over the deltoid (the "regimental badge" area).
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: shoulder abduction and the biceps reflex. Traction on C5-C6 at birth (Erb palsy) leaves the arm hanging in the "waiter's tip" posture.

info.description: A swelling on the dorsal (sensory) root of the C6 spinal nerve lying in the intervertebral foramen, just outside the dural sac, where the dorsal and ventral roots join. One of 31 pairs; three levels are shown as representatives.
info.function: Holds the cell bodies of the sensory neurons that bring touch, pain, temperature and position sense from its dermatome and muscles into the cord.
info.size: About 4-6 mm long
info.notes: The chickenpox virus lies dormant in dorsal root ganglia for decades and can reactivate as shingles, a painful rash confined to one dermatome.

info.description: The C6 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C5 and C6. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the brachial plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the lateral forearm, thumb and index finger.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: elbow flexion, wrist extension and the brachioradialis reflex; a C5/6 disc prolapse sends pain and tingling into the thumb.

info.description: The C7 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C6 and C7. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the brachial plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the middle finger.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: Test: elbow extension and the triceps reflex; C7 is the root most often compressed in the neck (C6/7 disc).

info.description: The C8 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between C7 and T1. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the brachial plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): the little finger and the medial forearm.
info.size: About 4-5 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: There are eight cervical nerves but only seven cervical vertebrae, so C8 exits below C7. Test: finger flexion and grip.

info.description: The heel bone, largest of the foot: a long block with a posterior tuberosity, a medial shelf (sustentaculum tali) supporting the talus, and a front facet for the cuboid.
info.function: Forms the heel, bears the body weight on landing and anchors the Achilles tendon.
info.size: ≈ 7.5–8 cm long, 4 cm tall
info.notes: Usually fractured by falls from a height landing on the heels.

info.description: The largest carpal bone, in the centre of the distal row, with a rounded head fitting into the lunate and scaphoid.
info.function: Distal-row carpal: forms a rigid unit with the metacarpals and transmits grip forces to the forearm.
info.notes: It is the first carpal to ossify, in the first months of life.

info.description: A C-shaped nucleus with a large head bulging into the anterior horn of the lateral ventricle, a body arching back along the ventricle wall above the thalamus and a thin tail curving down into the temporal lobe.
info.function: Part of the striatum: helps select and start wanted movements and behaviours and suppress unwanted ones, and supports habit and reward learning.
info.size: Head about 1.5-2 cm across; about 10 cm long along its curve
info.notes: In Huntington disease the caudate head wastes away so the anterior horns look ballooned on scans, producing chorea and dementia.

info.description: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that pierces the underside of the optic nerve about 1 cm behind the eye, runs in its centre to the optic disc and divides into superior and inferior, nasal and temporal branches arching over the retina (the temporal arcades curve around the macula).
info.function: Supplies the inner two-thirds of the retina; it is an end artery with no useful collaterals.
info.size: About 0.1-0.16 mm in diameter at the disc; the fovea itself is avascular.
info.notes: Sudden painless loss of vision from its occlusion is a stroke-equivalent emergency; retinal arterioles are the only arteries in the body that can be looked at directly.

info.description: Formed at the optic disc by four retinal venous branches that run beside the arteries; it leaves the optic nerve with the artery and drains into the superior ophthalmic vein or cavernous sinus.
info.function: Drains blood from the inner retina.
info.size: About 1.5 times the width of the matching artery (artery:vein ratio ~2:3).
info.notes: A central retinal vein occlusion gives a "blood-and-thunder" fundus with widespread haemorrhages; loss of spontaneous venous pulsation at the disc can hint at raised intracranial pressure.

info.description: A superficial vein that starts on the thumb side of the dorsal venous network of the hand, winds round to the front of the forearm, ascends lateral to biceps and runs in the deltopectoral groove before piercing the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.
info.function: Drains superficial tissues of the lateral hand, forearm and arm.
info.size: ~3–5 mm diameter.
info.notes: Easily visible at the wrist ("intern's vein") and used for cannulas; surgeons use it to insert pacemaker leads.

info.description: One of the two large lateral lobes of the cerebellum in the posterior cranial fossa, under the tentorium and behind the brainstem. Its surface is folded into thin parallel leaves (folia) separated by fissures; the horizontal fissure runs round its margin.
info.function: Coordinates movement on the SAME side of the body: timing, smoothness, balance and motor learning, comparing intended with actual movement.
info.size: Cerebellum about 10 cm wide, 5 cm high and 6 cm deep; ~150 g, 10% of brain weight but over half of all its neurons
info.notes: A hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral clumsiness: overshooting (dysmetria), intention tremor and inability to do rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia).

info.description: The core of each hemisphere beneath the 2-4 mm grey cortex: bundles of myelinated axons (corona radiata, internal capsule, association and commissural fibres) whose fatty myelin makes it pale.
info.function: Wires cortical areas to each other, to the other hemisphere and to the thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord.
info.size: About 40% of brain volume; roughly 150,000-180,000 km of myelinated fibres in a young adult
info.notes: Multiple sclerosis strips myelin from white-matter tracts; MRI shows the plaques as bright spots around the ventricles.

info.description: The deep cervical chain: a string of nodes running down the neck along the internal jugular vein, under the sternocleidomastoid muscle, from the angle of the jaw to the collarbone. The jugulodigastric node at the top is the largest. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Final drainage station for the whole head and neck (scalp, face, mouth, tonsils, pharynx, larynx, thyroid) before lymph enters the jugular trunk.
info.size: About 20-30 nodes per side, each 5-15 mm; the jugulodigastric node up to 15-20 mm
info.notes: They swell with tonsillitis and glandular fever. A hard, painless cervical node in an adult suggests a head-and-neck cancer; an enlarged left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node) can be the first sign of a stomach cancer.

info.description: A series of loops between the ventral rami of C1-C4, lying deep to the sternocleidomastoid. Its skin branches fan out from the middle of the muscle's back border (Erb's point): lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves; a loop on the carotid sheath (ansa cervicalis) supplies the strap muscles.
info.function: Sensation from the side of the neck, the ear lobe and the skin behind the ear, and the skin over the clavicle and upper chest; motor to the infrahyoid muscles and, through the phrenic nerve, the diaphragm.
info.size: Loops within ~4 cm of the spine; skin branches 1-2 mm thick, 6-10 cm long
info.notes: A superficial cervical plexus block at the mid-point of the sternocleidomastoid numbs the neck for carotid surgery. The great auricular nerve is the one most often injured in facelift surgery, leaving a numb ear lobe.

info.description: A dark, pigmented, blood-rich layer between the sclera and the retina, forming the back part of the uveal tract. Its capillary layer (choriocapillaris) lies against the retinal pigment epithelium.
info.function: Nourishes the outer retina (photoreceptors) and absorbs stray light inside the eye.
info.size: About 0.2-0.3 mm thick, thickest at the posterior pole; extends forward to the ora serrata.
info.notes: Choroidal melanoma is the commonest primary eye cancer in adults; the choroid receives one of the highest blood flows per gram of any tissue.

info.description: A ring of muscle and folded, vascular epithelium between the iris root and the ora serrata, part of the uveal tract. Its front part (pars plicata) carries about 70 radial ciliary processes; its back part (pars plana) is flat.
info.function: The ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour; the ciliary muscle contracts to slacken the zonules so the lens rounds up for near focus (accommodation).
info.size: Ring ~6 mm wide from front to back (pars plicata 2 mm, pars plana 4 mm); processes ~2 mm long and 0.5-1 mm high.
info.notes: Glaucoma drops and some laser treatments reduce aqueous production here; atropine paralyses the ciliary muscle (cycloplegia) for eye examinations.

info.description: The collarbone: an S-shaped strut, convex forward in its medial two-thirds and concave forward laterally, between the sternum and the acromion.
info.function: Holds the shoulder out from the trunk so the arm can swing freely and transmits forces from the arm to the axial skeleton.
info.size: ≈ 15 cm long, 1–2 cm thick
info.notes: The most frequently fractured bone, usually at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds after a fall on the outstretched hand.

info.description: The Co1 spinal nerve leaves the spinal canal between the sacral hiatus, below the fifth sacral nerve. Its sensory (dorsal) and motor (ventral) roots meet just beyond the dorsal root ganglion; the short mixed nerve then splits into a small dorsal ramus for the back muscles and skin and a larger ventral ramus, which joins the small coccygeal plexus.
info.function: Carries motor fibres to the muscles of its segment (myotome) and sensation back from its strip of skin (dermatome): a small patch of skin over the coccyx.
info.size: About 1 mm thick; the mixed nerve is only ~1 cm long before it divides
info.notes: The single coccygeal nerve is the last and smallest of the 31 pairs; its dorsal ramus supplies the skin over the tailbone.

info.description: The spiral organ of hearing: a bony tube coiled two and a half turns around a central core (the modiolus), like a snail shell, tapering from the wide basal turn to the apex. Inside, three fluid channels run its whole length: scala vestibuli, cochlear duct (scala media) and scala tympani.
info.function: Converts fluid pressure waves into nerve impulses, high frequencies at the base and low frequencies at the apex (tonotopy).
info.size: About 9 mm across the base and 5 mm high; uncoiled length 32-35 mm; 2.5-2.75 turns.
info.notes: Its apex points forward and outward; the basal turn bulges into the middle ear as the promontory. Cochlear implants thread an electrode along the scala tympani.

info.description: The membranous middle channel, triangular in cross-section, bounded by Reissner's membrane above, the basilar membrane below and the stria vascularis on the outer wall. It is filled with potassium-rich endolymph and carries the organ of Corti on its floor.
info.function: Houses the sensory organ of Corti and maintains the +80 mV endocochlear potential that powers hair-cell transduction.
info.size: About 35 mm long following the spiral; endolymph volume about 2 microlitres.
info.notes: Swelling of this duct (endolymphatic hydrops) underlies Meniere's disease: attacks of vertigo, tinnitus and fluctuating hearing loss.

info.description: The hearing part of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII): axons of the spiral ganglion neurons gather in the modiolus and run medially through the internal acoustic meatus to the cochlear nuclei of the brainstem.
info.function: Carries frequency-coded auditory signals from the hair cells to the brain.
info.size: About 30,000 fibres; about 1 mm in diameter at the meatus.
info.notes: A vestibular schwannoma ("acoustic neuroma") growing in the internal acoustic meatus typically presents with one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus.

info.description: Ascends in the carotid sheath beside the trachea and larynx, with the internal jugular vein lateral and the vagus nerve behind, dividing at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3–C4). The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk.
info.function: Carries blood to the head, neck and brain.
info.size: ~7–8 mm diameter; ~9 cm long.
info.notes: The carotid pulse is felt at the front border of sternocleidomastoid; the carotid sinus at the bifurcation senses blood pressure and atherosclerotic plaque there is a major cause of stroke.

info.description: The smaller, lateral division of the sciatic nerve. It follows the biceps femoris tendon to the back of the fibular head, winds around the neck of the fibula just under the skin and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (lateral compartment, then the top of the foot) and the deep fibular nerve (front compartment, then the first web space).
info.function: Motor to the muscles that lift the foot and toes (deep branch) and turn the sole outward (superficial branch); sensation from the outer leg, most of the top of the foot and the skin between the first two toes.
info.size: About 3 mm thick; ~15 cm before dividing, branches ~40 cm
info.notes: The most frequently injured nerve of the leg: a fibular-neck fracture, a tight plaster cast or habitual leg-crossing presses it against the bone, causing foot drop and a high-stepping gait.

info.description: One of the two terminal branches of the aorta, from its bifurcation at L4 running down and outwards to divide in front of the sacroiliac joint (L5/S1) into the external and internal iliac arteries.
info.function: Carries blood to the pelvis and the lower limb.
info.size: ~4–5 cm long, ~1 cm diameter.
info.notes: The right common iliac artery crosses in front of the start of the inferior vena cava; iliac narrowing causes buttock and thigh claudication.

info.description: Formed in front of the sacroiliac joint by the external and internal iliac veins; the short right vein ascends almost vertically to unite with its partner at L5, to the right of the aortic bifurcation, as the inferior vena cava.
info.function: Drains the pelvis and lower limb into the inferior vena cava.
info.size: ~5 cm long, ~1.5 cm wide.
info.notes: Lies behind and then lateral to its artery.

name: Right common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn)

info.description: A fibrous ring at the apex of the orbit surrounding the optic canal and the middle of the superior orbital fissure.
info.function: Gives origin to the four rectus muscles; the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, oculomotor, abducens and nasociliary nerves pass through it.
info.size: About 6-7 mm across.
info.notes: Pressure on structures inside it causes the orbital apex syndrome: vision loss plus paralysis of eye movements.

info.description: Slender muscle from the tip of the coracoid process (sharing a tendon with the short head of biceps) to the medial surface of the middle of the humerus.
info.function: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.
info.size: About 15 cm long, 2 cm wide.
info.notes: Pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve — a landmark when blocking that nerve in the axilla.

info.description: The clear, dome-shaped window at the front of the eye. It has no blood vessels and is kept transparent by the regular spacing of its collagen fibres and by its pumping endothelium.
info.function: Provides about two-thirds of the eye's focusing power (~43 dioptres) and protects the front of the eye.
info.size: About 11.5 mm wide (horizontal), central radius of curvature 7.8 mm, 0.55 mm thick centrally and ~0.7 mm at the edge.
info.notes: One of the most densely innervated tissues in the body, so a corneal scratch is intensely painful; LASIK and PRK reshape it to correct refractive error.

info.description: The 1-2 mm wide grey-blue transition zone where the clear cornea meets the white sclera. It houses the corneal stem cells and, on its inner side, the drainage angle with the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal.
info.function: Regenerates the corneal surface and drains aqueous humour out of the eye.
info.size: Ring ~11.7 mm across and 1-2 mm wide.
info.notes: Surgeons enter the eye at the limbus for cataract and glaucoma operations; a grey ring just inside it (arcus) can signal high cholesterol in younger adults.

info.description: Arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus, runs forward between the right auricle and the pulmonary trunk, then round the right atrioventricular groove to the back of the heart, where it usually gives the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery.
info.function: Supplies the right atrium and ventricle, the back third of the septum, and in most people the SA and AV nodes.
info.size: About 3–4 mm wide at its origin; acute marginal branch along the lower right border.
info.notes: The heart is "right-dominant" in ~70–80% of people (the RCA gives the posterior descending artery); RCA occlusion typically causes an inferior infarct and slow heart rhythms.

info.description: One of the two dorsal erectile cylinders of the penis. Each starts as a crus fixed to the ischiopubic ramus, and the pair run side by side inside the tough tunica albuginea to end under the glans.
info.function: Its spongy sinusoids fill with blood during erection, making the penis rigid.
info.size: About 15 cm long including the crus; ~1.5 cm across when flaccid.
info.notes: Carries the deep (cavernous) artery; PDE5 inhibitors act on its smooth muscle. A penile "fracture" is a tear of its tunica albuginea.

info.description: A transparent biconvex lens hung behind the iris by the zonules. It is built of long, tightly packed fibre cells laid down in layers like an onion, with no blood vessels or nerves.
info.function: Fine-tunes focus (about one-third of the eye's power, ~20 D) by changing shape: it becomes rounder for near vision when the ciliary muscle contracts.
info.size: 9 mm in diameter and 4 mm thick in an adult; the back surface is more curved than the front.
info.notes: It keeps growing all life and stiffens, causing presbyopia after ~45; clouding of the lens (cataract) is the leading cause of blindness worldwide.

info.description: One to three small nodes on the inner side of the elbow, 3-5 cm above the medial epicondyle beside the basilic vein. Each node is a bean-shaped filter 5-15 mm long with a fibrous capsule, an outer cortex of B-cell follicles, a T-cell paracortex and an inner medulla. Several afferent lymphatics enter its convex surface; one or two efferents leave at the hilum.
info.function: Drain the little-finger side of the hand and forearm along the basilic vein, then send lymph on to the axillary nodes.
info.size: 1-3 nodes of 5-8 mm
info.notes: Enlarged in infections of the hand and in secondary syphilis; classically checked when examining the lymphatic system of the arm.

info.description: Cube-shaped bone on the lateral side of the midfoot, in front of the calcaneus, grooved underneath by the fibularis longus tendon.
info.function: Forms part of the lateral longitudinal arch and supports the 4th and 5th metatarsals.
info.notes: Cuboid syndrome (subluxation) is a cause of lateral foot pain in dancers.

info.description: The largest branch of the femoral artery, arising ~4 cm below the inguinal ligament and running deep, close to the femur between the adductor muscles, giving the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and four perforating arteries.
info.function: Supplies the muscles of the thigh and the head and neck of the femur (via the circumflex arteries).
info.size: ~6–7 mm diameter.
info.notes: Damage to the medial circumflex femoral artery in a femoral neck fracture can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

info.description: Thick triangular muscle that caps the shoulder. It arises from the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula, wraps over the head of the humerus and converges on the deltoid tuberosity about 40% of the way down the humerus.
info.function: Abducts the arm beyond the first ~15° (middle fibres); anterior fibres flex and medially rotate it, posterior fibres extend and laterally rotate it.
info.size: About 15 cm long, up to 2.5 cm thick over the shoulder.
info.notes: A common intramuscular injection site; its axillary nerve can be damaged in shoulder dislocation or surgical-neck fracture, weakening abduction.

name: Right distal phalanx of the big toe (hallux)

info.description: Distal phalanx of the big toe (hallux): a short tubular bone ending in a tuft under the toenail.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 25 mm long
info.notes: The big toe has only two phalanges and bears most push-off force; gout classically attacks its first joint.

name: Right distal phalanx of the fourth toe

info.description: Distal phalanx of the fourth toe: a short tubular bone ending in a tuft under the toenail.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 9 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Right distal phalanx of the index finger

info.description: Distal phalanx of the index finger, ending in a rough tuft that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 17 mm long
info.notes: Crush injuries of the fingertip commonly fracture the distal tuft.

name: Right distal phalanx of the little finger

info.description: Distal phalanx of the little finger, ending in a rough tuft that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 13 mm long
info.notes: Crush injuries of the fingertip commonly fracture the distal tuft.

name: Right distal phalanx of the little toe

info.description: Distal phalanx of the little toe: a short tubular bone ending in a tuft under the toenail.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 8 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Right distal phalanx of the middle finger

info.description: Distal phalanx of the middle finger, ending in a rough tuft that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 18 mm long
info.notes: Crush injuries of the fingertip commonly fracture the distal tuft.

name: Right distal phalanx of the ring finger

info.description: Distal phalanx of the ring finger, ending in a rough tuft that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 17 mm long
info.notes: Crush injuries of the fingertip commonly fracture the distal tuft.

name: Right distal phalanx of the second toe

info.description: Distal phalanx of the second toe: a short tubular bone ending in a tuft under the toenail.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 11 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Right distal phalanx of the third toe

info.description: Distal phalanx of the third toe: a short tubular bone ending in a tuft under the toenail.
info.function: Toe bones help balance and push off during the last phase of each step.
info.size: ≈ 10 mm long
info.notes: The little toe's middle and distal phalanges are fused in many adults.

name: Right distal phalanx of the thumb

info.description: Distal phalanx of the thumb, ending in a rough tuft that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
info.function: Forms a lever of the finger moved by the long flexor and extensor tendons.
info.size: ≈ 21 mm long
info.notes: Crush injuries of the fingertip commonly fracture the distal tuft.

info.description: Continues the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, to the first intermetatarsal space, where it dives into the sole to complete the deep plantar arch.
info.function: Supplies the top of the foot and toes (arcuate and dorsal metatarsal arteries).
info.size: ~2–3 mm diameter.
info.notes: Its pulse, felt just lateral to the big-toe extensor tendon, is checked in diabetic and vascular foot examinations; it is congenitally absent in ~5–10% of people.

info.description: The external acoustic meatus: a slightly S-shaped tube from the concha to the eardrum. Its outer third is cartilage carrying hairs, sebaceous and ceruminous (wax) glands; the inner two-thirds run through the temporal bone under thin, hairless skin.
info.function: Conducts airborne sound to the eardrum and, by its length, resonates at about 3 kHz to boost speech-range frequencies by 10-15 dB.
info.size: About 25 mm long and 7 mm in diameter, narrowest at the bony isthmus.
info.notes: Because the canal curves, clinicians pull the auricle up and back to straighten it before looking in with an otoscope (down and back in infants).

info.description: The eardrum: a thin, pearly-grey, cone-shaped membrane closing the inner end of the ear canal, its apex (the umbo) pulled inward by the attached handle of the malleus. It has three layers: outer skin, a middle fibrous layer and inner mucosa.
info.function: Vibrates with incoming sound and passes the vibration to the ossicular chain.
info.size: About 9-10 mm across and 0.1 mm thick, set obliquely at roughly 55 degrees to the canal floor.
info.notes: Otoscopic landmarks are the malleus handle and the "cone of light" reflection in the antero-inferior quadrant; fluid in the middle ear makes the drum dull and bulging.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the eighth rib to the cartilage above, forming the costal margin.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 6 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The eighth rib, a false (vertebrochondral) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T8 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T8 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 27 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the eleventh rib (a short free tip).
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 1 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The eleventh rib, a floating rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T11, its tubercle with the T11 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 20 cm
info.notes: Floating ribs end free in the flank muscles and have no anterior attachment.

info.description: Comma-shaped organ along the back of the testis made of a single, tightly coiled duct, with a head on the upper pole, a body and a tail that becomes the vas deferens.
info.function: Stores sperm and lets them mature and gain the ability to swim over about 2 weeks.
info.size: About 5 cm long; the coiled duct is about 6 m long when uncoiled.
info.notes: Epididymitis, usually from infection, causes a painful swelling behind the testis.

info.description: A honeycomb of 3–18 small air cells in the ethmoid labyrinth, between the upper nasal cavity and the orbit, grouped as anterior, middle and posterior cells.
info.function: Lighten the skull and drain into the middle and superior meatuses.
info.size: Individual cells 2–10 mm; the labyrinth is ~4–5 cm long and 1–2.5 cm wide.
info.notes: The lateral wall (lamina papyracea) is paper-thin, so ethmoid sinusitis in children can spread into the orbit (orbital cellulitis).

info.description: The pharyngotympanic (auditory) tube runs downward, forward and medially from the front wall of the middle ear to the side wall of the nasopharynx. Its lateral third is bone; the medial two-thirds are a cartilage-supported slit that is normally closed.
info.function: Equalises middle-ear pressure with the atmosphere and drains middle-ear mucus into the throat.
info.size: About 36 mm long; 2 mm across at the isthmus, opening as an 8 mm slit in the pharynx.
info.notes: Opened by the palate muscles when swallowing or yawning, the "pop" felt in an aeroplane. Shorter and more horizontal in children, which favours middle-ear infections.

info.description: Arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle and inserts on the dorsal base of the third metacarpal.
info.function: Extends and radially deviates the wrist and steadies it during gripping.
info.size: About 22 cm long.
info.notes: Its origin is the main site of degeneration in lateral epicondylitis ("tennis elbow").

info.description: Arises from the lower lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and runs along the radial side of the forearm to the dorsal base of the second metacarpal.
info.function: Extends and radially deviates the wrist; keeps the wrist extended during a firm grip.
info.size: About 25 cm long; fleshy in its upper half.
info.notes: A frequent donor tendon for tendon transfers after nerve injuries.

info.description: Arises from the lateral epicondyle and the posterior border of the ulna and runs down the back of the ulna to the base of the fifth metacarpal.
info.function: Extends and adducts (ulnar-deviates) the wrist.
info.size: About 24 cm long.
info.notes: Its tendon can snap out of its groove over the ulnar head in tennis and golf players.

info.description: Arises from the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle; its belly divides into four tendons that cross the back of the hand to the extensor expansions of the index to little fingers.
info.function: Extends the fingers at the knuckle and, via the expansions, the finger joints; helps extend the wrist.
info.size: About 25 cm to the knuckles; tendons ~2 mm thick.
info.notes: Its tendons are linked by juncturae tendinum on the back of the hand, which is why the ring finger cannot be lifted fully on its own. The tendons are shown only as far as the knuckles.

info.description: The only muscle on the top of the foot: a small fleshy mass on the dorsolateral calcaneus whose four thin tendons run to toes 1-4 (the slip to the great toe is called extensor hallucis brevis) and join the long extensor tendons.
info.function: Extends toes 1-4 at the metatarsophalangeal joints.
info.size: Belly about 6-8 cm long.
info.notes: Its soft bulge in front of the lateral malleolus can be mistaken for swelling; it is a standard recording site for deep fibular nerve conduction studies.

info.description: Feather-shaped (unipennate) muscle lateral to tibialis anterior, arising from the lateral tibial condyle, the upper three-quarters of the anterior fibula and the interosseous membrane.
info.function: Extends the lateral four toes and dorsiflexes the ankle.
info.size: Belly about 25 cm long, 2-3 cm wide.
info.notes: Its lowest part often forms a separate slip, fibularis tertius, inserting on the fifth metatarsal.

info.description: A common tendon passes under the extensor retinacula in front of the ankle and fans into four slips on the dorsum of the foot, forming the dorsal (extensor) expansions of toes 2-5.
info.function: Lifts (extends) the lateral four toes.
info.size: Common tendon about 5 mm; slips about 2 mm wide.
info.notes: The slips stand out under the skin of the dorsum when the toes are raised - a quick test of the deep fibular nerve.

info.description: Thin muscle hidden between tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus, arising from the middle of the anterior fibula and the interosseous membrane.
info.function: Extends the great toe and helps dorsiflex the ankle.
info.size: Belly about 15 cm long.
info.notes: Testing the strength of great-toe extension is the classic check of the L5 nerve root.

info.description: Crosses the front of the ankle between the tendons of tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus and runs along the dorsum of the first metatarsal to the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.
info.function: Extends the great toe.
info.size: About 15 cm long, 4 mm diameter.
info.notes: Easily cut by lacerations on the top of the foot, leaving the big toe drooping.

info.description: Rises from the carotid bifurcation in front of the internal carotid and ascends behind the angle of the mandible into the parotid gland, ending as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. Shown with its facial artery (winding over the jaw to the corner of the mouth and side of the nose) and maxillary branches.
info.function: Supplies the face, scalp, jaws, teeth, tongue, thyroid and the dura (via the middle meningeal artery).
info.size: ~4–5 mm diameter at its origin; eight named branches.
info.notes: The facial pulse is felt where the artery crosses the jaw in front of masseter and the superficial temporal pulse just in front of the ear; a tear of its middle meningeal branch causes an extradural haematoma.

info.description: Follows the pelvic brim along the medial border of psoas to pass beneath the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point, where it becomes the femoral artery; gives the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries.
info.function: Carries blood to the lower limb and the lower anterior abdominal wall.
info.size: ~10 cm long, ~8–10 mm diameter.
info.notes: Commonly used for inflow when a kidney transplant is placed in the iliac fossa.

info.description: Continues the femoral vein above the inguinal ligament and runs along the pelvic brim, medial and then posterior to the external iliac artery, to join the internal iliac vein in front of the sacroiliac joint.
info.function: Drains the lower limb and lower abdominal wall.
info.size: ~1.2–1.5 cm diameter.
info.notes: Compression of the left iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery (May–Thurner syndrome) predisposes to left-leg DVT.

info.description: Eleven thin sheets, one in each intercostal space, whose fibres run from the lower border of one rib down and forwards to the upper border of the rib below; they reach from the rib tubercles to the costochondral junctions, beyond which the external intercostal membrane continues.
info.function: Raise the ribs in inspiration and stop the intercostal spaces bulging or being sucked in.
info.size: Each space ~1.5–2 cm tall; sheets ~3 mm thick.
info.notes: The intercostal nerve and vessels run under the rib above, so chest drains and needles are passed just over the upper border of a rib.

info.description: Largest and most superficial flat abdominal muscle. Fleshy digitations from the outer surfaces of ribs 5–12 (interlocking with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi) run down and forwards ("hands in pockets") into a broad aponeurosis reaching the linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior iliac crest; its folded lower edge is the inguinal ligament.
info.function: Compresses the abdomen, flexes the trunk and rotates it to the opposite side; assists forced expiration.
info.size: About 30 cm tall; fleshy part 5–7 mm thick.
info.notes: Its aponeurosis forms the front wall of the inguinal canal, and the superficial inguinal ring is a split in it. The part covering rectus (anterior rectus sheath) is omitted here.

info.description: An arched band of short, thick hairs on the skin over the superciliary arch of the frontal bone, pointing laterally.
info.function: Diverts sweat and rain away from the eye and is a major tool of facial expression (raised by frontalis, drawn together by corrugator supercilii).
info.size: ~5 cm long, 5–10 mm high; ~250 hairs; hairs live ~4 months
info.notes: Loss of the outer third of the eyebrow (Hertoghe sign) is a classic, though non-specific, sign of hypothyroidism.

info.description: Short, curved hairs in two to three rows along the front edge of each lid margin, absent from the lacrimal part medial to the puncta; the upper lashes curl upward, the lower ones downward.
info.function: Shield the eye from dust and trigger a protective blink when touched.
info.size: ~100-150 upper lashes 8-12 mm long, ~50-80 lower lashes 6-8 mm; each lasts 3-5 months (represented here by 25 + 12).
info.notes: Lashes turning in towards the cornea (trichiasis) cause scarring; repeated trachoma infection is a leading infectious cause of blindness through this mechanism.

info.description: Leaves the brainstem beside the vestibulocochlear nerve, enters the internal acoustic meatus, bends sharply at the geniculate ganglion, runs through the temporal bone along the inner wall of the middle ear, turns down behind it and exits the skull at the stylomastoid foramen just below the ear, then enters the parotid gland.
info.function: Motor to all the muscles of facial expression and the stapedius; taste from the front two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani); secretomotor to the lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands.
info.size: About 2 mm thick; ~3 cm inside the temporal bone
info.notes: Bell's palsy (swelling of the nerve in its narrow bony canal) paralyses one whole side of the face; a stroke spares the forehead because the upper face has bilateral cortical control.

name: Right facial nerve, terminal branches
latin: Rami temporales, zygomatici, buccales, marginalis mandibulae et colli

info.description: Inside the parotid gland the facial nerve fans out like a goose's foot (pes anserinus) into five branches - temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical - that spread across the face just under the skin.
info.function: Temporal: frontalis and eye closure; zygomatic: eye closure; buccal: cheek and upper lip; marginal mandibular: lower lip and chin; cervical: platysma.
info.size: Branches 0.5-1.5 mm thick, 4-8 cm long
info.notes: Surgeons removing the parotid dissect out this fan; a cut below the jaw can catch the marginal mandibular branch and leave a permanently lopsided smile.

info.description: Continues the external iliac artery below the inguinal ligament through the femoral triangle (lateral to the femoral vein), then runs down the front-medial thigh under sartorius in the adductor canal and passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery.
info.function: The main supply of the lower limb; its large deep branch (profunda femoris) supplies the thigh muscles.
info.size: ~1 cm diameter at the groin; ~30 cm long.
info.notes: The femoral pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point; it is the classic access route for catheter angiography and interventions.

info.description: Hyaline cartilage capping the trochlear groove and both femoral condyles.
info.function: Lets the femur roll and glide on the tibia and patella through 140° of knee flexion.
info.size: ≈ 2–3 mm thick
info.notes: Cartilage has no blood supply, so defects heal poorly; osteoarthritis of the knee is extremely common.

info.description: Hyaline cartilage covering the femoral head except for the small fovea where the ligament of the head attaches.
info.function: Provides a smooth, load-spreading bearing surface for the hip joint.
info.size: ≈ 2–3 mm thick
info.notes: Wear of this cartilage is hip osteoarthritis, the most common reason for hip replacement.

info.description: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus (L2-L4). It emerges from the lateral border of psoas, runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus, passes under the inguinal ligament just lateral to the femoral artery and within a few centimetres fans out in the femoral triangle; its longest branch, the saphenous nerve, follows the adductor canal to the inner knee and runs down the inner leg to the foot.
info.function: Motor to iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and the four heads of quadriceps (knee extension); sensation from the front of the thigh and, via the saphenous nerve, the inner leg and foot.
info.size: About 4 mm thick at the groin; the saphenous nerve ~50 cm long
info.notes: The knee-jerk reflex tests it (L3-L4). A femoral nerve block lateral to the pulse in the groin (order N-A-V: nerve, artery, vein from outside in) relieves the pain of a hip fracture.

info.description: Accompanies the femoral artery from the adductor hiatus, lying behind it in the thigh and medial to it in the femoral triangle, and becomes the external iliac vein under the inguinal ligament. It receives the great saphenous and deep femoral veins.
info.function: The main deep vein of the lower limb.
info.size: ~1–1.5 cm diameter; has 3–4 valves.
info.notes: Deep vein thrombosis here can break off as a pulmonary embolus; it is used for emergency central access just medial to the femoral pulse.

info.description: The thigh bone, longest and strongest in the body: a spherical head on an angled neck (≈125°), greater and lesser trochanters, a shaft bowed forward with the linea aspera behind, and two large condyles at the knee.
info.function: Carries the body weight from hip to knee and gives leverage to the most powerful muscles of the body.
info.size: ≈ 44 cm long (≈ ¼ of height); head Ø 48 mm; shaft Ø 27 mm
info.notes: Hip fractures through the femoral neck are common in older people with osteoporosis and can cut off the blood supply to the head.

info.description: Slender lateral bone of the leg with a knob-like head below the knee and a lower end forming the lateral malleolus of the ankle.
info.function: Carries little weight (≈ 15%) but anchors leg muscles and stabilises the ankle mortise.
info.size: ≈ 40 cm long, 1–1.5 cm thick
info.notes: The common fibular nerve winds around its neck, where it is easily injured, causing foot drop.

info.description: Lies deep to fibularis longus, arising from the lower two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula.
info.function: Everts the foot and weakly plantarflexes the ankle.
info.size: Belly about 15 cm long.
info.notes: Its tendon can avulse the tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal during an inversion sprain ("pseudo-Jones" fracture).

info.description: Runs behind the lateral malleolus in front of the fibularis longus tendon, above the fibular trochlea, to the tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal.
info.function: Everts the foot.
info.size: About 12 cm long, 5 mm diameter.
info.notes: Longitudinal splits of this tendon against the back of the fibula are a common finding after chronic ankle instability.

info.description: Superficial muscle of the lateral compartment, arising from the head and upper two-thirds of the lateral fibula (also called peroneus longus).
info.function: Everts the foot and plantarflexes the ankle; with tibialis anterior it forms a "stirrup" under the foot that supports the transverse arch.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm long.
info.notes: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck deep to its origin - a vulnerable spot for compression by casts, braces or leg-crossing.

info.description: Passes behind the lateral malleolus, along the side of the calcaneus and through the groove of the cuboid, then obliquely across the deep sole to the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.
info.function: Everts the foot and depresses the first metatarsal head.
info.size: About 25 cm long, 5 mm diameter.
info.notes: Tears or subluxation of the fibular tendons behind the malleolus follow ankle sprains and cause persistent lateral ankle pain.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the fifth rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 10 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: Long bone of the palm behind the little finger, with a base at the carpus, a slender shaft and a rounded head forming the knuckle.
info.function: Forms the skeleton of the palm and the knuckle joint of its finger.
info.size: ≈ 50 mm long
info.notes: A "boxer's fracture" breaks the neck of the fifth metacarpal.

info.description: Long bone of the forefoot behind the little toe, with a wedge-shaped base, slender shaft and rounded head at the ball of the foot.
info.function: Forms a spoke of the foot's arches and a lever for walking.
info.size: ≈ 72 mm long
info.notes: Fractures of the base of the fifth metatarsal (Jones fracture) follow inversion injuries.

info.description: The fifth rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T5 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T5 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 30 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

name: Right fimbriae of the uterine tube

info.description: Finger-like fringes around the open end of the infundibulum; one longer ovarian fimbria reaches the ovary.
info.function: At ovulation they engorge and sweep over the ovary, guiding the released egg into the tube.
info.size: About 1–1.5 cm long.
info.notes: The open tubal end means the peritoneal cavity communicates with the outside via the uterus and vagina in women.

info.description: Five translucent plates of hard keratin on the backs of the distal phalanges, each growing from a matrix under the proximal nail fold; the pale half-moon (lunula) is the visible front of the matrix.
info.function: Protect the fingertips, provide counter-pressure that sharpens fine touch, and help pick up small objects.
info.size: ~10–12 mm long, ~0.5 mm thick; grow ~3 mm per month (a whole nail regrows in ~6 months)
info.notes: Nail changes can reveal systemic disease: clubbing (lung disease), spoon nails (iron deficiency), pitting (psoriasis), Beau lines (a past severe illness).

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the first rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 4 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: Long bone of the palm behind the thumb, with a base at the carpus, a slender shaft and a rounded head forming the knuckle.
info.function: Its mobile saddle joint lets the thumb oppose the fingers.
info.size: ≈ 37 mm long
info.notes: A Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture of its base.

info.description: Long bone of the forefoot behind the big toe (hallux), with a wedge-shaped base, slender shaft and rounded head at the ball of the foot.
info.function: Short and thick, it carries about a third of forefoot load during push-off.
info.size: ≈ 65 mm long
info.notes: Bunions (hallux valgus) develop at the first metatarsal head.

info.description: The first rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T1, its tubercle with the T1 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Forms the rim of the thoracic inlet; the subclavian artery and vein and the brachial plexus cross its upper surface.
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 19 cm
info.notes: A cervical rib or tight first rib can compress the brachial plexus (thoracic outlet syndrome).

info.description: Arises from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle; its long tendon runs in its own groove on the trapezium to the base of the second (and third) metacarpal.
info.function: Flexes the wrist and deviates it radially.
info.size: About 25 cm long, tendinous in the distal half.
info.notes: The radial pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon at the wrist.

info.description: The most medial superficial flexor, arising from the medial epicondyle and from the olecranon and posterior border of the ulna, and inserting on the pisiform (and via ligaments on the hamate and fifth metacarpal).
info.function: Flexes and adducts (ulnar-deviates) the wrist.
info.size: About 25 cm long, fleshy almost to the wrist.
info.notes: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between its two heads — the cubital tunnel.

info.description: Central muscle of the first layer of the sole, lying directly on the plantar fascia; from the medial calcaneal tuberosity it sends four tendons that split to insert on the middle phalanges of toes 2-5, letting the long flexor tendons pass through.
info.function: Flexes the lateral four toes at the proximal interphalangeal joints and helps support the arch.
info.size: Belly about 10-12 cm long, 3 cm wide.
info.notes: Together with abductor hallucis and abductor digiti minimi it forms the first of the four muscle layers of the sole.

info.description: Arises from the posterior surface of the tibia below the soleal line, on the medial side of the deep posterior compartment.
info.function: Flexes the lateral four toes and helps plantarflex and invert the foot.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm; about 35 cm with its tendons.
info.notes: Just above the ankle it crosses superficial to tibialis posterior (the crural chiasm); its tendon is transferred to replace a failed tibialis posterior tendon.

info.description: The FDL tendon passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole, receives quadratus plantae and gives origin to the lumbricals, then splits into four tendons that pierce the flexor digitorum brevis tendons to reach the distal phalanges of toes 2-5.
info.function: Curls the lateral four toes and helps grip the ground in push-off.
info.size: Main tendon about 5 mm diameter; digital slips 2 mm.
info.notes: Weakness of the long and short toe flexors against the pull of the extensors contributes to claw and hammer toes.

info.description: Deep flexor from the upper anterior and medial ulna and the interosseous membrane; its four tendons run through the carpal tunnel beneath and then through the split superficialis tendons to the distal phalanges.
info.function: The only muscle that bends the fingertips (distal interphalangeal joints); also flexes the other finger joints and the wrist.
info.size: About 25 cm to the palm.
info.notes: "Jersey finger" is avulsion of its ring-finger tendon when grabbing a shirt. The tendons are shown only as far as the knuckles.

info.description: Broad intermediate-layer flexor from the medial epicondyle, coronoid process and anterior radius; its four tendons pass through the carpal tunnel and split to insert on the middle phalanges of the fingers.
info.function: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal and knuckle joints of the fingers and helps flex the wrist.
info.size: About 25 cm to the palm.
info.notes: Tested by holding the other fingers straight and bending one finger at its middle joint. The tendons are shown only as far as the knuckles.

info.description: Powerful deep calf muscle arising from the lower two-thirds of the posterior fibula and interosseous membrane, lateral in the deep compartment; its fleshy fibres extend almost to the ankle.
info.function: Flexes the great toe - essential for the final push-off in walking - and assists plantarflexion and inversion.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm; about 35 cm with its tendon.
info.notes: Tendinitis where it passes behind the talus is common in ballet dancers ("dancer's tendinitis") from repeated pointe work.

info.description: Grooves the back of the talus, runs beneath the sustentaculum tali (which acts as its pulley) and along the sole between the sesamoids of the great toe to its distal phalanx.
info.function: Flexes the great toe and supports the medial arch.
info.size: About 20 cm long, 5 mm diameter.
info.notes: Can be trapped behind the talus (posterior ankle impingement), producing pain and triggering of the big toe.

info.description: Deep flexor arising from the anterior surface of the radius and interosseous membrane; its tendon passes through the carpal tunnel to the distal phalanx of the thumb.
info.function: Flexes the thumb, especially its tip joint.
info.size: About 20 cm long.
info.notes: Inability to bend the thumb tip (with an intact index fingertip) points to anterior interosseous nerve palsy. The tendon is shown only as far as the thumb's metacarpal.

info.description: Skin of the foot: very thick glabrous skin on the sole over the heel and ball, a raised medial longitudinal arch, thin skin on the dorsum and five toes (the big toe has two phalanges, the others three).
info.function: Bears body weight and friction in standing and walking and senses ground contact for balance.
info.size: Foot ~26 cm long, ~9.5 cm wide at the ball; plantar epidermis up to ~1.5 mm, heel skin several mm in total
info.notes: Loss of protective sensation in the sole (diabetic neuropathy) lets painless pressure ulcers develop — the commonest cause of non-traumatic amputation.

info.description: Subcutaneous fat of the foot, forming a specialised honeycomb heel pad of fat chambers walled by fibrous septa under the calcaneus, and a thin layer on the dorsum.
info.function: The heel pad absorbs the impact of heel strike, which reaches ~1–1.5 times body weight in walking.
info.size: Heel pad ~15–20 mm thick; dorsal fat ~2–3 mm
info.notes: Heel-pad atrophy with age is a common cause of heel pain that is mistaken for plantar fasciitis.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the fourth rib to the sternum.
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 9 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: Long bone of the palm behind the ring finger, with a base at the carpus, a slender shaft and a rounded head forming the knuckle.
info.function: Forms the skeleton of the palm and the knuckle joint of its finger.
info.size: ≈ 55 mm long
info.notes: The metacarpal heads are the knuckles seen when making a fist.

info.description: Long bone of the forefoot behind the fourth toe, with a wedge-shaped base, slender shaft and rounded head at the ball of the foot.
info.function: Forms a spoke of the foot's arches and a lever for walking.
info.size: ≈ 78 mm long
info.notes: Bunions (hallux valgus) develop at the first metatarsal head.

info.description: The fourth rib, a true (vertebrosternal) rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T4 and the vertebra above, its tubercle with the T4 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 29 cm
info.notes: Rib fractures are most common at the angle of the rib, the weakest point of the curve.

info.description: A small pit in the centre of the macula where the inner retinal layers are pushed aside so light falls directly on densely packed cones; it contains no rods and no blood vessels.
info.function: The point of sharpest vision: we move our eyes to put whatever we look at onto the fovea.
info.size: 1.5 mm across; central foveola 0.35 mm with ~150,000-200,000 cones per mm2.
info.notes: In a central retinal artery occlusion the fovea stands out as a "cherry-red spot" against the pale, swollen retina.

info.description: The largest lobe, forming the front of each hemisphere from the frontal pole back to the central sulcus and down to the lateral fissure; its flat underside (orbital surface) rests on the roofs of the orbits.
info.function: Planning, decisions, working memory, personality and social behaviour (prefrontal cortex), voluntary movement (primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus) and, usually on the left, speech production (Broca area).
info.size: About 7 cm from the frontal pole to the central sulcus; roughly a third of the cortical surface
info.notes: Prefrontal damage can change personality while sparing intelligence (Phineas Gage, 1848); a lesion of the left inferior frontal gyrus causes non-fluent (Broca) aphasia.

info.description: Air-filled space in the frontal bone behind the eyebrow, usually asymmetric and separated from its partner by a thin bony septum.
info.function: Lightens the skull, adds resonance to the voice and may act as a crumple zone protecting the brain.
info.size: About 3 cm high, 2.5 cm wide and 2 cm deep; absent at birth, it develops after about age 7.
info.notes: It drains through the frontonasal duct into the middle meatus; infection can spread to the orbit or through the thin posterior wall to the brain.

info.description: Frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis: a thin quadrilateral sheet over the forehead that arises from the galea aponeurotica (epicranial aponeurosis) and inserts into the skin of the eyebrow, blending with orbicularis oculi. It has no bony attachment.
info.function: Raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead horizontally.
info.size: About 6 cm tall and 5 cm wide per side, 1–2 mm thick.
info.notes: Supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve: in Bell's palsy the forehead cannot be wrinkled on that side, whereas it is spared in a stroke.

info.description: The smaller, shorter head of gastrocnemius, arising from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and joining the medial head in the calcaneal tendon.
info.function: Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee.
info.size: Belly about 15-18 cm long, 4-5 cm wide.
info.notes: A small sesamoid bone, the fabella, is found in its tendon in a minority of people and can be mistaken for a loose body on knee X-rays.

info.description: The larger head of gastrocnemius, arising from the back of the medial femoral condyle. It forms the prominent inner bulge of the calf, extends lower than the lateral head and blends into the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
info.function: Plantarflexes the ankle (push-off, standing on tiptoe) and flexes the knee.
info.size: Belly about 20 cm long, 6-7 cm wide.
info.notes: "Tennis leg" is a tear of its musculotendinous junction on the inner calf, typically in middle-aged recreational athletes.

name: Right gemelli and quadratus femoris
latin: Musculi gemelli superior et inferior; musculus quadratus femoris

info.description: Three small deep rotators behind the hip: the superior gemellus (from the ischial spine) and inferior gemellus (from the ischial tuberosity) run alongside the obturator internus tendon to the greater trochanter; below them quadratus femoris, a flat rectangle, passes from the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest.
info.function: Laterally rotate the hip and hold the femoral head in its socket.
info.size: Gemelli about 6-8 cm long and 1 cm thick; quadratus femoris about 7 x 4 cm.
info.notes: With piriformis and the obturators they form the "short external rotators" that are detached and repaired in the posterior approach to hip replacement.

info.description: Ring of fibrocartilage around the rim of the glenoid cavity, to which the long head of biceps is anchored above.
