info.function: Upper fibres elevate the shoulder (shrug) and extend the neck, middle fibres retract the scapula, lower fibres depress it; upper and lower parts together rotate the glenoid upwards for overhead reaching.
info.size: About 45 cm tall along the spine, up to ~1 cm thick in the neck.
info.notes: Supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI), which can be injured in surgery of the posterior triangle of the neck, leaving a drooping shoulder; note the tendinous "diamond" at the neck–back junction.

info.description: Small wedge-shaped distal-row bone at the base of the index metacarpal.
info.function: Distal-row carpal: forms a rigid unit with the metacarpals and transmits grip forces to the forearm.
info.notes: The least commonly fractured carpal bone.

info.description: The only muscle on the back of the arm, with three heads: the long head from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, the lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial groove and the deep medial head from below it. They join a broad flat tendon on the olecranon of the ulna.
info.function: The main extensor of the elbow; the long head also extends and adducts the shoulder.
info.size: About 30 cm long; the bulkiest muscle of the arm.
info.notes: The radial nerve spirals between its lateral and medial heads in the radial groove, where humeral shaft fractures injure it (wrist drop); the triceps reflex tests C7.

info.description: A crescent-shaped sensory ganglion the size of a fingernail, lodged in a dural pocket (Meckel's cave) on the tip of the petrous temporal bone. It holds the cell bodies of the facial sensory neurons; its convex front edge gives off the three divisions.
info.function: Relay station equivalent to a dorsal root ganglion for the face: the first-order sensory neurons of touch, pain and temperature sit here.
info.size: About 15-20 x 5 mm
info.notes: The ganglion can be reached with a needle through the foramen ovale to inject or heat it for intractable trigeminal neuralgia; it is also where the chickenpox virus hides before shingles of the face.

info.description: The largest cranial nerve. Its thick sensory root and small motor root leave the side of the pons and run forward over the petrous ridge to the trigeminal (Gasserian) ganglion in Meckel's cave.
info.function: Sensation for the whole face, scalp to the vertex, cornea, teeth, mouth and the front two-thirds of the tongue; motor to the chewing muscles.
info.size: Sensory root about 4-5 mm wide; 1.5 cm to the ganglion
info.notes: Trigeminal neuralgia - lightning stabs of facial pain - is usually caused by a looping artery pressing on this root where it enters the pons.

info.description: Pyramidal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row.
info.function: Proximal-row carpal: adapts its position as the wrist bends so the hand moves smoothly on the forearm.
info.notes: Second most commonly fractured carpal, often as a dorsal chip.

name: Right trochlea of the superior oblique

info.description: A small U-shaped loop of fibrocartilage attached to the trochlear fossa of the frontal bone, just inside the upper inner orbital rim, lined by a synovial sheath.
info.function: Acts as a pulley that redirects the pull of the superior oblique tendon backward and outward.
info.size: ~4-6 mm long; lies about 17 mm medial and 17 mm above the eye centre, just behind the rim.
info.notes: Inflammation here (trochleitis) causes pain at the inner upper corner of the orbit on looking up; the Brown syndrome is a tight tendon-trochlea complex that limits elevation in adduction.

info.description: The thinnest cranial nerve and the only one to leave the back of the brainstem. It winds around the midbrain, runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and enters the orbit to reach the superior oblique muscle.
info.function: Supplies the superior oblique, which turns the eye down and in and rotates it inward (intorsion) - essential for looking down stairs.
info.size: About 1 mm thick; the longest intracranial course (~7.5 cm)
info.notes: Its long, thin course makes it the cranial nerve most often damaged by closed head injury; patients tilt the head away from the weak side to fuse double images.

info.description: Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the twelfth rib (a short free tip).
info.function: Gives the rib cage the elasticity it needs for breathing and to absorb blows.
info.size: ≈ 1 cm long
info.notes: Costal cartilage often calcifies with age, stiffening the chest wall; inflammation of the costochondral joints (costochondritis) mimics heart pain.

info.description: The twelfth rib, a floating rib: a curved flattened bar whose head articulates with T12, its tubercle with the T12 transverse process, sloping down and forward to its costal cartilage.
info.function: Protects the thoracic organs and moves up and out with the intercostal muscles during breathing (bucket-handle motion).
info.size: Cross-section ≈ 6 × 11 mm; arc length ≈ 17 cm
info.notes: Floating ribs end free in the flank muscles and have no anterior attachment.

info.description: The medial (little-finger-side) forearm bone: a large hooked upper end (olecranon and coronoid process around the trochlear notch) that grips the humeral trochlea, tapering to a small head and styloid process at the wrist.
info.function: Forms the hinge of the elbow and the stable axis around which the radius rotates.
info.size: ≈ 25 cm long
info.notes: The olecranon is the point of the elbow; it is fractured by falls directly onto the elbow.

info.description: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery; it passes deep to the flexor muscles, descends along the medial (little-finger) side of the forearm with the ulnar nerve and crosses the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum beside the pisiform bone.
info.function: Supplies the medial forearm (including the common interosseous artery) and forms most of the superficial palmar arch.
info.size: ~3 mm diameter; ~23 cm long.
info.notes: The Allen test checks that the ulnar artery alone can supply the hand before the radial artery is cannulated or harvested for bypass grafts.

info.description: The main continuation of the medial cord. It runs down the medial arm, passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus (the "funny bone"), enters the forearm through flexor carpi ulnaris, runs under that muscle to the wrist and enters the hand through Guyon's canal beside the pisiform bone.
info.function: Motor to flexor carpi ulnaris, the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus and most small muscles of the hand (interossei, hypothenar muscles, medial lumbricals, adductor pollicis); sensation from the little finger and half of the ring finger.
info.size: About 4 mm thick; ~65 cm from the axilla to the little finger
info.notes: Knocking the funny bone jolts this nerve against the epicondyle. Chronic compression at the elbow (cubital tunnel) or wrist gives tingling in the little finger, a weak pinch (Froment sign) and eventually a claw hand.

info.description: A mobile fold of very thin skin over a layer of orbicularis muscle, a stiff tarsal plate and the palpebral conjunctiva. Its margin carries the lashes in front and the openings of the meibomian glands behind; a skin crease marks where the levator aponeurosis inserts.
info.function: Protects the cornea, spreads the tear film with every blink (15-20 per minute) and shuts out light during sleep.
info.size: Covers the top 1-2 mm of the cornea; crease ~8-10 mm above the margin; lid skin <1 mm thick, the thinnest in the body.
info.notes: A drooping upper lid (ptosis) can come from a stretched levator aponeurosis, a third-nerve palsy, Horner syndrome or myasthenia gravis.

info.description: Arises from the right main bronchus only 1–2 cm below the carina, above the pulmonary artery (hence "eparterial"), and splits into apical, posterior and anterior segmental bronchi.
info.function: Secondary (lobar) bronchus: conducts air to one lobe of the lung.
info.size: About 1–1.5 cm long, 8–10 mm wide.
info.notes: Lobar bronchi are the level at which the lung is removed in a lobectomy; their walls contain irregular cartilage plates instead of rings.

info.description: A plate of dense fibrous tissue that forms the skeleton of the upper lid, D-shaped and tallest in the middle. About 25-30 tall meibomian glands lie embedded in it vertically.
info.function: Keeps the lid stiff and curved to fit the globe; its glands secrete the oily layer of the tear film.
info.size: ~29 mm long, 10 mm tall centrally, 1 mm thick.
info.notes: A blocked meibomian gland forms a chalazion, a painless lump in the tarsus; everting the upper lid over the tarsus is how foreign bodies are found.

info.description: Muscular tube that carries urine from the renal pelvis down along the front of psoas major, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, runs down the pelvic side wall and pierces the bladder base obliquely.
info.function: Moves urine to the bladder by peristaltic waves (1–5 per minute); its oblique course through the bladder wall acts as a one-way valve against reflux.
info.size: 25–30 cm long, 3–5 mm in diameter.
info.notes: In men the vas deferens crosses above it near the bladder; in women the uterine artery passes over it beside the cervix ("water under the bridge").

info.description: Slender muscular tube in the upper edge of the broad ligament running from the uterine corner (intramural part) through the narrow isthmus and the wide, curving ampulla to the funnel-shaped infundibulum over the ovary.
info.function: Catches the ovulated egg, is the usual site of fertilisation (ampulla) and carries the early embryo to the uterus over 3–4 days by cilia and peristalsis.
info.size: 10–12 cm long; lumen about 1 mm at the isthmus and up to 1 cm in the ampulla.
info.notes: The ampulla is the commonest site of ectopic pregnancy; tying or removing the tubes gives permanent contraception.

info.description: An oblong membranous sac in the upper back part of the vestibule into which all three semicircular ducts open. On its floor lies a horizontal sensory patch (macula) covered by a gelatinous membrane studded with calcium-carbonate crystals, the otoconia.
info.function: Senses horizontal linear acceleration and tilt of the head relative to gravity.
info.size: About 3-4 mm long and 2 mm across.
info.notes: Otoconia that break loose and fall into the posterior semicircular canal cause benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), treated with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre.

info.description: Runs down the right side of the neck in the carotid sheath, crosses in front of the right subclavian artery (looping its recurrent laryngeal nerve under it), descends beside the trachea, passes behind the root of the right lung and spreads over the back of the oesophagus to become the posterior vagal trunk, which reaches the back of the stomach and sends a large branch to the coeliac plexus.
info.function: Parasympathetic and sensory supply to the heart (mainly the sinoatrial node), lungs and gut; via the coeliac branch it reaches the liver, pancreas, kidneys and intestine.
info.size: About 2-3 mm thick; ~55 cm long
info.notes: The right vagus mostly innervates the SA node and the left the AV node, so right-sided stimulation slows the heart rate more. Vagus nerve stimulators for epilepsy are implanted on the left to spare the heart.

info.description: Thick-walled muscular duct that continues from the tail of the epididymis, climbs in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal, hooks over the ureter and widens into the ampulla behind the bladder.
info.function: Propels sperm toward the ejaculatory duct by powerful peristalsis during ejaculation.
info.size: About 30–45 cm long and 2–3 mm thick, with a narrow lumen.
info.notes: It is the cord cut and tied in a vasectomy; it feels like a firm string in the upper scrotum.

info.description: Deepest head of the quadriceps, wrapped directly around the front and outer side of the femoral shaft beneath rectus femoris. It arises from the upper two-thirds of the anterior and lateral femur and inserts through the deep layer of the quadriceps tendon.
info.function: Extends the knee.
info.size: About 30 cm long, 1.5-2 cm thick.
info.notes: A small slip (articularis genus) lifts the suprapatellar bursa during extension; a "dead leg" contusion crushes it against the femur and can lead to myositis ossificans.

info.description: Largest head of the quadriceps, forming the bulk of the outer thigh. It arises from the greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the linea aspera, and inserts through the quadriceps tendon on the lateral border of the patella.
info.function: Extends the knee.
info.size: About 40 cm long and up to 8 cm wide; roughly 3 cm thick at mid-thigh.
info.notes: Common site for intramuscular injections in infants and for muscle biopsies; its lateral pull on the patella is balanced by vastus medialis.

info.description: The teardrop-shaped bulge above and inside the knee. It arises from the intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera; its lowest, almost horizontal fibres (vastus medialis obliquus) insert on the medial border of the patella and the quadriceps tendon.
info.function: Extends the knee and holds the patella medially in its groove during the last degrees of extension.
info.size: About 30 cm long; the teardrop is about 7 cm wide and 3 cm thick above the knee.
info.notes: Wastes quickly after knee injury or surgery; weakness of its oblique fibres is linked to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar maltracking.

info.description: The crescent-shaped chamber that forms most of the front (sternocostal) surface of the heart, wrapped around the left ventricle. It narrows upward into the smooth conus arteriosus (infundibulum) that leads to the pulmonary valve.
info.function: Pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and the lungs.
info.size: Wall 3–5 mm thick; volume similar to the left ventricle; systolic pressure only ~25 mmHg.
info.notes: Its inner wall is ridged by trabeculae carneae; the septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle.

info.description: The first branch of the subclavian artery. It climbs through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1, winds backwards over the arch of the atlas, enters the skull through the foramen magnum and joins its partner at the lower border of the pons to form the basilar artery.
info.function: Supplies the spinal cord, brainstem, cerebellum and the back of the cerebrum (posterior circulation).
info.size: ~3–4 mm diameter; the left is often larger.
info.notes: Can be torn (dissected) by sudden neck twisting, a cause of stroke in young adults; about 20% of brain blood flow comes through the two vertebral arteries.

info.description: The balance part of CN VIII: a superior division from the utricle and the anterior and lateral ampullae, and an inferior division from the saccule and the posterior ampulla. The cell bodies form Scarpa's ganglion in the internal acoustic meatus, where it joins the cochlear nerve.
info.function: Carries signals of head rotation, tilt and acceleration to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum.
info.size: About 20,000 fibres.
info.notes: Vestibular neuritis, a viral inflammation of this nerve, causes days of severe spinning vertigo without hearing loss.

info.description: The central chamber of the bony labyrinth, between the cochlea in front and the semicircular canals behind, with the oval window in its lateral wall. It contains the two otolith organs, the utricle and the saccule.
info.function: Houses the gravity and linear-acceleration sensors and connects the cochlea to the semicircular canals.
info.size: About 4 mm wide, 5 mm long and 3 mm deep.
info.notes: Its medial wall borders the internal acoustic meatus, through which the vestibular nerves leave for the brainstem.

info.description: A short, thick sensory nerve that crosses the cerebellopontine angle from the brainstem to the internal acoustic meatus together with the facial nerve. Inside the temporal bone it splits into the cochlear nerve (hearing) and the vestibular nerve (balance).
info.function: Hearing from the cochlea and head position and motion from the utricle, saccule and semicircular canals.
info.size: About 3 mm thick, 2 cm from brainstem to meatus
info.notes: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) grows on its vestibular part in the meatus, causing slowly progressive one-sided deafness and tinnitus before it presses on the facial nerve and cerebellum.

info.description: A thin, glistening serous membrane that tightly covers the lung surface and dips into the fissures between the lobes.
info.function: Secretes and spreads pleural fluid so the lung glides smoothly against the chest wall during breathing.
info.size: A single layer of mesothelial cells on connective tissue, roughly 30–80 µm thick.
info.notes: The visceral pleura has no pain fibres; chest pain in pneumonia (pleurisy) starts only when inflammation reaches the parietal pleura.

info.description: The clear gel that fills the large cavity behind the lens (about 80% of the eye's volume). It is 99% water held in a mesh of collagen fibrils and hyaluronic acid, attached firmly at the ora serrata and optic disc.
info.function: Keeps the globe inflated, holds the retina in place and transmits light to it.
info.size: Volume ~4 ml; about 16-17 mm from lens to retina.
info.notes: With age it liquefies and can peel off the retina (posterior vitreous detachment), causing floaters; vitreous samples are used in forensic medicine.

info.description: The true vocal cord: a fold of mucosa over the vocal ligament and vocalis muscle, running from the inside of the thyroid angle to the arytenoid vocal process; the two folds bound the V-shaped rima glottidis.
info.function: Vibrates in the exhaled airstream to produce voice, and closes tightly to protect the airway and build pressure for a cough.
info.size: About 17–23 mm long in men and 12–17 mm in women; vibrates at ~100–150 Hz (men) and ~180–250 Hz (women) in speech.
info.notes: Swelling of its loose superficial layer (Reinke's oedema) in smokers deepens the voice; hoarseness lasting more than 3 weeks warrants laryngoscopy.

name: Right zonular fibres (suspensory ligament of the lens)

info.description: Hundreds of fine, transparent fibrillin threads running from the ciliary processes and pars plana to the capsule in front of, at, and behind the lens equator.
info.function: Hold the lens centred behind the pupil and transmit the pull of the ciliary body: taut zonules flatten the lens for distance vision.
info.size: Each fibre 5-30 micrometres thick; the zonular gap spans ~0.5-2 mm.
info.notes: In Marfan syndrome (fibrillin defect) the zonules are weak and the lens often dislocates upward (ectopia lentis).

info.description: The cheekbone: a four-sided body forming the prominence of the cheek, with a frontal process up the lateral orbital rim and a temporal process joining the temporal bone to complete the zygomatic arch.
info.function: Shapes the cheek, forms the lateral wall and floor of the orbit and anchors the masseter.
info.size: ≈ 5 cm wide, 4 cm tall
info.notes: A "tripod" fracture separates it at its three sutures after a blow to the cheek.

info.description: Slender strap from the lateral surface of the zygomatic bone running down and forwards to the modiolus at the corner of the mouth.
info.function: Draws the angle of the mouth upwards and outwards — the principal smiling muscle.
info.size: About 6 cm long and 1 cm wide.
info.notes: A bifid zygomaticus major is thought to cause cheek dimples; a genuine (Duchenne) smile combines it with orbicularis oculi.

info.description: Wedge-shaped bone of five fused sacral vertebrae, curved concave-forward, with four pairs of sacral foramina and a median crest behind.
info.function: Transmits the weight of the trunk to the hip bones through the sacroiliac joints and forms the back wall of the pelvis.
info.size: ≈ 105 mm wide at the base, 110 mm tall
info.notes: The sacral promontory (front edge of S1) is an obstetric landmark for measuring the pelvic inlet.

info.description: Short scalp hair covering the vault of the skull from the frontal hairline and temples to the nape. Each hair is a dead keratin shaft growing from a living follicle in the dermis.
info.function: Insulates the head against heat loss and sunlight, cushions minor blows and has social and sensory roles (hair follicles are wrapped by touch receptors).
info.size: ~100 000 follicles; each hair 50–100 µm thick, growing ~1 cm per month for 2–7 years (anagen) before shedding
info.notes: Losing 50–100 scalp hairs a day is normal. Male-pattern baldness is driven by dihydrotestosterone shrinking follicles at the temples and crown.

info.description: Pouch of thin, wrinkled, pigmented skin containing the dartos smooth muscle, divided by a midline raphe and septum into two compartments, each holding a testis, epididymis and the lower spermatic cord.
info.function: Keeps the testes 2–3 °C below body temperature by wrinkling or relaxing (dartos) and by the cremaster muscle raising or lowering them.
info.size: About 7 cm across and 8–10 cm tall.
info.notes: The raphe marks where the two labioscrotal swellings fused in the embryo; their female counterpart is the labia majora.

info.description: A cluster of grape-like alveoli beside the upper follicle that empties into the follicle canal by holocrine secretion (whole cells burst to release their contents).
info.function: Secretes sebum, an oily mix of triglycerides, wax esters and squalene that waterproofs and softens skin and hair.
info.size: ~0.2–2 mm; largest on the face, scalp and upper trunk
info.notes: Acne develops when a sebaceous follicle is plugged by sebum and keratin and colonised by Cutibacterium acnes.

info.description: A cutaneous nerve fibre branching to an onion-like lamellated (Pacinian) corpuscle in the deep dermis, an encapsulated Meissner corpuscle in a dermal papilla, and bare free nerve endings that penetrate the epidermis.
info.function: Pacinian corpuscles sense vibration and deep pressure, Meissner corpuscles light touch, and free endings pain, itch and temperature.
info.size: Pacinian ~1 × 0.5 mm, Meissner ~0.1 mm (magnified here)
info.notes: Meissner corpuscles are densest in the fingertips and lips and decline with age, one reason fine touch fades in the elderly.

info.description: S-shaped loop on its own mesentery (sigmoid mesocolon) from the pelvic brim to the rectum in front of the third sacral vertebra.
info.function: Stores faeces until defecation.
info.size: About 40 cm long (very variable) and 3-4 cm wide.
info.notes: Its long mobile mesentery lets it twist (sigmoid volvulus), and it is the commonest site of diverticulitis.

info.description: A small crescent of specialised pacemaker cells in the wall of the right atrium where the superior vena cava enters, at the top of the crista terminalis.
info.function: Fires spontaneously 60–100 times a minute, starting every normal heartbeat (sinus rhythm).
info.size: About 10–20 mm long, 3–5 mm wide, ~1 mm deep under the epicardium.
info.notes: Supplied by the SA-nodal artery (from the right coronary artery in ~60% of people); its rate is sped up by sympathetic nerves and slowed by the vagus.

name: Skin of the head (face and scalp)

info.description: The skin covering the face and scalp, sculpted over the skull: forehead, brow ridges, orbits, nose, cheekbones, lips, chin and jaw line. Facial skin is thin, very vascular and rich in sebaceous glands; scalp skin is thick and carries about 100 000 hair follicles.
info.function: Protects the head, senses touch, pain and temperature (trigeminal nerve), and is moved by the muscles of facial expression, which insert directly into it.
info.size: Face–scalp height ~23 cm (chin to crown), head width ~15.5 cm, length ~19.5 cm; skin 0.5 mm (eyelids) to 3–5 mm (scalp) thick
info.notes: Scalp wounds bleed heavily because the vessels are held open by dense connective tissue. The scalp layers spell SCALP: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

info.description: Thin, mobile skin of the neck showing the sternocleidomastoid ridges running from behind the ears to the top of the sternum and, in front, the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple, larger in men).
info.function: Covers and allows free movement of the neck; its natural horizontal skin creases are used by surgeons to hide scars.
info.size: Neck ~12 cm long, ~37 cm circumference (adult male); skin ~1–1.5 mm thick
info.notes: The platysma muscle lies directly under this skin; thyroid surgery is done through a transverse "collar" incision in a skin crease about 2 cm above the sternal notch.

info.description: Thin, hairless, loosely attached skin over the shaft that slides freely and folds over the glans as the prepuce (foreskin).
info.function: Covers the erectile bodies while allowing large changes in size.
info.size: Flaccid penis about 9 cm long and 9–10 cm around (average).
info.notes: Lymph from the penile skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes, whereas the glans also drains to deep nodes.

info.description: The skin of the chest, abdomen, back, shoulders and buttocks, showing the relief of the clavicles, pectoral muscles, rectus abdominis, umbilicus, inguinal grooves, spine furrow, scapulae, deltoids and buttocks.
info.function: Barrier against water loss, microbes and UV; thermoregulation through sweat and blood flow; touch, pressure and pain sensing; vitamin D synthesis.
info.size: Largest part of the ~1.8 m² body surface (trunk ≈ 36 % by the rule of nines); 1–2 mm thick on the front, up to ~4 mm on the upper back
info.notes: The skin of the back has the thickest dermis in the body. Skin tension (Langer) lines run mostly horizontally on the trunk, so horizontal incisions heal with finer scars.

info.description: Mobile muscular fold covered with mucosa that hangs from the back edge of the hard palate and ends in the uvula; laterally it continues into the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
info.function: Rises and tenses during swallowing and speech to seal off the nasopharynx so food and air go the right way.
info.size: About 3 cm long and up to 1 cm thick.
info.notes: If it is paralysed (e.g. vagus nerve injury) fluids regurgitate into the nose and speech sounds nasal; it is also a major site of vibration in snoring.

info.description: Butterfly-shaped bone at the centre of the skull base: a hollow body with the sella turcica (seat of the pituitary), greater and lesser wings, and pterygoid plates hanging below.
info.function: Keystone of the cranial base, joining with every other cranial bone; transmits the optic nerves and many other nerves and vessels.
info.size: ≈ 7 cm across the greater wings
info.notes: The pituitary gland is reached surgically through the sphenoid sinus (transsphenoidal surgery).

info.description: Paired, often unequal air spaces in the body of the sphenoid bone, directly below the pituitary gland and between the cavernous sinuses.
info.function: Lightens the skull base; drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior turbinate.
info.size: About 2 cm in each dimension (combined volume ~7 ml).
info.notes: Surgeons reach pituitary tumours through the nose and this sinus (transsphenoidal surgery); the optic nerves and internal carotids bulge into its walls.

info.description: The cable of nervous tissue continuing the medulla from the foramen magnum down the vertebral canal to the conus medullaris at the L1/L2 disc. It is thicker in the cervical enlargement (C4-T1, for the arms) and the lumbar enlargement (T11-L1, for the legs), with an anterior median fissure in front.
info.function: Carries sensory tracts up and motor tracts down between brain and body, and contains the circuits for spinal reflexes and rhythmic walking patterns; 31 pairs of spinal nerves leave it.
info.size: About 42-45 cm long; ~1 cm across (1.3-1.4 cm wide at the cervical enlargement); ~35 g
info.notes: Because the cord stops at L1/L2 while the canal continues, lumbar punctures are done at L3/L4 or L4/L5, below the cord, where the needle only meets floating nerve roots.

info.description: The tough tube of dura that continues the cranial dura through the foramen magnum and encloses the spinal cord, CSF and cauda equina, ending as a blind sac at the level of S2; each nerve root takes a sleeve of it into its foramen.
info.function: Protects the cord and holds the CSF of the spinal subarachnoid space; the fat-filled epidural space outside it cushions it against the bone.
info.size: About 45-50 cm long; 1.5-2 cm across; ends at S2
info.notes: Epidural anaesthesia is injected outside this sac; a spinal anaesthetic or lumbar puncture pierces it (and the arachnoid) below L2 to reach the CSF.

info.description: The thickened connective-tissue shelf on the modiolar side of the cochlear duct, from whose lip the tectorial membrane hangs.
info.function: Anchors the tectorial membrane over the hair cells.
info.size: Real height about 50 micrometres.
info.notes: Its interdental cells secrete the tectorial membrane during development.

info.description: A soft, dark-purple, fist-sized organ tucked under the left dome of the diaphragm behind the stomach, lying along the 9th-11th ribs and fully protected by the rib cage. Its smooth outer (diaphragmatic) surface is convex; the inner (visceral) surface is concave and carries the hilum where the splenic vessels enter. A thin fibrous capsule wraps it.
info.function: Filters the blood: old and damaged red cells are destroyed by macrophages in the red pulp, while the white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne microbes.
info.size: About 12 x 7 x 4 cm, 150 g (range 80-300 g); the "odd numbers" rule: 1 x 3 x 5 inches, 7 oz, ribs 9-11
info.notes: The organ most often injured in blunt abdominal trauma; it can bleed massively and sometimes must be removed. After splenectomy, patients are vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Haemophilus) and need vaccination. A normal spleen cannot be felt: it must enlarge 2-3 times to be palpable below the ribs.

info.description: The largest coeliac branch; it runs a markedly tortuous course to the left along the upper border of the pancreas, behind the stomach, and divides into several branches at the hilum of the spleen.
info.function: Supplies the spleen, the body and tail of the pancreas, and via short gastric and left gastro-omental branches the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach.
info.size: ~5–6 mm diameter; ~10–12 cm long.
info.notes: Its coiling allows for movement of the stomach and spleen; splenic artery aneurysms are the commonest visceral aneurysms and can rupture in pregnancy.

info.description: The slit on the concave visceral surface where the splenic artery and vein, lymphatics and nerves enter and leave, wrapped in the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments. The tail of the pancreas reaches right into the hilum.
info.function: Entry and exit for the spleen's rich blood supply, about 5 % of the cardiac output (250-300 ml per minute).
info.size: About 5-6 cm long; the splenic artery splits into 5-7 hilar branches
info.notes: Because the pancreatic tail sits in the hilum, splenectomy can injure it and cause a pancreatic fistula. Accessory spleens (splenunculi) are found near the hilum in 10-15 % of people.

info.description: The bulk of the spleen: a spongy meshwork of blood-filled sinusoids and cords (of Billroth) packed with macrophages, which gives the organ its dark red colour.
info.function: Removes old, rigid or parasite-laden red cells, recycles their iron, and holds about a third of the body's platelets in reserve.
info.size: About 75-80 % of the spleen's volume
info.notes: Red cells must squeeze through 1-3 micrometre slits between the sinusoid lining cells; sickle cells and spherocytes cannot, so they are trapped and destroyed, which is why sickle cell disease causes haemolysis and eventually a scarred, non-functioning "autosplenectomised" spleen.

info.description: Leaves the hilum of the spleen and runs to the right in a groove on the back of the body of the pancreas, below the splenic artery, to join the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck. It receives the inferior mesenteric vein.
info.function: Drains the spleen, pancreas and part of the stomach into the portal system.
info.size: ~1 cm diameter.
info.notes: Pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer can cause it to clot, producing isolated gastric varices.

info.description: Millimetre-sized whitish nodules (Malpighian corpuscles) scattered through the red pulp: sheaths of T lymphocytes around the central arterioles, with B-cell follicles attached to them.
info.function: Mounts antibody responses against antigens carried in the blood; the spleen holds about a quarter of the body's lymphocytes.
info.size: Each nodule 0.5-1 mm; together 20-25 % of the spleen
info.notes: Visible to the naked eye as pale specks on the cut surface; the nodules enlarge dramatically in glandular fever (infectious mononucleosis) and in lymphoma.

info.description: J-shaped muscular sac in the left upper abdomen: the cardia where the esophagus enters, the dome-shaped fundus under the left diaphragm, the body, and the antrum narrowing to the pylorus. The short concave right border is the lesser curvature, the long convex left border the greater curvature.
info.function: Stores a meal and churns it with acid and pepsin into semi-liquid chyme, which it releases a little at a time into the duodenum.
info.size: About 25 cm long along the greater curvature; holds 1-1.5 L after a meal (up to about 4 L when stretched), about 50 mL when empty.
info.notes: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid (pH 1.5-3.5) and intrinsic factor, without which vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed (pernicious anaemia).

info.description: The fatty layer (hypodermis) under the skin of the face and scalp. On the scalp it is a dense fibro-fatty layer carrying the vessels; in the face it forms discrete fat compartments, including the buccal fat pad in the cheek.
info.function: Pads and shapes the face, insulates, and carries the blood vessels and nerves to the skin.
info.size: About 2–6 mm thick on the scalp; facial compartments up to ~1–2 cm (buccal pad ~10 ml)
info.notes: Facial fat compartments shrink and descend with age, which is a major cause of hollow temples, tear troughs and jowls.

info.description: The layer of fat and loose connective tissue between the neck skin and the platysma / deep cervical fascia.
info.function: Lets the skin glide over the neck muscles and stores energy.
info.size: Usually 3–10 mm thick; thickest under the chin (submental fat)
info.notes: Excess submental fat produces a "double chin"; the external jugular vein runs in this layer and is visible when venous pressure is raised.

info.description: The hypodermis of the trunk: fat lobules separated by fibrous septa, split over the lower abdomen into a fatty superficial layer (Camper fascia) and a membranous deep layer (Scarpa fascia).
info.function: Energy store, thermal insulation and shock absorber; also an endocrine organ secreting leptin and adiponectin.
info.size: Typically 5–30 mm; thickest over the lower abdomen, flanks and buttocks
info.notes: Men tend to store fat centrally (abdomen), women on the hips and buttocks; waist circumference is a better predictor of cardiovascular risk than body weight.

info.description: The superior hypogastric plexus is a flat band of fibres in front of the fifth lumbar vertebra, just below the aortic bifurcation. It divides into right and left hypogastric nerves that descend to the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses on the sides of the rectum, where the parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) join them.
info.function: Controls the bladder, rectum and sexual organs: parasympathetic fibres empty the bladder and cause erection, sympathetic fibres close the bladder neck and drive ejaculation.
info.size: Superior plexus ~4-5 cm long; each inferior plexus ~4 cm across
info.notes: Injury to these plexuses during rectal or prostate surgery can cause bladder and erectile dysfunction, so surgeons use nerve-sparing techniques; blocking the superior plexus relieves pelvic cancer pain.

info.description: Leaves the front of the aorta at L1, about 1 cm below the coeliac trunk, passes behind the neck of the pancreas and over the left renal vein and third part of the duodenum, then runs down in the root of the mesentery towards the right iliac fossa, giving jejunal, ileal and colic branches.
info.function: Supplies the midgut: the duodenum beyond the bile duct, jejunum, ileum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and two-thirds of the transverse colon.
info.size: ~6–8 mm diameter; ~20 cm long.
info.notes: Sudden blockage (usually an embolus) causes acute mesenteric ischaemia with pain out of proportion to the examination findings; the narrow aorto-mesenteric angle can squeeze the duodenum or left renal vein ("nutcracker").

info.description: A continuation of the celiac plexus that surrounds the superior mesenteric artery like a sleeve, with a small superior mesenteric ganglion at the artery's origin; its fibres follow the arterial branches into the mesentery.
info.function: Autonomic supply to the small intestine, caecum, appendix, ascending and most of the transverse colon (midgut): sympathetic fibres slow peristalsis and narrow vessels, vagal fibres stimulate secretion and motility.
info.size: Sleeve ~1 cm wide along 5-10 cm of the artery
info.notes: Midgut pain from these fibres is felt around the umbilicus, which is why appendicitis begins as vague central abdominal pain before settling in the right lower quadrant.

info.description: Runs up in the root of the mesentery to the right of the superior mesenteric artery, passing in front of the third part of the duodenum and the uncinate process, to end behind the pancreatic neck by joining the splenic vein.
info.function: Drains the small intestine, caecum, appendix, ascending and transverse colon into the portal vein.
info.size: ~1 cm diameter.
info.notes: On CT a whirlpool of the SMV around the SMA is the sign of midgut volvulus.

info.description: A large valveless vein formed behind the right first costal cartilage by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins. It descends to the right of the ascending aorta, receives the azygos vein from behind and opens into the top of the right atrium.
info.function: Returns blood from the head, neck, upper limbs and chest wall to the heart.
info.size: ~7 cm long, ~2 cm diameter.
info.notes: Compression by lung cancer or lymphoma causes superior vena cava syndrome (swollen face and arms, distended neck veins); central venous catheter tips are placed at its junction with the right atrium.

info.description: The axon ends in fine terminal branches whose swollen tips (boutons) come within 20-40 nanometres of the next cell. Each bouton is packed with vesicles of neurotransmitter lined up at the release zone facing the synaptic cleft.
info.function: Converts the electrical impulse into a chemical message: calcium entering the bouton triggers vesicles to release transmitter (e.g. acetylcholine or glutamate) that binds receptors on the next cell.
info.size: Boutons 1-2 micrometres; synaptic cleft 20-40 nanometres
info.notes: Most nerve drugs and toxins act here - antidepressants, botulinum toxin (blocks acetylcholine release) and nerve agents; in myasthenia gravis antibodies attack the acetylcholine receptors.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 28 mm wide × 22 mm deep × 20 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 39 mm wide × 29 mm deep × 25 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 40 mm wide × 30 mm deep × 25 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 41 mm wide × 31 mm deep × 26 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 29 mm wide × 23 mm deep × 21 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.

info.size: Body 30 mm wide × 24 mm deep × 21 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.size: Body 32 mm wide × 24 mm deep × 22 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.size: Body 33 mm wide × 25 mm deep × 22 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 34 mm wide × 26 mm deep × 23 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 35 mm wide × 27 mm deep × 23 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 36 mm wide × 28 mm deep × 24 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: A thoracic vertebra: heart-shaped body with costal facets for the ribs, long spinous process angled downward and sturdy transverse processes.
info.function: Anchors the ribs and protects the spinal cord while allowing limited rotation of the chest.
info.size: Body 38 mm wide × 28 mm deep × 24 mm tall; canal ≈ 16 mm
info.notes: Overlapping, downward-sloping spines limit extension of the thoracic spine.

info.description: Narrow left end running in the splenorenal ligament to the hilum of the spleen; it has the highest density of islets.
info.function: Its acinar cells secrete about 1.5 L a day of enzyme-rich alkaline juice into the duodenum; scattered islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
info.size: About 2 cm high, tapering to a blunt tip.
info.notes: Its closeness to the splenic hilum means it can be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.

info.description: A gelatinous, acellular ribbon anchored to the spiral limbus that floats over the hair cells; the tallest stereocilia of the outer hair cells are embedded in its underside, while those of the inner hair cells stand free just beneath it.
info.function: Shears against the stereocilia when the basilar membrane moves, bending them and opening their ion channels.
info.size: Real thickness about 30 micrometres, width 0.1-0.2 mm.
info.notes: Mutations in its collagen and tectorin proteins cause inherited forms of deafness.

info.description: A tent-shaped sheet of dura roofing the posterior cranial fossa: it separates the occipital lobes above from the cerebellum below, is attached to the transverse sinus grooves and petrous ridges, and has a U-shaped free edge (the tentorial notch) around the midbrain.
info.function: Supports the occipital lobes so they do not press on the cerebellum and divides the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments.
info.size: About 10-11 cm wide; the notch is ~3 cm wide and 5 cm long
info.notes: Raised supratentorial pressure can squeeze the uncus of the temporal lobe through the notch (uncal herniation), stretching the oculomotor nerve and dilating the pupil.

info.description: Magnified view (~×10) of one pulmonary acinus: a terminal bronchiole, the last purely conducting airway, splits into respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts.
info.function: Carries air into the gas-exchanging acinus; beyond this point the walls are lined by alveoli.
info.size: Real terminal bronchioles are about 0.5 mm wide; an acinus is 6–10 mm across and there are ~30,000 of them.
info.notes: Club (Clara) cells in the bronchiolar lining secrete protective proteins; centrilobular emphysema from smoking begins at the respiratory bronchioles.

info.description: A narrow vertical slit in the midline between the two thalami, floored by the hypothalamus; small recesses point toward the optic chiasm, the pituitary stalk and the pineal gland.
info.function: Passes CSF from the lateral ventricles (via the foramina of Monro) back to the cerebral aqueduct.
info.size: About 2-3 cm long, 2 cm high and only 3-5 mm wide
info.notes: Its width on CT is a sensitive sign of hydrocephalus or brain atrophy; a colloid cyst at its roof can block both foramina of Monro suddenly.

info.description: The largest lymph vessel in the body. It begins at the cisterna chyli, passes up through the aortic opening of the diaphragm, climbs the back of the chest between the aorta and the azygos vein, crosses from right to left behind the oesophagus at the level of T4-T6, arches over the top of the left lung at the root of the neck and empties into the junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins.
info.function: Returns 2-4 litres of lymph a day, from everything except the right arm and right side of the head and chest, back into the bloodstream.
info.size: About 38-45 cm long, 3-5 mm in diameter, with valves along its length and at its mouth
info.notes: Tearing it during chest surgery or by a penetrating injury fills the pleural space with milky chyle (chylothorax), which can drain litres a day and starve the patient of fat and lymphocytes.

info.description: Three nerves on each side that leave the thoracic sympathetic ganglia and run down and forward over the sides of the vertebral bodies, piercing the crura of the diaphragm: the greater splanchnic (roots T5-T9) ends in the celiac ganglion, the lesser (T10-T11) in the aorticorenal ganglion and the least (T12) in the renal plexus.
info.function: Carry preganglionic sympathetic fibres that pass through the chain without synapsing, to relay in the abdominal prevertebral ganglia (and directly to the adrenal medulla), plus pain fibres from the upper abdominal organs.
info.size: Greater splanchnic ~2-3 mm thick and ~20 cm long; lesser and least thinner
info.notes: Because they carry visceral pain, blocking or cutting them (splanchnicectomy) relieves the severe pain of pancreatic cancer and chronic pancreatitis.

info.description: A soft, pinkish-grey, two-lobed gland in the front of the upper chest, tucked behind the breastbone (manubrium) and in front of the pericardium and great vessels. It is largest in childhood and, after puberty, slowly shrinks and is replaced by fat (involution).
info.function: Trains T lymphocytes: immature cells arriving from the bone marrow mature here and are selected so that they attack foreign antigens but tolerate the body's own tissues.
info.size: About 5 x 4 x 1-2 cm in an adult (10-20 g); heaviest at puberty (30-40 g), relatively largest in infancy
info.notes: Thymomas are linked to myasthenia gravis (10-15 % of patients have one) and removing the thymus can improve the disease. DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) leaves the thymus absent or tiny, with too few T cells.

info.description: The largest laryngeal cartilage: two quadrilateral plates of hyaline cartilage fused in front at an angle that forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple), with superior and inferior horns on the posterior borders.
info.function: Shields the larynx and anchors the vocal folds, which attach to the inside of its angle.
info.size: About 3–4 cm wide and 2.5–3 cm high; the laminae meet at ~90° in men and ~120° in women.
info.notes: The cricothyroid muscle tilts it forward on the cricoid to stretch the vocal folds and raise pitch; it often ossifies with age.

info.description: The narrow bridge of thyroid tissue joining the two lobes across the front of the windpipe, at the level of the 2nd to 4th tracheal rings.
info.function: Same follicular tissue as the lobes — makes T4/T3 — and physically links them into one gland.
info.size: About 1.25 cm tall and wide, 3–6 mm thick
info.notes: In about half of people a pyramidal lobe rises from the isthmus towards the hyoid, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct. Surgeons doing a tracheostomy either divide the isthmus or work just below it.

info.description: Muscular organ filling the floor of the mouth. Its upper surface (dorsum) is covered with papillae; a V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, separates the oral two-thirds from the lumpy pharyngeal third, with a row of 8-12 large circumvallate papillae just in front of it.
info.function: Moves food during chewing, pushes the bolus into the pharynx when swallowing, carries most taste buds and shapes speech sounds.
info.size: About 10 cm from tip to root (about 6.5 cm lies in the mouth), about 5 cm wide; roughly 70 g.
info.notes: All its muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII) except palatoglossus (vagus). A tongue that deviates when protruded points to the side of a hypoglossal nerve lesion.

info.description: The windpipe: a flexible tube running from the cricoid cartilage (C6) down to the carina at the sternal angle (T4/T5), held open by C-shaped cartilage rings.
info.function: Conducts air between the larynx and the bronchi; its ciliated mucosa sweeps mucus and trapped particles up towards the throat (mucociliary escalator).
info.size: 10–12 cm long and about 2 cm in outer diameter in adults, with 16–20 cartilage rings.
info.notes: It shifts away from a tension pneumothorax and towards a collapsed lung; a tracheostomy is made through the 2nd–4th rings, just below the thyroid isthmus.

info.description: Eighteen horseshoe-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage embedded in the tracheal wall, open at the back where the trachea touches the oesophagus.
info.function: Keep the airway from collapsing under the negative pressure of inspiration while leaving the posterior wall flexible.
info.size: Each ring is about 4 mm high and 1 mm thick, joined to its neighbours by fibrous annular ligaments.
info.notes: The rings often calcify with age; congenital complete "O-rings" are a cause of tracheal stenosis in infants.

info.description: A band of smooth muscle and fibro-elastic membrane that closes the gap between the ends of the C-rings on the back of the trachea, directly in front of the oesophagus.
info.function: Contracts to narrow the trachea and speed up airflow when coughing; its pliability lets a swallowed food bolus bulge forwards.
info.size: About 1.5 cm wide and 1–2 mm thick along the whole tracheal length.
info.notes: Because the back wall is membranous, an oesophageal foreign body can compress the airway, and tracheo-oesophageal fistulas form here.

info.description: Most mobile part of the colon, slung on the transverse mesocolon from the hepatic flexure to the higher splenic flexure and sagging below the stomach; the greater omentum hangs from it.
info.function: Continues water absorption and bacterial fermentation, compacting the contents into faeces.
info.size: About 45 cm long and about 5 cm wide.
info.notes: The region near the splenic flexure is a watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries, so it is vulnerable to ischaemic colitis.

info.description: The right atrioventricular valve, with anterior, posterior and septal leaflets anchored by chordae tendineae to the papillary muscles of the right ventricle.
info.function: Allows blood to pass from the right atrium to the right ventricle and closes in systole to prevent regurgitation into the right atrium and veins.
info.size: Largest valve: annulus ~3.5–4 cm diameter (circumference 11–13 cm); opening area 5–8 cm².
info.notes: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves makes the first heart sound (S1); tricuspid endocarditis is typical in people who inject drugs.

info.description: The thick sensory root and small motor root leave the lateral side of the mid-pons where it joins the middle cerebellar peduncle. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Sensation from the face, mouth and cornea; motor to the muscles of chewing.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 5.2 mm thick
info.notes: Trigeminal neuralgia is often caused by an artery looping against this root entry zone; microvascular decompression can cure it.

info.description: The only cranial nerve to leave the back of the brainstem, just below the inferior colliculus; its fibres cross before exiting. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Motor to the superior oblique muscle, which turns the eye down and in.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 1.2 mm thick
info.notes: The thinnest cranial nerve (~1 mm); its long course makes it vulnerable in head injury.

info.description: The longest tooth, with one pointed cusp and a single very long root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grips and tears food and guides the jaw in side-to-side movements.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.5 × 8.0 mm, 10.0 mm tall; root ≈ 17 mm
info.notes: Canine roots can reach 17 mm; upper canines are often called eye teeth.

info.description: Chisel-shaped tooth with a thin cutting edge and a single conical root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 8.5 × 7.0 mm, 10.5 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: Central incisors erupt at about 7 years (lower first) and are the teeth most often chipped in falls.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and three roots (two buccal, one palatal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 10.0 × 11.0 mm, 7.5 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: The first molar erupts at about 6 years (the "six-year molar") and is the key to the bite.

info.description: Transitional tooth with two cusps (buccal and lingual) on its biting surface and usually two roots. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 7.0 × 9.0 mm, 8.5 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: First premolars are the teeth most often extracted to make space in orthodontics.

info.description: Chisel-shaped tooth with a thin cutting edge and a single conical root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Bites and cuts food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 6.5 × 6.0 mm, 9.0 mm tall; root ≈ 13 mm
info.notes: Upper lateral incisors are the most often congenitally missing teeth after wisdom teeth.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and three roots (two buccal, one palatal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 9.0 × 11.0 mm, 7.0 mm tall; root ≈ 12 mm
info.notes: The second molar erupts at about 12 years.

info.description: Transitional tooth with two cusps (buccal and lingual) on its biting surface and a single root. The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Holds and crushes food.
info.size: Crown ≈ 6.5 × 9.0 mm, 7.8 mm tall; root ≈ 14 mm
info.notes: Premolars replace the deciduous molars at 10–12 years.

info.description: Large grinding tooth with four cusps around a central fossa and three roots (two buccal, one palatal). The crown is covered with enamel, the hardest substance in the body.
info.function: Grinds food into a paste during chewing.
info.size: Crown ≈ 8.5 × 10.0 mm, 6.5 mm tall; root ≈ 11 mm
info.notes: The wisdom tooth erupts at 17–25 years, if at all, and is often impacted.

info.description: The upper lip vermilion, with the central tubercle and the Cupid's-bow border below the philtrum. The red colour comes from blood in capillaries seen through a thin, non-keratinised, hair-less epithelium.
info.function: Closes the mouth, seals around food and drink, shapes speech sounds and is one of the most touch-sensitive areas of the body.
info.size: Vermilion ~5 cm wide, ~8–9 mm high at the midline
info.notes: The lips lack sweat and sebaceous glands and so dry and crack easily; the vermilion border must be realigned exactly when repairing a cut lip or cleft lip.

info.description: Hollow muscular reservoir behind the pubic symphysis. Its wall is the detrusor muscle (interlacing smooth-muscle bundles) lined by stretchy urothelium that folds into rugae when empty.
info.function: Stores urine at low pressure and empties it during micturition, when the detrusor contracts and the urethral sphincters relax.
info.size: Capacity 400–600 mL (urge at ~150–250 mL); shown moderately full, about 8 cm across.
info.notes: As it fills it rises above the pubis into the extraperitoneal space, so a full bladder can be drained by a suprapubic catheter without entering the peritoneum.

info.description: Slit-like space, triangular when seen from the front, with the tubal openings at its upper corners and the internal os below, continuing through the spindle-shaped cervical canal to the external os.
info.function: Pathway for sperm upward and menstrual blood and the baby downward; the site of implantation.
info.size: About 6–7 cm from external os to fundus (cavity ~4 cm, cervical canal ~2.5–3 cm).
info.notes: An intrauterine device (IUD) sits in this cavity with its arms in the upper corners.

info.description: Thick-walled, pear-shaped muscular organ between the bladder and the rectum, normally tipped forward over the bladder (anteverted and anteflexed). Its dome-shaped fundus lies above the openings of the uterine tubes, above the body and isthmus.
info.function: Receives the embryo, nourishes the growing fetus and expels it by powerful myometrial contractions in labour; sheds its lining each month as menstruation.
info.size: About 7.5 × 5 × 2.5 cm and 50–70 g in a woman who has not given birth; the wall (myometrium) is 1.5–2 cm thick.
info.notes: In pregnancy it grows to about 1 kg and reaches the ribs; fibroids (leiomyomas) are common benign tumours of its muscle.

info.description: Small conical fleshy projection hanging from the middle of the free edge of the soft palate.
info.function: Helps the soft palate close the nasopharynx during swallowing and secretes thin saliva.
info.size: About 1-1.5 cm long and 0.8 cm wide.
info.notes: With a vagus nerve lesion the uvula deviates away from the injured side when the patient says "ah".

info.description: Fibromuscular canal running up and back from the vestibule to the cervix, normally collapsed front-to-back into an H-shaped slit and lined by folded (rugose) stratified squamous epithelium. The cervix projects into its upper end, surrounded by the fornices.
info.function: Receives the penis and semen, lets menstrual flow out and forms the lower birth canal.
info.size: About 7–9 cm long (posterior wall longer), highly distensible.
info.notes: Lactobacilli keep its pH around 4; the posterior fornix lies right against the rectouterine pouch.

info.description: A fan of eight to ten rootlets leaving the postolivary sulcus of the medulla below the glossopharyngeal rootlets and uniting into one trunk. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Parasympathetic supply to the heart, lungs and gut; motor to the palate, pharynx and larynx; sensation from the viscera.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 2.4 mm thick
info.notes: Its motor nucleus (nucleus ambiguus) lies in the lateral medulla, so a lateral medullary (Wallenberg) stroke causes hoarseness and swallowing difficulty.

info.description: Narrow, worm-like blind tube opening from the posteromedial wall of the cecum about 2 cm below the ileocecal valve, where the three taeniae coli converge; shown in the common pelvic-hanging position (retrocecal is most common).
info.function: Its wall is packed with lymphoid tissue, and it may serve as a safe-house that re-seeds the colon with helpful bacteria after diarrhoeal illness.
info.size: Usually 6-10 cm long (average about 8 cm), about 6 mm wide.
info.notes: Appendicitis is the commonest abdominal surgical emergency; pain classically moves from the umbilicus to McBurney's point, one-third of the way from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus.

info.description: Enters the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle just behind the facial nerve, beside the flocculus of the cerebellum. Shown as a short stub on both sides; the nerve continues in the peripheral nervous system.
info.function: Carries hearing and balance from the inner ear.
info.size: Stub about 1 cm; root 3.4 mm thick
info.notes: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) grows from its vestibular part: one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus are the first signs.

info.description: Small pointed tail of the sternum, cartilaginous in youth and gradually ossifying in adults.
info.function: Gives attachment to the diaphragm, the linea alba and the rectus abdominis.
info.size: ≈ 30 mm long
info.notes: Hand position for chest compressions is kept above it because a broken xiphoid can injure the liver.
